title: Admin DB export (entire control plane + all tenants) reachable by support-role admins — full-platform data exfiltration
description: Controller is `@Controller('admin/exports') @UseGuards(AdminAuthGuard)` (lines 29-30) with NO AdminRolesGuard and NO @AdminRoles on `create` (line 49) or `download` (line 61). `CreateAdminExportDto.scope` accepts `['tenant','control','all']` (export.dto.ts:5,18). `ExportService.createForAdmin` passes scope straight through (export.service.ts:54-83). The worker `resolveTargets` maps scope 'control' → `{label:'control', dbUrl: superuserUrl}` and scope 'all' → control DB + every non-archived tenant DB (export-processors.ts:176-188), then `readTables`/`dumpSql` dump every public table including `admin_users` (mfaSecretCipher/mfaNonce/passwordHash) and all billing/tenant tables (export-processors.ts:191-220). `AdminUser.role @default(support)` (schema.prisma:727). `download` calls `svc.get(id)` then `streamExport` with no ownership/role check — and `streamExport`'s own doc says 'Ownership is checked by the caller' (export-download.ts:6-7), which the admin caller never does. Contrast the tenant controller which DOES scope downloads (tenant-export.controller.ts:62-65).
impact: A low-privilege (default 'support') admin can exfiltrate the entire platform: every tenant's member PII + catalog, plus the control DB (other admins' encrypted MFA secrets, password hashes, all billing). Complete confidentiality breach of all tenants from one low-trust account. The controller docblock even calls this 'Owner-admin database export', confirming an owner gate was intended but is absent.
fix: Add `@UseGuards(AdminAuthGuard, AdminRolesGuard)` to the controller and `@AdminRoles('owner')` on `create` and `download` (matching the pattern already used by admin-tenants/admin-plans/admin-overrides/admin-subscriptions/system-mode). Add an integration test asserting a support session gets 403 on POST /admin/exports and on GET /admin/exports/:id/download.

The export controller has no such decorator, so the roles guard would no-op even if it were attached — and it isn't attached.

title: Admin billing mutations (set-plan / set-paid-until) not owner-gated — support admins can grant paid entitlements to any tenant
description: `@Controller('admin/billing/tenants/:tenantId') @UseGuards(AdminAuthGuard)` (lines 17-18); neither `setPlan` (line 44) nor `setPaidUntil` (line 50) carries `@AdminRoles('owner')` and no AdminRolesGuard on the class. `applyAdminPlanChange` sets `planId`, `billingMode`, forces `status:'active'`, `graceUntil:null`, then `effectivePlan.invalidate(tenantId)` so entitlement takes effect immediately (billing.service.ts:356-375). `applyManualPayment` sets `status:'active'`, arbitrary future `paidUntil`, `graceUntil:null` + cache invalidate (billing.service.ts:378-399). Schema default role is 'support' (schema.prisma:727).
impact: A support-role admin can move any tenant to any plan and mark them paid indefinitely (direct revenue loss / free upgrades), force-reactivate suspended/past-due subscriptions, and silently alter competitors' billing state. Money/billing-integrity breach + privilege escalation. (applyManualPayment does correctly reject stripe-billed tenants at billing.service.ts:384-388, but set-plan has no such restriction and both remain support-reachable.)
fix: Add `AdminRolesGuard` to the controller and `@AdminRoles('owner')` to `set-plan` and `set-paid-until`; the read GET may stay broadly admin-readable. Cover with an integration test using a support-role session expecting 403.

title: pg_dump failure leaks Postgres superuser credentials into tenant-visible export error
description: dumpSql() passes the full connection string as an argv element: `await execFileP('pg_dump', ['--no-owner','--no-privileges','--format=plain','--file',outPath, dbUrl], { maxBuffer: 16*1024*1024 })` (export-processors.ts:192-196). dbUrl for a tenant comes from tenants.dbUrl, which tenant-provisioning.service.ts builds via urlForDb(): `const u = new URL(this.env.pgSuperuserUrl); u.pathname = '/'+dbName; return u.toString()` (lines 105-108) and stores on the tenant (line 61 `const dbUrl = this.urlForDb(dbName)`, returned line 75). pgSuperuserUrl defaults to `postgresql://libriant:libriant@localhost:5432/libriant_control` (env.ts:205-207), so the tenant dbUrl embeds the live superuser user+password. I empirically confirmed Node's promisified execFile, on a NON-ENOENT non-zero exit (the common pg_dump failure: connection refused, auth failure, `server version mismatch`), rejects with `err.message = 'Command failed: <binary> <argv...>\n<stderr>'` — the full URL incl. password is verbatim on line 1. oneLine = `s.split('\n').slice(0,4).join(' ').slice(0,500)` (line 13) keeps the first line, so the credential survives (it is far inside 500 chars). processExportJob's catch stores `error: oneLine((err as Error).message)` (line 46). publicExportJob exposes `error: job.error` (export.service.ts:19) and TenantExportController.list maps listForTenant through publicExportJob (tenant-export.controller.ts:40), reachable by any owner/admin on GET /t/:slug/exports. CreateTenantExportDto permits format:'sql' (export.dto.ts:4,9) and createForTenant passes it straight through with scope:'tenant' (export.service.ts:34-52). Grep for redact/sanitize/scrub/password in export/* returns nothing — no mitigation. (Note: pg's own PgClient.connect error does NOT leak the URL — I verified it returns only `connect ECONNREFUSED host:port` — so this leak is specific to the pg_dump argv path, but that path is fully reachable by a tenant via the sql format.)
impact: A logged-in tenant owner/admin can recover the shared Postgres SUPERUSER password by requesting a SQL export of their own DB and reading the returned job.error when pg_dump fails (transient DB outage, auth error, or the very common pg_dump/server version skew — all non-ENOENT non-zero exits). That credential grants access to the control DB and every tenant DB: full cross-tenant breach and total platform compromise.
fix: Never pass the connection string as argv. Set PGHOST/PGPORT/PGUSER/PGPASSWORD/PGDATABASE (or PGPASSFILE) in execFile's env and drop dbUrl from argv. Additionally scrub URL userinfo inside oneLine() (e.g. `.replace(/(postgres(?:ql)?:\/\/[^:@\/]+:)[^@]*@/gi,'$1***@')`) and stop returning raw job.error to tenant-scoped callers — return a generic message and log detail server-side.
skepticReasoning:
CONFIRMED. Every link in the exploit chain holds against the real code, and I empirically reproduced the load-bearing behavior.

1. Credential embedding (provisioning/tenant-provisioning.service.ts:105-108): urlForDb() does `const u = new URL(this.env.pgSuperuserUrl); u.pathname = '/'+dbName; return u.toString()` — it only swaps the DB path, so user+password are preserved. provision() stores this on tenants.dbUrl (lines 61,75). pgSuperuserUrl defaults to `postgresql://libriant:libriant@localhost:5432/libriant_control` (config/env.ts:205-208). So tenants.dbUrl embeds the live shared-superuser credentials.

2. Argv leak (export-processors.ts:192-196): dumpSql() passes dbUrl as a positional argv element to pg_dump. I empirically confirmed with Node's promisified execFile that on a non-ENOENT non-zero exit, err.message line 1 is `Command failed: <binary> <full argv...>\n<stderr>` — the credentialed URL appears verbatim. My test output: stored job.error = `...--file /tmp/out.sql postgresql://libriant:SUPERSECRETpw@localhost:5432/tenant_abc ...`, contains password = true. oneLine() (line 13) keeps the first 4 lines joined and slices to 500 chars; with a realistic pg_dump command line the password sits at index ~141, well inside 500 — confirmed not truncated.

3. Storage (export-processors.ts:46): the catch stores `error: oneLine((err as Error).message)` — raw, unredacted.

4. Exposure (export.service.ts:19 + tenant-export.controller.ts:38-41): publicExportJob returns `error: job.error`; TenantExportController.list maps listForTenant through publicExportJob on GET /t/:slug/exports, guarded only by TenantGuard + RolesGuard @Roles('owner','admin') (lines 33-34). Any owner/admin of the tenant reaches it.

5. sql-format reachability (export.dto.ts:4,9 + export.service.ts:34-52): CreateTenantExportDto allows format:'sql'; createForTenant forwards it with scope:'tenant'. A tenant-scoped sql export resolves the target's dbUrl (resolveTargets lines 167-174) and calls dumpSql with it.

6. No mitigation: grep for redact/sanitize/scrub/password-replacement across export/, config/, provisioning/, common/ returned nothing relevant (only an unrelated Redis password reference). No URL scrubbing exists anywhere in the path.

Refutation attempts that FAILED to refute: (a) The only non-leaking failure mode is ENOENT (binary missing), which yields `spawn pg_dump ENOENT` with no argv — but the line-190 comment "Requires postgresql-client in the image" plus the fact that SQL export is a supported format means pg_dump IS present in prod, so realistic failures (connection refused, auth failure, server version skew) are all non-ENOENT non-zero exits that DO leak. (b) The readTables/PgClient path does NOT leak the URL on connect errors (returns only `connect ECONNREFUSED host:port`) — but that is the json/csv/xlsx path; the sql path is a fully independent, tenant-reachable code path that does leak. (c) Authorization is correctly scoped (a tenant only sees its own exports) — but that does not help, because the leaked secret is the SHARED superuser credential common to the control DB and every tenant DB, so a single tenant's own export job is sufficient to recover it.

Impact: a logged-in tenant owner/admin requests an sql export of their own library; when pg_dump fails for any common transient reason (DB blip, auth error, pg_dump/server version skew), the returned job.error contains the shared Postgres superuser user+password. That credential grants access to the control plane DB and every tenant DB — full cross-tenant breach and total platform compromise. Critical is the correct severity.
exploit:
Exploit (authenticated tenant owner/admin on slug `acme`):

1. POST /t/acme/exports  with body {"format":"sql"}  → 202, returns { export: { id, status:"queued" } }.
2. The export worker runs dumpSql(tenants.dbUrl, outPath) = execFile('pg_dump', [..., '<dbUrl-with-superuser-creds>']). When pg_dump exits non-zero for ANY non-ENOENT reason (transient connection refused, auth failure, or the very common pg_dump/server-version mismatch), processExportJob's catch stores error = oneLine(err.message).
3. GET /t/acme/exports  → { exports: [ { id, status:"failed", error:"Command failed: pg_dump --no-owner --no-privileges --format=plain --file /srv/.../<id>.sql postgresql://libriant:<SUPERUSER_PASSWORD>@host:5432/tenant_xxx pg_dump: error: ..." } ] }
4. Attacker reads the URL userinfo → recovers the shared Postgres superuser password → connects directly to the control DB and every tenant DB.

Empirical proof of the leak (run locally with promisified execFile, since the real pg_dump binary is the one shipped in the prod image per the line-190 comment):

  execFileP('sh', ['-c','echo "pg_dump: error: connection to server failed" 1>&2; exit 1', '--no-owner','--no-privileges','--format=plain','--file','/tmp/out.sql','postgresql://libriant:SUPERSECRETpw@localhost:5432/tenant_abc'])

  catch err → oneLine(err.message) =
  "Command failed: sh -c echo \"pg_dump: error: connection to server failed\"; exit 1 --no-owner --no-privileges --format=plain --file /tmp/out.sql postgresql://libriant:SUPERSECRETpw@localhost:5432/tenant_abc pg_dump: error: connection to server failed"
  stored.includes('SUPERSECRETpw') === true.

Fix: pass connection params via env (PGHOST/PGPORT/PGUSER/PGPASSWORD/PGDATABASE or PGPASSFILE) in execFile's env and drop dbUrl from argv; additionally scrub URL userinfo inside oneLine() (e.g. .replace(/(postgres(?:ql)?:\/\/[^:@\/]+:)[^@]*@/gi,'$1***@')) and return a generic error to tenant-scoped callers while logging detail server-side.

title: ReDoS guard (patternLooksCatastrophic) is bypassable — single record write freezes the event loop for the whole process (all tenants)
description: patternLooksCatastrophic (field-types.ts:48-59) only matches three narrow shapes: `/\([^)]*[*+][^)]*\)\s*[*+]/`, `/\([^)]*[*+][^)]*\)\s*\{\d*,?\d*\}/`, and `/[*+]\s*[*+]/`. I ran the exact guard against a corpus in Node: `(([a-z])*)*$` => blocked:false, `(a|a)*$` => blocked:false, `([a-z]|[a-z])+$` => blocked:false, `(\w|\w)*$` => blocked:false, `(a{1,9}){1,9}$` => blocked:false; only `(a+)+$` and `(.*)*$` are blocked. I then ran the allowed pattern on the production match path: `new RegExp('(([a-z])*)*$').test('a'.repeat(28)+'1')` took 75708.7 ms — a 75.7-second synchronous freeze of the single Node event loop. Nested grouping, overlapping alternation, and nested bounded quantifiers are entirely unconsidered by the heuristic. REGEX_INPUT_CAP=4000 (line 35) does not help because explosion occurs at ~29 chars, far below the cap. field-types.ts:148-150 compiles and runs the stored pattern synchronously with no worker thread, RE2, or timeout. The doc-comment at line 46 ('it never lets a known-dangerous one run on the request path') is false.
impact: Any actor who can plant a validation pattern plus any record write whose value mismatches near the end of the string hangs the entire Node process for over a minute. Node is single-threaded; this blocks every request for every tenant co-located on the instance, repeatable at will. An attacker can even trigger it with a write to their own tenant.
fix: Do not rely on a regex blocklist for ReDoS. Run user-authored regex in a worker thread with a hard wall-clock timeout, OR use a non-backtracking engine (RE2 / node-re2). At minimum, extend patternLooksCatastrophic to reject overlapping/duplicate alternation, nested bounded quantifiers ({n,m} on a group containing a quantifier or another {n,m}), and any quantified group that is itself quantified by any quantifier including {n,m}; add a spec asserting OWASP evil-regex corpus is rejected. Treat the current guard as near-zero protection.

title: rotate MFA_MASTER_KEY: 'never' guard is cosmetic — it warns then rotates anyway, orphaning all admin TOTP
description: actionRotate's `never` branch only prints and does NOT return: lines 932-934 `if (def.rotation === 'never') { console.log(col(\`⛔ ${key} is marked DO-NOT-ROTATE.\`, C.red)); if (def.rotationNote) console.log(...); }` — no `return`. Control falls through to the confirm at 939 `if (!assumeYes && !(await confirm(\`Rotate ${key} now?\`)))` and then the actual rotation at 943-945 `const value = generateFor(def)!; setValue(model, key, value); saveModel(model);`. MFA_MASTER_KEY has gen `HEX32` (kind 'hex', secrets.ts:162), so it passes the gate `def.gen.kind === 'none' || 'ssh-ed25519'` at 923 and is offered in the interactive rotate menu (chooseKey filter `d.store === 'env' && d.gen.kind !== 'none'`, lines 1058-1061). With `--yes`, `!assumeYes` is false so even the confirm is skipped. rotationNote (160-161) states rotating it 'ORPHANS every admin TOTP enrollment.'
impact: `pnpm secrets rotate MFA_MASTER_KEY --yes` silently replaces the AES-256-GCM key decrypting every admin's stored TOTP secret (MFA_MASTER_KEY is injected required at docker-compose.prod.yml:48 `${MFA_MASTER_KEY:?...}`). All platform admins lose MFA — an irreversible auth-availability/data-loss event on the most safety-critical secret.
fix: Make the `never` branch return before the confirm/rotate. Gate any forced rotation behind an explicit flag (e.g. --force-orphan-mfa) plus a typed confirmation phrase, and never let --yes bypass a `never` rotation.

title: rotate POSTGRES_PASSWORD regenerates the DB password in-file with no ALTER ROLE and no pg_data_initialized guard — locks app out of its DB
description: POSTGRES_PASSWORD is `rotation: 'caution'` with `gen: { kind: 'hex', bytes: 24 }` (secrets.ts:181-184), so it passes the gate at 923 and reaches the `caution` branch (935-937) which only prints the note, then rotates at 943-945, writing a brand-new password to the env file with no Postgres-side change. The rotationNote (182-183) itself says 'Change it ONLY together with `ALTER ROLE libriant PASSWORD ...` ... never edit it here alone.' ensure-env.sh has a CRITICAL guard (ensure-env.sh:80 `if [ -z "$(getv POSTGRES_PASSWORD)" ] && pg_data_initialized; then ... exit 3`) refusing to mint a fresh password over an initialized volume; actionRotate has NO equivalent. Verified the value is interpolated verbatim into the DB URLs: docker-compose.prod.yml:36 `CONTROL_DATABASE_URL: postgresql://libriant:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@pgbouncer:5432/...` and :71 `PG_SUPERUSER_URL: postgresql://libriant:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@postgres:5432/...`. (Cited path is repo-root docker-compose.prod.yml; actual path is infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml — substance unchanged.)
impact: `pnpm secrets rotate POSTGRES_PASSWORD --yes` desyncs the env-file password from the password baked into the running cluster. On next deploy/restart the app cannot authenticate to Postgres — total outage until the old password is restored from backup. Exactly the lockout class ensure-env.sh's guard was added to prevent.
fix: Treat POSTGRES_PASSWORD as effectively `never` in actionRotate (block auto-rotation), or require an explicit two-step flow that performs/prompts for the `ALTER ROLE` and refuses when a data volume exists, mirroring ensure-env.sh's pg_data_initialized() guard.

title: RolesGuard checks role membership but not user status or tenant membership — a disabled admin retains access to admin-only tenant routes
description: RolesGuard re-reads the live role precisely to avoid the stale JWT: `controlDb.user.findUnique({ where: { id: req.session.sub }, select: { role: true } })` (roles.guard.ts:44-47), then `if (!user || !roles.includes(user.role))` (line 48). The select pulls ONLY `role`; it never reads `status` and never re-confirms `user.tenantId === req.tenant.id`. Deactivation (staff.service.ts:124) sets `status: 'disabled'` while leaving `role` intact, so a disabled admin still has `role: 'admin'`, which is in the `@Roles('owner','admin')` set every admin-tenant controller requires (tenant-settings, branding, audit, staff, export, import, billing, field-definitions, library-support). NOTE: the finding's 'disabled OWNER' framing is partly inaccurate — requireManaged (staff.service.ts:156) throws ForbiddenException for `role === 'owner'`, so an owner cannot be deactivated via the staff API. A disabled ADMIN is the real, fully-reachable case. The underlying defect (status/tenantId not checked) is confirmed regardless.
impact: A disabled library admin keeps access to admin-only tenant surfaces (staff management, audit log, branding, tenant-settings, billing, data export/import, support keys, field definitions) for the JWT lifetime. Because the same controllers also lack AuthGuard (TEN-01), nothing in the request path catches the disabled state. Severity kept at high (admin scope, not owner; owner-via-staff-API is blocked).

title: Password reset/change does not invalidate existing sessions — attacker keeps access after takeover recovery

A repo-wide grep for passwordChangedAt|tokenVersion|sessionEpoch|sessionsValidAfter|invalidateSessions returns ONLY the comment at auth.guard.ts:23. PasswordResetService.complete() updates `data: { passwordHash, failedLogins: 0, lockedUntil: null }` (password-reset.service.ts:132) with no revocation. AuthGuard only revalidates user.status / tenant.status (auth.guard.ts:50-58) and, worse, caches a positive result for 60s (`authcheck:${session.sub}`, REVALIDATE_TTL_SEC=60, lines 28,39-41,62) — so even a status-based change is deferred up to 60s. Bump it on password reset, completeSetup, staff resetPassword, and admin-forced deactivate. Also key/clear the 60s authcheck cache on bump (or skip the positive cache for sensitive transitions) so revocation isn't delayed.

title: Targeted account-lockout DoS + account enumeration via login lockout
description: Lockout is keyed solely on the victim row: recordFailure writes `failedLogins: nextCount` and `lockedUntil` when nextCount>=maxFailedLogins (login.service.ts:161-167), with no IP/device dimension. The locked branch throws a DISTINCT message `Too many failed attempts. Please try again in ${minutes} minute(s).` (login.service.ts:100-102), only ever reachable for a real, locked account, whereas all other failures (unknown tenant/user/inactive/wrong-pw) throw the generic `We couldn't sign you in with those details.` (login.service.ts:180). The per-IP login limit is 20/5min (auth.controller.ts:45), far above maxFailedLogins=5 (env.ts:201), so 5 wrong guesses (the lockout trigger) are well under it.
impact: Anyone knowing tenant slug + a user email/username can submit 5 wrong passwords to lock that account for loginLockoutMs (default 15 min, env.ts:202), repeatable indefinitely → sustained targeted DoS. The differential lockout message is a reliable account-existence oracle that defeats the otherwise-careful uniform-timing/uniform-message design (dummyVerify on every miss).
fix: Return the generic invalid-credentials message even when locked (still apply lockout server-side) so lockout state isn't observable, OR only reveal lockout after an otherwise-correct password. Couple lockout to an (account, IP) dimension or exponential per-IP backoff so a single attacker can't lock an account for everyone.

CONFIRMED against the real code. Both halves of the finding hold with concrete exploit paths, and no mitigating guard (CAPTCHA/Turnstile, progressive challenge, or per-IP coupling of the lockout) exists anywhere in apps/api/src or apps/web/src.

1) Targeted account-lockout DoS — REAL and repeatable.
- recordFailure (apps/api/src/auth/login.service.ts:160-169) increments `failedLogins` and sets `lockedUntil` keyed SOLELY on `userId` (`controlDb.user.update({ where: { id: userId } ...})`). There is no IP/device dimension, so the locked state is account-global.
- Trigger threshold is maxFailedLogins=5 (env.ts:201) and lockout duration loginLockoutMs=15min (env.ts:202).
- Exploit path per attempt with a valid identifier: user found (login.service.ts:89-92) → active (93-95) → not-yet-locked (97) → verify fails (105) → recordFailure (107). After the 5th failure `lockedUntil = now+15min`; the next legitimate login by the real user hits the locked branch (97-103) and is denied. Attacker repeats indefinitely.
- The per-IP login limit (auth.controller.ts:45, RL.loginPerIp = 20/5min) does NOT protect the targeted account: lockout is account-global, so locking happens regardless of source IP. 20/5min still permits ~4 full lockout cycles per IP per window, and an attacker with multiple IPs is effectively unbounded. Anyone knowing tenant slug + a user email/username can keep that account locked out continuously.

2) Account-existence oracle via differential lockout message — REAL.
- The lockout branch throws a DISTINCT message `Too many failed attempts. Please try again in N minute(s).` (login.service.ts:100-102), reachable ONLY when `user.lockedUntil > now`, which requires a real, existing, active account that has been locked.
- Every other failure path returns the uniform generic `We couldn't sign you in with those details.`: unknown tenant (63), inactive tenant (68), unknown/no-hash user (91), inactive user (95), wrong password (108→180). recordFailure is never reached for a non-existent identifier (the lookup short-circuits at 89-92), so a non-existent identifier NEVER produces the lockout message.
- Therefore: drive 5 failures at an identifier; if the next response is the distinct lockout message, the account provably exists; otherwise it does not. This defeats the deliberate uniform-timing/uniform-message design built around dummyVerify (password.service.ts:39-42, called on every miss).

Refutation attempts that failed: (a) No CAPTCHA/Turnstile/recaptcha/hcaptcha anywhere (grep returned nothing in api/web src). (b) No progressive/exponential backoff on the auth path (the only backoff hits are Redis client retry and BullMQ email retry, unrelated). (c) clientIp (platform/client-ip.ts) is trustworthy under the documented Cloudflare→Caddy topology, but that only strengthens per-IP limiting — it has no bearing on the account-global lockout, which is the DoS vector. (d) The same account-keyed, no-IP-dimension pattern is mirrored in admin-auth.service.ts:63-68, confirming this is the intended (flawed) design, not a one-off.

Honest calibration: the enumeration oracle is noisier than a single-request oracle (attacker must burn 5 attempts to arm the lock), but it is 100% reliable. The targeted DoS is the dominant, unambiguous impact. Severity high is correct — exploitable availability attack on any known account plus a reliable existence oracle, no privileged access required, but it is availability/info-disclosure rather than direct account-takeover or money/data loss (which would be critical).
exploit:
Preconditions: attacker knows a tenant slug (public, in URLs) and a target user's email or staff username (e.g. owner email, or predictable `staff_3`).

Targeted DoS (repeatable):
1. POST /auth/login {"slug":"victim-lib","identifier":"owner@victim.com","password":"wrong1"} → 401 generic. Repeat with wrong2..wrong5.
2. On the 5th wrong password, recordFailure (login.service.ts:161-167) sets lockedUntil = now+15min for that user row (account-global, no IP key).
3. The real owner now logs in with the CORRECT password → hits the locked branch (login.service.ts:97-103) → 401 "Too many failed attempts. Please try again in 15 minute(s)." Legitimate user is denied.

- For a NON-EXISTENT identifier: all attempts return generic "We couldn't sign you in with those details." (login.service.ts:180), and recordFailure is never called (89-92 short-circuit) → no lock, message never changes.
- For a REAL identifier: after 5 wrong passwords, the next attempt returns the DISTINCT "Too many failed attempts..." message (100-102). Observing this distinct message proves the (slug, identifier) account exists, defeating the dummyVerify uniform-timing/uniform-message defense.

Suggested fix (matches proposal): (a) return the generic invalid-credentials message even when locked (apply lockout silently) so lockout state is unobservable, or only reveal lockout after an otherwise-correct password; and (b) couple lockout to an (account, IP) dimension or add exponential per-IP backoff / CAPTCHA so a single actor cannot lock an account for the legitimate user. Apply the same fix to admin-auth.service.ts:63-68.

5. The sweep cannot rescue what was never written. `sweepFailedStripeWebhooks` only `findMany`s existing rows where `processedAt: null` (stripe-retry.job.ts:41-49); it never inserts and never calls Stripe's events.list API. A grep confirms NO reconciliation/backfill/events.list job exists anywhere — registry.ts:22-71 lists only the one sweep. So an event that produced no row is permanently invisible to recovery.

I tried hard to refute this and found no mitigation: no `.exclude()`, no global-prefix carve-out, no raw-body/controller-level pre-middleware, no Stripe-side reconciliation poll, no impersonation path for an unauthenticated third-party POST. The premise and exploit path are real.

Severity high, not critical, because permanent loss is conditional: it requires an operator-set GLOBAL read_only/maintenance/out_of_order window (per-tenant windows don't gate the webhook since tenantId is undefined) AND the window must outlast Stripe's ~3-day delivery-retry envelope for a given event. A short maintenance window lets Stripe redeliver afterward with no loss. Multi-day global outage/maintenance windows are plausible (the modes exist precisely for that), and the consequence — silent billing desync from a dropped customer.subscription.deleted / invoice.payment_failed with no durable trace — is a serious money/correctness defect. Hence high.

Repro (operator-triggered, no attacker needed):
1. Operator opens a GLOBAL maintenance (or out_of_order, or read_only) window via /admin/system-mode/* — e.g. a multi-day planned migration. SystemModeService writes the active global event; resolveGlobal() now returns mode='maintenance'.
2. During the window, Stripe delivers `POST /webhooks/stripe` for, say, `customer.subscription.deleted` (a customer cancelled) or `invoice.payment_failed`.
3. SessionMiddleware/AdminMiddleware/ImpersonationMiddleware are no-ops (no cookies on a Stripe request). SystemModeMiddleware.use runs: fullPath='/webhooks/stripe' matches no ALWAYS_PASS/ADMIN_BYPASS entry; tenantIdFromPath returns undefined (path doesn't start with '/t/'); resolveEffective returns the global maintenance mode. Line 132 (or 125 for read_only POST) sends `res.status(503).json(...)` and returns WITHOUT next().
4. StripeWebhookController.handle never runs ⇒ the upsert at lines 73-85 never writes a stripe_webhook_events row.
5. Stripe sees 503, retries with backoff for ~3 days. If the maintenance window outlasts that envelope (or a backlog pushes retries out), Stripe gives up. No DB row was ever created.
6. The 5-min stripe-webhook-retry sweep (registry.ts:34-37 → stripe-retry.job.ts:41-49) only `findMany`s existing rows; it finds nothing to retry and never queries Stripe. The cancellation/payment-failure is silently lost — the tenant keeps paid features (or stays incorrectly gated) with zero durable trace.

Fix (matches proposal): add `/^\/webhooks\/stripe(\/|$)/` to ALWAYS_PASS in system-mode.middleware.ts so the signature-verified, idempotent, control-plane-only handler always runs and at minimum writes the durable row (then the existing sweep can rescue dispatch failures). Apply the same carve-out to any other inbound third-party webhook routes. Verify with stripe-webhook.controller.spec.ts that the upsert still fires, and add a middleware test asserting POST /webhooks/stripe returns the controller's 200, not 503, under a global maintenance event.

title: Storage-delete + recompute endpoints have no role guard — any staff (incl. volunteer) can wipe files and bypass branding's owner/admin gate
description: DELETE handler (lines 103-113) and recompute handler (lines 143-148) are decorated ONLY with `@UseGuards(TenantGuard)` — no `@Roles`/`RolesGuard`. TenantGuard (tenant.guard.ts:46-54) only verifies `req.session.tid === req.tenant.id` (tenant membership), NOT role. UserRole enum confirms `volunteer` is the lowest role (schema.prisma:41-46). `'branding'` IS in RESOURCE_TYPES (storage-demo.controller.ts:33) and parseResourceType accepts it (line 174), so `DELETE /t/:slug/storage/branding/<file>` reaches `this.storage.delete(tenant, 'branding/<file>')`. BrandingController is correctly gated `@UseGuards(TenantGuard, RolesGuard) @Roles('owner','admin')` (branding.controller.ts:33-35) — so the generic delete path bypasses that gate. controlDb.tenant.brandLogoRef is NOT nulled on generic delete, leaving a dangling ref → broken header logo. StorageModule is registered in app.module.ts:54 (live in prod despite the 'demo' name). No `@nestjs/throttler` anywhere (grep found zero), and recompute calls `recomputeUsage` → `walkSize()` (local-driver.ts:149-168), an unbounded recursive fs.readdir+fs.stat over the whole tenant tree — repeatable with no rate limit.
impact: Intra-tenant privilege escalation + destructive data loss: a volunteer can delete branding logos (bypassing owner/admin), book covers, and member photos by ref, leaving dangling DB refs and broken assets; and can repeatedly trigger a full-filesystem-walk recompute as a CPU/IO DoS.
fix: Add `RolesGuard` + `@Roles('owner','admin')` (or 'librarian' for covers/members) to the DELETE and recompute handlers; reject `resourceType === 'branding'` on the generic delete path (force branding deletes through BrandingController, which also nulls brandLogoRef). After any delete, null the owning entity ref so DB and storage stay consistent. Rate-limit recompute and make it admin-only.
skepticReasoning:
CONFIRMED. I re-derived every link of the chain against the real code and tried hard to refute it; no mitigation exists.

1) Missing role gate. The DELETE handler (storage-demo.controller.ts:103-113) and recompute handler (lines 143-148) are decorated ONLY with `@UseGuards(TenantGuard)`. No `@Roles`/`RolesGuard`. There is no global APP_GUARD — app.module.ts:73-78 registers only an APP_INTERCEPTOR (SupportAuditInterceptor) — and no middleware enforces roles. So nothing else compensates.

2) TenantGuard is role-blind. tenant.guard.ts:46-54 only checks `req.session` exists and `req.session.tid === req.tenant.id` (tenant membership). It never looks at the user's role. session.middleware.ts:22-26 attaches `req.session` for ANY valid session cookie regardless of role. So a signed-in volunteer of the tenant passes TenantGuard cleanly.

3) Lowest role confirmed. schema.prisma:41-46 — `volunteer` is the lowest UserRole.

4) Branding bypass is real. `'branding'` is in RESOURCE_TYPES (storage-demo.controller.ts:33) and parseResourceType accepts it (line 173-178). A branding logo ref is `branding/<cuidLike()+ext>` (local-driver.ts:56-57) — a single filename segment — so `DELETE /t/:slug/storage/branding/<file>` binds resourceType=branding, filename=<file> and reaches `this.storage.delete(tenant, 'branding/<file>')` (line 111). StorageService.delete (storage.service.ts:135-159) → LocalDriver.delete (local-driver.ts:75-79) → `fs.rm(p,{force:true})`. The file is actually destroyed. Meanwhile BrandingController is correctly gated `@UseGuards(TenantGuard, RolesGuard) @Roles('owner','admin')` (branding.controller.ts:33-35) and its removeLogo nulls brandLogoRef (line 91). The generic delete path nulls NOTHING, so controlDb.tenant.brandLogoRef is left dangling → header logo 404s. This is a genuine bypass of the owner/admin branding gate plus a consistency bug.

5) Same gap lets a volunteer delete ANY file within their own tenant (covers, member photos, attachments, marc) by ref, leaving dangling entity refs (coverAssetRef etc.) — destructive data loss with no role check.

6) DoS sub-claim holds. recompute (line 143-148) → recomputeUsage (storage.service.ts:162-170) → driver.totalBytes() → walkSize() (local-driver.ts:149-168), an unbounded recursive readdir+stat over the whole tenant tree, with no rate limit on this endpoint.

Failed refutations: (a) No global guard. (b) No role-enforcing middleware. (c) SystemModeMiddleware would 503 these mutations only in read_only/maintenance mode; in normal operation they pass. (d) Cross-tenant is correctly prevented — safeResolve (local-driver.ts:99-108) blocks `..`/escape and TenantGuard blocks foreign tids — so this is INTRA-tenant privilege escalation, not a cross-tenant breach, which is why high (not critical) is the honest severity.

Minor corrections to the finding's wording (do not change the verdict): the finding says "no @nestjs/throttler anywhere" implying zero rate limiting; in fact a homegrown RateLimitService exists at apps/api/src/platform/rate-limit.service.ts but is wired only into auth/admin-auth/password-reset/support controllers, NOT storage — so the recompute endpoint is indeed unthrottled. Also the recompute route is `t/:slug/storage-admin/recompute` (line 143), not `t/:slug/storage/recompute` as the class docstring (line 47) claims; the cited handler line numbers and the substance are correct.
exploit:
Setup: a tenant "acme" with a volunteer user signed in (lowest role). Tenant storage is local (file://). The owner has uploaded a header logo, so controlDb.tenant.brandLogoRef = "branding/c<...>.png" and the file exists on disk.

A) Bypass the owner/admin branding gate + break the header logo (intra-tenant privesc + data loss):
  1. As the volunteer, read the logo ref from /auth/me (brandLogoRef rides into the shell) or just enumerate via the listing.
  2. curl -X DELETE \
       --cookie "<volunteer session cookie>" \
       https://app/t/acme/storage/branding/c<...>.png
  3. TenantGuard passes (session.tid === tenant.id); no RolesGuard runs. storage.delete → LocalDriver.delete → fs.rm removes the logo file.
  4. controlDb.tenant.brandLogoRef is NOT nulled → every page renders a broken/404 header logo for the whole library. The owner/admin-only DELETE /t/acme/branding/logo path was bypassed entirely.

B) Delete other members' photos / book covers (data loss):
  curl -X DELETE --cookie "<volunteer cookie>" https://app/t/acme/storage/members/<photoFile>
  curl -X DELETE --cookie "<volunteer cookie>" https://app/t/acme/storage/covers/<coverFile>
  Files are destroyed; the owning entity rows still point at the now-missing ref.

C) CPU/IO DoS via unthrottled full-tree recompute:
  for i in $(seq 1 1000); do
    curl -s -X POST --cookie "<volunteer cookie>" https://app/t/acme/storage-admin/recompute &
  done
  Each call runs walkSize() — a recursive readdir+stat over the entire tenant storage tree — with no rate limit, saturating the event loop and disk.

Fix: add `RolesGuard` + appropriate `@Roles(...)` to the DELETE and recompute handlers; reject resourceType==='branding' on the generic delete (force branding deletes through BrandingController, which nulls brandLogoRef); after any delete, null the owning entity ref; rate-limit recompute via the existing RateLimitService and make it admin-only.

title: Worker parses entire untrusted file into memory with no row cap or zip-bomb guard (OOM)
description: import-worker.ts:100-101 `const data = await readStaged(batch.stagingPath); const table = await parseByFormat(batch.format as SourceFormat, data, {...})` is called with NO maxRows, so the full row set is materialized. For CSV this routes through parseDelimited→tokenize over the FULL text (csv-parser.ts:131-132 `const matrix = tokenize(text, delimiter)`) which builds the entire string[][] matrix before tabular.ts:69 applies any cap. For XLSX, xlsx-parser.ts:42 `await wb.xlsx.load(ab)` decompresses the whole zip with no uncompressed-size limit, then xlsx-parser.ts:54-61 builds the full string[][] matrix. Upload cap is only 64MB compressed (import.constants.ts:7). Worker concurrency is 1 (import-worker.ts:253 `{ connection, concurrency: 1, prefix: IMPORT_QUEUE_PREFIX }`), shared across all tenants.
impact: An authenticated owner/admin can upload a sub-64MB file (esp. XLSX with a giant sharedStrings table or a hugely-repeated cell) that inflates to gigabytes of JS strings, OOM-killing the single-concurrency import worker. Because concurrency is 1, this blocks every tenant's imports — a cross-tenant DoS via the shared worker process.
fix: Pass a hard maxRows ceiling and reject before materializing all rows; for XLSX inspect the zip central directory / cap uncompressed entry sizes before wb.xlsx.load; stream CSV rather than tokenizing the whole text; add a per-tenant row/byte budget independent of the 64MB compressed cap.
skepticReasoning:
CONFIRMED. I read the full chain and could not refute it; the finding's premise holds and no guard mitigates it.

Worker materializes the whole untrusted file with no row/byte cap:
- apps/api/src/import/import-worker.ts:100-106 calls `readStaged(batch.stagingPath)` then `parseByFormat(batch.format, data, { encoding, delimiter, sheetName, noHeader })` — note there is NO `maxRows` key. Compare import.service.ts:48-49 where the PREVIEW path DOES pass `maxRows: PREVIEW_ROWS` (=20). So the cap exists only at preview, not at the real import.
- CSV: parsers/csv-parser.ts:132 `const matrix = tokenize(text, delimiter)` builds the entire string[][] over the full decoded text before anything is capped.
- XLSX: parsers/xlsx-parser.ts:42 `await wb.xlsx.load(ab)` decompresses the whole zip with no uncompressed-size limit (exceljs 4.4.0, confirmed installed), then 54-61 builds the full string[][].
- The `maxRows` cap only runs in parsers/tabular.ts:69 AFTER the full matrix is already in memory, so even if maxRows were passed it would not stop the OOM during tokenize/wb.xlsx.load.

Only size guard is the 64MB COMPRESSED multer cap: import.constants.ts:7 + import.controller.ts:70 `FileInterceptor('file', { limits: { fileSize: IMPORT_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES } })`. There is NO import row-count or byte-budget plan feature — packages/shared/src/features.ts:99 `bulk_import_enabled` is a boolean gate only. requireRunnable (import.service.ts:317-326) checks only mapping + status; startValidate/startCommit enqueue with no size check. `totalRows` is only written AFTER parse (import-worker.ts:110), proving parse-then-count ordering with no pre-parse gate.

Refutation attempts that FAILED:
1. "Plan getLimit rejects first" — no. Parse (import-worker.ts:101) precedes executeImport (line 160); engine/runner.ts:50 reads `table.rows.length` on an already-materialized table. The OOM is during parse, before any per-row plan check.
2. "Preview already validated the file is small" — no. Preview uses maxRows:20 for ROWS but for XLSX still calls wb.xlsx.load on the whole zip (xlsx-parser.ts:42), and the staged file is the FULL upload (import.service.ts:86 stages input.file.buffer), re-parsed uncapped by the worker.
3. "Container memory limit / NODE_OPTIONS contains it" — no. infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml worker block (209-237) has NO mem_limit, NO deploy.resources, NO NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size.

Blast radius (why high, bordering critical for availability): the single worker PROCESS hosts EVERY queue — email-outbox, scheduled-jobs (Stripe webhook retry sweep, reservation/hold pickup-expiry, support-session expiry), import, maintenance, export (worker.ts:123-173) — at concurrency 1 (import-worker.ts:253). An OOM crash kills all of them for ALL tenants: a cross-tenant DoS, and the absence of mem_limit means the ballooning process can also OOM-pressure sibling containers (postgres/redis/api) on the same host. attempts:1 + removeOnFail:200 (import-queue.service.ts:35-37) prevents an infinite crash-loop on the same file, but every crash still drops in-flight jobs across all queues (e.g. a pending Stripe webhook retry), and the attacker can simply re-upload. Severity high (not critical) because it is availability/DoS, not data loss or cross-tenant data disclosure, and requires an authenticated owner/admin on a bulk_import-enabled plan.
exploit:
Preconditions: authenticated owner/admin of a tenant whose plan has bulk_import_enabled=true.

XLSX zip-bomb (strongest path — OOMs even before commit):
1. Craft a .xlsx (a ZIP) under 64MB whose xl/sharedStrings.xml or a single worksheet defines an enormous used range / hugely repeated long string, so the uncompressed payload is multiple GB. ZIP/deflate easily yields >100x ratios on repetitive text.
2. POST multipart to /t/:slug/imports with field `file`=the xlsx and `entityKind`=books. Multer admits it (compressed size < 64MB, import.controller.ts:70).
3. createBatch (import.service.ts:48) calls parseByFormat with maxRows:20 — but parseXlsx (xlsx-parser.ts:42) must `wb.xlsx.load(ab)` the WHOLE zip first, decompressing GBs into JS strings/ArrayBuffers → V8 heap exhaustion / container OOM. The worker (or api, depending on where load runs) process is killed. Because the worker hosts all queues at concurrency 1, every tenant's email/scheduled/import/export jobs stop. Even if upload survives, startCommit re-parses the full staged file uncapped in the worker (import-worker.ts:100-106) → guaranteed OOM there.

CSV path (simpler, kills the worker on validate/commit):
1. Upload a ~64MB .csv (e.g. one column, millions of short rows). Preview reads 20 rows but stageFile writes the full 64MB buffer (import.service.ts:86).
2. Set any mapping, POST /t/:slug/imports/:id/validate. Worker reads the full 64MB (readStaged) and runs tokenize over the entire string plus buildTableFromMatrix producing millions of {rowNumber, cells} objects in `rows` — peak memory many multiples of 64MB → OOM kills the shared worker.

Repro locally without a host: run processImportJob directly (it is exported for tests) against a batch whose stagingPath points at a multi-GB-uncompressing xlsx, with the worker started under `node --max-old-space-size=512` to make the crash deterministic; observe the process exit with JS heap OOM during parseByFormat.

Fixes: (a) pass a hard maxRows ceiling into parseByFormat in import-worker.ts:101 AND stream/cap inside the parsers (reject in tokenize / during ws.eachRow once the cap is hit) rather than only in tabular.ts:69; (b) for XLSX, inspect the zip central directory and cap total/ per-entry uncompressed size before wb.xlsx.load; (c) add a per-tenant uncompressed byte + row budget enforced at upload AND before enqueue, independent of the 64MB compressed cap; (d) set mem_limit and NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size on the worker container and ideally isolate the import queue in its own process so an import OOM cannot take down email/Stripe-webhook/expiry sweeps.

title: Unauthenticated fleet-wide metrics exposed publicly via the /lbr-api/* proxy (Caddy short-circuit claim is false)
description: HealthController is @Controller() (health.controller.ts:22) with @Get('metrics') (line 61) and NO guard — verified no @UseGuards on the class/method and no APP_GUARD provider in app.module.ts (providers only registers SupportAuditInterceptor as APP_INTERCEPTOR). main.ts installs no global guard. The metrics body emits fleet-wide gauges: libriant_tenants_total{status=...} (line 106), libriant_storage_used_bytes (line 113), libriant_pg_connections + libriant_pg_connections_max (lines 120,123), libriant_pg_cache_hit_ratio (line 130), libriant_redis_used_memory_bytes (line 139). Caddyfile:59 `@is_probe path /healthz /readyz /metrics` matches only the LITERAL path /metrics; a request to /lbr-api/metrics does NOT match it and falls through to `handle_path /lbr-api/* { reverse_proxy api:3001 }` (Caddyfile:139), which strips the prefix to /metrics and forwards to the unguarded handler. The same exposure exists via the Next.js rewrite `{ source: '/lbr-api/:path*', destination: `${apiTarget}/:path*` }` (next.config.mjs:23). The comment at health.controller.ts:55 ("`/metrics` is internal-only (Caddy short-circuits the public path)") is therefore false. The middleware chain (Session/Admin/Impersonation/SystemMode/Tenant on forRoutes('*'), app.module.ts:111-118) does not block /metrics — each is a no-op without its signal.
impact: Any anonymous internet user can read fleet-wide business + infra telemetry: total libraries by status (customer count / churn signal), total stored bytes across all tenants, live Postgres backend count and the max_connections ceiling, buffer-cache hit ratio, and Redis memory. The pg_connections + pg_connections_max pair gives an attacker a direct saturation signal to time a connection-pool exhaustion attack. Reachable through the documented web-facing proxy with no credentials.
fix: Do not rely on the edge to hide /metrics. Guard at the app layer: bind metrics to the internal worker port only (apps/api/src/worker.ts already serves /metrics on WORKER_PORT=3002, worker.ts:85) and remove the main-port handler, OR require an internal bearer token / source-IP allowlist on HealthController.metrics(). Additionally add an explicit Caddy block before `handle_path /lbr-api/*` that 404s `/lbr-api/metrics`, and mirror it in the Next.js rewrite. Fix the misleading comment at health.controller.ts:55. Verify with `curl https://<host>/lbr-api/metrics`.
skepticReasoning:
CONFIRMED. The exploit path is real and unmitigated; I refuted every candidate guard and the premise holds.

APP-LAYER: HealthController is @Controller() with @Get('metrics') (health.controller.ts:22,61) and NO @UseGuards on class or method. PlatformModule (platform.module.ts) registers the controller with no guard. app.module.ts:73-78 registers only SupportAuditInterceptor as APP_INTERCEPTOR — there is NO APP_GUARD provider anywhere (grep for APP_GUARD/useGlobalGuards across apps/api/src returns nothing). main.ts installs no global guard. So the handler is genuinely unauthenticated.

METRICS BODY is fleet-wide: libriant_tenants_total{status} (line 106 — customer/churn signal), libriant_storage_used_bytes summed across tenants (line 113), libriant_pg_connections + libriant_pg_connections_max (lines 120,123), libriant_pg_cache_hit_ratio (line 130), libriant_redis_used_memory_bytes (line 139).

CADDY ROUTING (the load-bearing claim): @is_probe uses the `path` matcher with literals /healthz /readyz /metrics (Caddyfile:59). Caddy's `path` matcher matches the FULL request URI path. A request to /lbr-api/metrics has full path /lbr-api/metrics, which is NOT equal to /metrics, so @is_probe does not fire. handle_path /lbr-api/* (Caddyfile:139) matches /lbr-api/metrics, strips the /lbr-api prefix, and reverse-proxies /metrics to api:3001 — the unguarded handler. handle/handle_path are mutually exclusive and sorted by matcher specificity, so the literal-path probe block cannot intercept the prefixed path. The comment at health.controller.ts:55 ("Caddy short-circuits the public path") is therefore false.

MIDDLEWARE does not block: SystemModeMiddleware's ALWAYS_PASS contains /^\/metrics\/?$/ (system-mode.middleware.ts:33) — an explicit BYPASS that lets the request through, not a block. Session/Admin/Impersonation/Tenant middleware are all no-ops without their respective signals (app.module.ts:98-99 documents this).

CORROBORATION: prometheus.yml scrapes api:3001/metrics directly over the private `app` network (line 41-44), NOT via Caddy — proving the edge "short-circuit" was never the real access control; it is only a maintenance fallback for the literal /metrics. The same false belief is repeated in prometheus.yml:40. The Next.js dev rewrite (next.config.mjs:23) reproduces the exposure in dev.

SEVERITY: This is information disclosure of business + infra telemetry, not data loss / cross-tenant record breach / write access / PII. The pg_connections+max pair is genuine recon for timing a pool-exhaustion attack but is not the attack itself. Honest severity is high, not critical (matches the finding).

Anonymous, no credentials:

  curl https://libriant.com/lbr-api/metrics

Expected response (HTTP 200, text/plain; version=0.0.4) includes fleet-wide gauges, e.g.:
  libriant_api_uptime_seconds 12345
  libriant_tenants_total{status="active"} 42
  libriant_tenants_total{status="suspended"} 3
  libriant_storage_used_bytes 1098765432
  libriant_pg_connections 37
  libriant_pg_connections_max 100
  libriant_pg_cache_hit_ratio 0.992
  libriant_redis_used_memory_bytes 20480000

Why it reaches the handler: Caddy @is_probe (Caddyfile:59) matches only full path /metrics; request path is /lbr-api/metrics → no match → falls to handle_path /lbr-api/* (Caddyfile:139) → prefix stripped to /metrics → proxied to api:3001 → unguarded HealthController.metrics() (health.controller.ts:61). SystemModeMiddleware ALWAYS_PASS /^\/metrics\/?$/ (system-mode.middleware.ts:33) explicitly bypasses, all other middleware no-op. Same in dev via Next rewrite (next.config.mjs:23): GET http://localhost:3000/lbr-api/metrics.

Reconnaissance value: total libraries by status (customer count + churn), total stored bytes across all tenants, live PG backend count vs max_connections ceiling (saturation timing signal), buffer-cache hit ratio, Redis memory.

Fix (per finding): bind metrics to the internal worker port only / require an internal bearer token or source-IP allowlist on HealthController.metrics(); add an explicit Caddy 404 block for /lbr-api/metrics before handle_path; mirror in the Next rewrite; correct the false comments at health.controller.ts:55 and prometheus.yml:40.

title: storage-migrate.ts crashes on every real run — references undeclared `toSize` (remediation regression)
description: Line 141 inside the control-plane transaction callback: `afterJson: { storageUrl: toUrl, byteCount: toSize },`. Only `fromSize` is declared (line 125: `const fromSize = await dirSize(from.path).catch(() => 0);`). `grep -rn 'toSize' scripts/` returns exactly one hit (the use at :141, no declaration). Scripts run via `tsx` (esbuild, no type-check): root package.json:36 `"storage:migrate": "tsx scripts/storage-migrate.ts"`. No tsconfig includes scripts/ (only tsconfig.base.json exists at root; `grep scripts tsconfig*.json` is empty) so they are NOT in `turbo run typecheck`. ESLint cannot catch it either: eslint.config.mjs:45 sets `'no-undef': 'off'` for **/*.{ts,tsx}. The ReferenceError throws inside `controlDb.$transaction(...)` (line 128) which runs AFTER the `rsync -a --delete` cutover (line 100) and the identical-tree verification (line 109) but BEFORE the storageUrl cutover commits. The catch (line 153) does NOT close the read_only window opened at line 95 (closeEvent is only at line 150).
impact: Every non-dry-run `pnpm storage:migrate` throws `ReferenceError: toSize is not defined` after fully mirroring files to the destination but before the tenant.storageUrl cutover. Tenant stays on OLD storage (no data loss) but: destination holds a full orphaned copy, the per-tenant read_only system-mode window is left OPEN (tenant rejects writes until an admin manually closes it — and unlike tenant-relocate this script's openReadOnly creates an event with no endsAt, so it never auto-expires), and the migration can never complete. The storage-migration drill the remediation hardened is non-functional.
fix: Recompute `const toSize = await dirSize(to.path).catch(() => 0);` before the transaction (trees are verified identical at that point), or drop the `byteCount: toSize` field. Add scripts/ to a typecheck task (a scripts tsconfig wired into `turbo run typecheck`) since tsx + no-undef:off give zero coverage. Also bound/close the read_only window on the error path (it currently leaks indefinitely).

CONFIRMED. Every premise of the finding holds against the real code.

1) Undeclared identifier is real. scripts/storage-migrate.ts:141 reads `afterJson: { storageUrl: toUrl, byteCount: toSize }`. A repo-wide grep for `toSize` (incl. *.d.ts) returns exactly one hit — that use — with NO declaration, parameter, destructuring, or global augmentation anywhere. Only `fromSize` is declared (line 125: `const fromSize = await dirSize(from.path).catch(() => 0);`).

2) It actually throws at runtime. I reproduced the exact pattern under `tsx` (the runner; root package.json:36 `"storage:migrate": "tsx scripts/storage-migrate.ts"`): it emits `ReferenceError: toSize is not defined`. tsx uses esbuild (no type-check), so the bad reference reaches the JS runtime.

title: restore.sh DROPs databases against a still-running cluster under ON_ERROR_STOP=1 — restore fails in a real DR event
description: Lines 62-64 pipe the dump straight into psql with ON_ERROR_STOP=1: `gunzip -c "$dir/postgres.sql.gz" | docker compose ... exec -T postgres psql -U libriant -d postgres -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1`. The dump is created with `pg_dumpall -U libriant --clean --if-exists` (backup.sh:47), which emits `DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS ...` statements. `grep -c` for any compose stop/down/docker stop/pg_terminate_backend in restore.sh returns 0 — the script never quiesces api/worker (which hold live pools to libriant_control and each tenant DB). Postgres rejects `DROP DATABASE` with 'is being accessed by other users' while sessions exist, and ON_ERROR_STOP=1 aborts on the first such failure.
impact: The DR restore path is unreliable exactly when needed (live host, containers up). It aborts on the first DROP DATABASE that still has connections, potentially after some DROP/CREATE statements ran, leaving a half-restored, inconsistent cluster. An operator under pressure hits a cryptic 'being accessed by other users' failure. Note the deployment doc's hand-written restore snippet (deployment-hetzner.md ~514) does NOT pass ON_ERROR_STOP, so the script itself is the more brittle path.
fix: Before the psql restore, stop app services (`docker compose ... stop api worker web migrate`) and/or `SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE datname NOT IN ('postgres') AND pid <> pg_backend_pid();`; restart afterward. Document that the app must be quiesced for restore.
skepticReasoning:
CONFIRMED. I tried hard to refute this and could not — every load-bearing claim holds, and the codebase itself proves the team knows the correct pattern that restore.sh omits.

Mechanism (all verified by reading the code):

1) The dump DROPs every database. scripts/backup.sh:47 creates the dump with `pg_dumpall -U libriant --clean --if-exists`. pg_dumpall --clean emits `DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS "<db>";` immediately before each `CREATE DATABASE`. restore.sh's own header comment confirms this intent: lines 8-10 say the dump "DROPs + recreates every database, including the per-tenant DBs."

2) restore.sh never quiesces the app. scripts/restore.sh:62-64 pipes the dump straight into `psql -U libriant -d postgres -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1`. A grep over restore.sh for `terminate|stop|down|FORCE|disconnect|pg_terminate_backend` returns 0 — the script never stops api/worker/web/migrate and never terminates backends.

3) Live sessions DO exist on the very DBs being dropped, during a real DR run (live host, containers up):
   - api & worker (same image, compose lines 149/209-225) keep an LRU of up to 50 hot tenant PrismaClients (apps/api/src/tenancy/tenant-prisma.service.ts:37-54; cache size default 50, idle TTL 30 min, updateAgeOnGet:true) — each a persistent connection to a tenant_* DB.
   - Those tenant connections go DIRECTLY to postgres, not through pgbouncer: the per-tenant dbUrl is built from PG_SUPERUSER_URL (apps/api/src/provisioning/tenant-provisioning.service.ts:105-108 `urlForDb`), and PG_SUPERUSER_URL = postgresql://libriant:...@postgres:5432/libriant_control (infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:71). So DROP DATABASE on each tenant_* DB hits active sessions.
   - pgbouncer runs POOL_MODE: transaction with DEFAULT_POOL_SIZE 20 (compose:275-278) and holds persistent server connections to libriant_control; plus the control-plane Prisma connection. So DROP DATABASE on libriant_control also hits active sessions.
   - `restart: unless-stopped` (compose:74) keeps all containers up throughout.

4) Postgres rejects `DROP DATABASE` with "database ... is being accessed by other users" while sessions exist (no WITH (FORCE), no datallowconn handling anywhere — grep confirmed). With ON_ERROR_STOP=1 (restore.sh:64), psql aborts on the FIRST such failure — after pg_dumpall has already emitted globals/roles and possibly dropped/recreated some idle DBs — leaving a half-restored, inconsistent cluster and a cryptic error for the operator.

5) The team already knows the correct guard but applied it only to the single-tenant drop path, NOT to the DR restore path: scripts/tenant-create.ts:297-303 runs `SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE datname = $1 AND pid <> pg_backend_pid()` immediately before `DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS`. restore.sh — which drops EVERY DB — has no equivalent.

(b) "maybe idle TTL closes the connections" — TTL is 30 min with updateAgeOnGet, so under any traffic they stay open. (c) "maybe the dump uses FORCE drop" — grep shows no FORCE anywhere. (d) The deployment doc's hand-written snippet (docs/deployment-hetzner.md:511-512) omits ON_ERROR_STOP, so it would limp past the failed DROPs differently — but that makes the script (restore.sh) the more brittle of the two paths, reinforcing the finding rather than refuting it.

Severity high (not critical): this is a DR-reliability/availability failure, not a routine-operation data-loss or security breach. But it defeats recovery exactly when needed and can leave a half-restored cluster, so it is a genuine production-blocking gap in the documented recovery procedure.

One correction to the finding's metadata: the deployment doc restore snippet is at docs/deployment-hetzner.md:511-512 (not docs/audit/...~514), and tenant DB connections bypass pgbouncer (direct to postgres) — which strengthens, not weakens, the claim about live sessions on the dropped DBs.

Repro (real DR scenario, containers up):
1. Deploy prod stack (infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml): postgres + pgbouncer + api + worker + web, all `restart: unless-stopped`.
2. Drive normal traffic so api/worker populate the tenant PrismaClient LRU (tenant-prisma.service.ts) — each tenant now has a live direct connection to its tenant_* DB on postgres:5432, and pgbouncer holds a warm transaction-mode server pool to libriant_control.
3. Run the documented restore: `scripts/restore.sh <YYYYMMDD> --yes`.
4. At restore.sh:62-64, `pg_dumpall --clean` output reaches `DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS "tenant_..."` (or "libriant_control"). Postgres returns: `ERROR: database "tenant_..." is being accessed by other users / There is 1 other session using the database.`
5. Because of `-v ON_ERROR_STOP=1` (restore.sh:64), psql aborts immediately. The restore stops mid-stream — globals/roles and any idle DBs may already have been dropped/recreated — leaving an inconsistent, half-restored cluster.

- `grep -cE 'terminate|stop|down|FORCE|disconnect' scripts/restore.sh` → 0

    "SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE datname <> 'postgres' AND pid <> pg_backend_pid();"

title: Backups silently omit all tenant uploads by default — STORAGE_DIR/BACKUP_ROOT never set; defaults point at in-container paths
description: backup.sh:27 `STORAGE_DIR="${STORAGE_DIR:-/srv/libriant/storage}"` and :22 `BACKUP_ROOT="${BACKUP_ROOT:-/srv/libriant/backups}"`. On the HOST, storage is the bind-mounted volume at `${LIBRIANT_DATA_ROOT:-/mnt/libriant}/storage` (docker-compose.volume.yml:35-40); `/srv/libriant/storage` is the IN-CONTAINER mount (docker-compose.prod.yml:168 `storage:/srv/libriant/storage`) and does not exist on the host, so `[ -d "$STORAGE_DIR" ]` (:58) is false → 'skipping storage tar' (:64). ensure-env.sh only writes LIBRIANT_DATA_ROOT (:104) and BACKUP_KEEP_DAYS (:105) — never STORAGE_DIR or BACKUP_ROOT. .env.prod.example contains only RCLONE_REMOTE (line 81), no STORAGE_DIR/BACKUP_ROOT. The cron in deployment-hetzner.md:503 sources `.env.prod` (which lacks them) and only overrides COMPOSE_FILE, so the scheduled cron has no STORAGE_DIR. The doc at lines 477-478 falsely claims 'your env points BACKUP_ROOT and STORAGE_DIR at the volume'.

A disk loss loses all per-tenant files with no recovery, and the documented restore drill reads a storage.tar.gz that was never created. Latent total-file-loss. The only mitigation is the manual one-shot in the doc that doesn't set STORAGE_DIR either — so even that produces no storage tar.

Make backup.sh exit non-zero when STORAGE_DIR is missing instead of silently skipping, so a missing-uploads backup can't go unnoticed.

title: workflow_dispatch "rollback" rebuilds current code under the old tag and runs new migrations against the old image
description: The `build` job has only `needs: verify` (line 81) — there is NO `if:` guard, so it ALWAYS runs and rebuilds from `actions/checkout@v4` (line 86, which checks out github.sha = main HEAD). The meta step sets `TAG="${{ github.event.inputs.image_tag }}"` (line 90) and build-push-action tags `libriant-api:${{ steps.meta.outputs.tag }}` AND `libriant-api:latest` (lines 113-114), push: true (line 111). So `workflow_dispatch` with `image_tag=<old-sha>` rebuilds HEAD code and force-pushes it over the historical `<old-sha>` image and over `:latest`. Independently, the deploy step pins `GIT_SHA: ${{ github.sha }}` (line 191) and runs `git reset --hard ${GIT_SHA}` (line 205) — github.sha is the trigger ref (main HEAD), NOT the image_tag — then runs `bash scripts/ensure-env.sh` and `docker compose ... up` against the NEW compose file. The `migrate` service (prod.yml:128-160) gates api/worker via `service_completed_successfully` and runs `scripts/prod-bootstrap.sh`, which executes `pnpm db:migrate:deploy` (prod-bootstrap.sh:27) + `pnpm tenant:migrate` (line 36) — forward-only migrations — while api/worker pull the OLD IMAGE_TAG. New schema + old code.
impact: The documented rollback lever (line 21 'Override the tag to deploy ... roll back') is unusable and dangerous: it overwrites the good historical image with current/broken code and re-pushes :latest, and it applies forward migrations against the old image's code. An operator reaching for workflow_dispatch during an incident destroys the artifact they were trying to restore and can wedge the stack with new-schema/old-code.
fix: Gate the build job: `build.if: github.event.inputs.image_tag == ''` so a tag override never rebuilds/re-pushes. On rollback, resolve GIT_SHA from the supplied tag (so `git reset --hard` matches the deployed image) instead of using github.sha. Never re-tag an existing SHA. Refuse a deploy whose IMAGE_TAG predates the latest migration.

CONFIRMED after reading deploy.yml in full plus the compose file, prod-bootstrap.sh, fleet.yml and grepping every checkout/ref/needs/if in the workflow. The core mechanism is exactly as cited and the documented rollback lever is broken and destructive. BUT one sub-claim in the finding is factually wrong and the report copy must be corrected before it ships.

GHCR tags are mutable (no immutability config found anywhere in .github/ or infra/), so the re-push overwrites the historical good image's tag and re-poisons :latest.
- deploy step: `GIT_SHA: ${{ github.sha }}` (line 191) → `git reset --hard ${GIT_SHA}` (line 205). github.sha on workflow_dispatch is main HEAD, NOT the requested image_tag. So the host checkout (and the scripts/locales bind-mounted into migrate, compose lines 144-146) come from HEAD, not the rolled-back commit.
- migrate, api, worker all pull the SAME `libriant-api:${IMAGE_TAG}` (compose lines 129, 150, 210).

REAL, CONFIRMED DAMAGE (the finding's leading impact holds): the inline-documented rollback lever — `image_tag` input description "Override the tag to deploy ... roll back" (line 21) — is functionally inert AND destructive. workflow_dispatch with image_tag=<old-sha> rebuilds current HEAD, tags it with the old SHA + :latest, force-pushes both, then `git reset --hard` to HEAD and force-recreates the fleet on the rebuilt-HEAD image. An operator reaching for this during an incident to restore a known-good version instead (a) deploys HEAD — the very code they were trying to roll away from, so the "rollback" does nothing, and (b) overwrites the good historical image at that tag in GHCR plus :latest — destroying the artifact they meant to restore and the documented manual `dc pull` fallback path.

New schema + old code." This does NOT occur. Because the same workflow run's build job re-pushed HEAD to the <old> tag, the migrate service AND api/worker all pull the rebuilt-HEAD image (compose 129/150/210 share IMAGE_TAG) and the mounted scripts are HEAD (reset to github.sha). migrate runs HEAD migrations and api runs HEAD code — they are version-consistent. There is no schema/code split within a workflow_dispatch run.

NET: premise (a documented rollback lever the build job sabotages) and primary impact (inert + destructive rollback, clobbered historical artifact, poisoned :latest, lost manual fallback) are genuine and code-confirmed → confirmed=true. The migration-wedge framing is inaccurate and the report wording must be corrected. title: Concurrent hold-promotion paths take no per-book lock and no CAS — double-allocates a copy / orphans inventory
description: Confirmed in code. The only `reservation:<bookId>` advisory lock in the whole circulation subsystem is in placeHold (reservations.service.ts:189: `SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended(${`reservation:${input.bookId}`}, 0))`). A grep for FOR UPDATE/isolationLevel/advisory returned ONLY the two placeHold/member-archive advisory locks — none in the promotion paths, so they run at READ COMMITTED. returnLoan reads the head with a plain SELECT `tx.reservation.findFirst({ where: { bookId: loan.copy.bookId, status: 'queued' }, orderBy: { queuePosition: 'asc' } })` (loans.service.ts:404-412) then promotes via `tx.reservation.update({ where: { id: head.id }, data: { status: 'ready', fulfilledByCopyId: loan.copyId, ... } })` (loans.service.ts:416-425) — the WHERE is `id` only, NO status predicate. promoteNextHoldInTx (reservations.service.ts:493-502) and the expiry job (reservation-expiry.job.ts:149-161) are identical bare `update`s. Under two concurrent returns of copy-A and copy-B of the same book: both findFirst read the same head R; Tx1 updates R (blocks no one, no status guard); Tx2's `update R` blocks on Tx1's row lock, then under READ COMMITTED re-evaluates its WHERE (`id=R` still matches since there is no status predicate) and overwrites fulfilledByCopyId from A to B. Each tx also flips its own copy on_loan->reserved guarded only on `status='on_loan'` (loans.service.ts:462-465), so BOTH copies succeed. Final state: R points at copy-B; copy-A is left in `reserved` with no reservation referencing it.
impact: Under concurrent returns/expiries of multiple copies of a popular title, a physical copy is silently stranded in `reserved` with no hold pointing at it, removing it from circulation until staff manually notice and reset it. Queue fairness is also violated. The advisory lock added to fix the placeHold race does not cover the dominant promotion paths (returnLoan, resolveReservation/promoteNextHoldInTx, expiry job).
fix: Take the same `reservation:<bookId>` advisory xact lock at the top of every queue-mutating transaction (returnLoan promotion tx, resolveReservation tx, and the expiry job's per-reservation tx) so all promotions for a book serialize. At minimum guard the reservation promotion with a CAS: `tx.reservation.updateMany({ where: { id: head.id, status: 'queued' }, data: {...} })` and abort/skip when count===0, mirroring the copy CAS already used.
skepticReasoning:
CONFIRMED. I tried to refute this finding and could not — the exploit path is real and reachable.

Evidence (re-read from source, not the finding's quotes):

1. Advisory locks: `grep -rn "pg_advisory"` over apps/api/src + packages returns exactly 5 hits — loans.service.ts:229 (`member:${input.memberId}`, checkout), reservations.service.ts:189 (`reservation:${input.bookId}`, placeHold ONLY), plus quota/staff/members. NONE in any promotion path. No `FOR UPDATE` / `isolationLevel` / `Serializable` anywhere in the two services or jobs. So all three promotion txns run at the connection default READ COMMITTED.

2. returnLoan (loans.service.ts:404-441): `tx.reservation.findFirst({ where: { bookId, status: 'queued' }, orderBy: { queuePosition: 'asc' }})` (plain SELECT, no lock) then `tx.reservation.update({ where: { id: head.id }, data: { status:'ready', fulfilledByCopyId: loan.copyId, ... }})`. The WHERE is `id` only — no `status` predicate. The freed copy is flipped at loans.service.ts:462-465 via `updateMany({ where: { id: loan.copyId, status: 'on_loan' }, ...})`.

3. resolveReservation (reservations.service.ts:316-359) opens `$transaction` with NO advisory lock and calls promoteNextHoldInTx (493-502), which does the identical bare `tx.reservation.update({ where: { id: head.id }, ...})`.

4. Expiry job (reservation-expiry.job.ts:100-161): `$transaction` with no advisory lock; reservation promotion at 149-161 is a bare `tx.reservation.update({ where: { id: next.id }, ...})` with no status predicate. (Note: this path DOES have a copy CAS at 139-143, so it avoids double-copy-allocation, but still allows the head-overwrite. returnLoan has neither guard and is the cleanest exploit.)

5. Schema (db-tenant/prisma/schema.prisma:390-421): `fulfilledByCopyId String?` with NO @unique; `queuePosition Int?` with NO @unique; only @@index([bookId, status, queuePosition]). So nothing at the DB layer prevents two reservations/copies colliding or a copy being orphaned.

6. returnLoan is HTTP-reachable concurrently: loans.controller.ts:100-108 `@Post(':id/return')`.

Concurrency derivation (READ COMMITTED, EvalPlanQual semantics): Tx1 returns copy-A, Tx2 returns copy-B of the same book; queue head = reservation R. Both findFirst (plain SELECT, non-blocking) read R as the queued head. Tx1 `update R SET fulfilledByCopyId=A` takes R's row lock; Tx2 `update R` blocks. Tx1 commits. Tx2 re-evaluates its WHERE against the new committed row — `id=R` STILL matches because there is no status predicate — so Tx2 overwrites fulfilledByCopyId from A to B. Each txn independently flips its own returned copy on_loan→reserved (distinct rows A and B, both pass the `status='on_loan'` CAS). Final state: R.fulfilledByCopyId=B; copy A=reserved with NO reservation referencing it (orphaned out of circulation); copy B also reserved for R. Queue fairness and inventory integrity both violated.

Mitigations I checked and ruled out: (a) no FOR UPDATE on the head read; (b) no unique constraint on fulfilledByCopyId or queuePosition; (c) the on_loan→reserved CAS does NOT catch the conflict because A and B are different rows; (d) the placeHold advisory lock keyed on `reservation:${bookId}` does NOT cover these txns (different code paths, lock never taken). The only way the bug is avoided is the benign interleaving where Tx1 commits before Tx2's findFirst runs (Tx2 then sees no queued head) — but that is just timing luck, not a guard. The window is wide because findFirst, the queue-bump executeRaw, loan updateMany, and copy updateMany all execute between the read and commit.

Severity high (not critical): consequence is stranded inventory + queue-fairness violation requiring manual staff correction, not cross-tenant breach or money loss. Highly plausible on popular multi-copy titles at a busy return desk / during the expiry sweep overlapping a return.
exploit:
Repro (single tenant, one book with >=2 undamaged copies A and B, both on_loan, and a queue with head reservation R, status='queued'):

1. Open two concurrent POST requests:
   - Req1: POST /loans/{loanId-A}/return  (returns copy A)
   - Req2: POST /loans/{loanId-B}/return  (returns copy B)
   Fire them so both enter returnLoan's $transaction before either commits (e.g. add a breakpoint after the findFirst at loans.service.ts:404, or hammer with two parallel clients; the read→commit window spans 4+ statements so collisions occur naturally under load).

2. Both transactions' findFirst (loans.service.ts:404-412) read R as the queued head.
3. Tx1 `update R` (416-425) sets fulfilledByCopyId=A, takes R's row lock; flips copy A on_loan→reserved (462-465); commits.
4. Tx2's `update R` (416-425) was blocked on R; after Tx1 commits, under READ COMMITTED it re-checks WHERE id=R (no status predicate) — still matches — and overwrites fulfilledByCopyId A→B; flips copy B on_loan→reserved; commits.

Expected buggy outcome (verifiable with SQL):
  SELECT id, status, "fulfilledByCopyId" FROM reservations WHERE id='R';  -- status=ready, fulfilledByCopyId=B
  SELECT id, status FROM book_copies WHERE id IN ('A','B');               -- both 'reserved'
  -- Copy A is 'reserved' but NO reservation has fulfilledByCopyId='A' → orphaned, removed from circulation until staff manually reset it.

The same head-overwrite reproduces via concurrent resolveReservation (cancel/expire) calls and via the expiry sweep overlapping a return (reservation-expiry.job.ts:149-161 bare update on next.id).

Fix: take `SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended('reservation:'||bookId, 0))` at the TOP of the returnLoan promotion txn, the resolveReservation txn, and the expiry job's per-reservation txn (mirroring placeHold at reservations.service.ts:189) so all promotions for a book serialize. At minimum, make every head promotion a CAS: `tx.reservation.updateMany({ where: { id: head.id, status: 'queued' }, data: {...} })` and abort/skip when count===0, mirroring the copy CAS already present in the expiry job.

title: Expiry-job reservation promotion lacks a status CAS, so it races returnLoan/cancel even though it CAS-guards the copy
description: The expiry job carefully claims the copy with a compare-and-swap (`tx.bookCopy.updateMany({ where: { id: copy.id, status: 'available' }, data: { status: 'reserved' } })` at line 139-142, aborting when claimed.count===0), but then promotes the queued hold with an UNGUARDED `tx.reservation.update({ where: { id: next.id }, data: { status: 'ready', fulfilledByCopyId: copy.id, ... } })` at line 149-161 — no `status: 'queued'` predicate. The expiring reservation itself is CAS-guarded (updateMany where status='ready' at line 102-106), but the *promoted* reservation is not. Because the job takes no `reservation:<bookId>` advisory lock either, a concurrent returnLoan (loans.service.ts:404-425) or admin cancel/expire (reservations.service.ts promoteNextHoldInTx) reading the same `next` head can promote it against a DIFFERENT freed copy. The copy CAS prevents two reservations claiming the SAME copy, but it does NOT prevent the same reservation being promoted twice against two different copies: tx-A claims copy X + sets next.ready/fulfilledByCopyId=X; tx-B claims copy Y + overwrites next.fulfilledByCopyId=Y. Copy X is then left 'reserved' with no reservation pointing at it — orphaned inventory, identical failure mode to circ-1.
impact: Same silent stranded-copy corruption as circ-1, but specifically demonstrating that the remediation's copy-CAS (added in this job) is insufficient: it protects the physical copy from double-claim but leaves the reservation->copy pointer unguarded, so a physical copy still gets orphaned in 'reserved' when the cron sweep races a return/cancel of another copy of the same title.
fix: Guard the promotion with a reservation CAS: `tx.reservation.updateMany({ where: { id: next.id, status: 'queued' }, data: {...} })` and, if count===0, release the just-claimed copy back to 'available' before returning. Better: take the `reservation:<bookId>` advisory xact lock at the top of the per-reservation transaction so all promotions for a book serialize across job/return/cancel.
skepticReasoning:
CONFIRMED. The exploit path genuinely exists; every potential mitigation was checked and none closes it.

Premise verification:
1. Isolation: No isolation level is set on any `client.$transaction(...)` (grep for Isolation/Serializable/RepeatableRead returns nothing), so Postgres default READ COMMITTED applies. Under READ COMMITTED, a second UPDATE that blocks on a row lock re-reads the latest committed row when it unblocks and re-applies its SET — it does NOT see a stale snapshot that would error.

2. Unguarded promotion (the bug): apps/api/src/jobs/reservation-expiry.job.ts:149-161 promotes the queued head with `tx.reservation.update({ where: { id: next.id }, data: { status: 'ready', fulfilledByCopyId: copy.id, ... } })` — a single-row update by PK with NO `status: 'queued'` predicate and (being `.update`, not `.updateMany`) no count check. The copy-CAS added by the remediation (lines 139-142) only protects the physical copy from double-claim; it leaves the reservation→copy pointer unguarded. Confirmed against the 151f579 diff: the CAS + readyAt were added, but the reservation.update stayed unconditional. The sibling promotion paths are identically unguarded: loans.service.ts returnLoan line 416 (`tx.reservation.update({where:{id:head.id}})`, no status filter) and reservations.service.ts promoteNextHoldInTx line 493 (same).

3. No serialization: The only `reservation:<bookId>` advisory xact lock in the whole circulation lane is in placeHold (reservations.service.ts:189). returnLoan, the expiry job, and resolveReservation (admin cancel/expire) take NO such lock (returnLoan/expire take none; checkout takes only `member:<id>`). So returnLoan ↔ expiry-job ↔ cancel/expire do not serialize on the book — they contend only via per-row PK locks.
