4. Separate processes: apps/api/src/worker.ts runs the cron sweep (registry.ts:29-31) while the API serves returnLoan/cancel HTTP — genuine cross-process concurrency; the Node event loop does not serialize them, and there is no Redis/per-book app lock.

5. No DB backstop: There is no trigger and no check constraint tying a copy's `reserved` status to an existing reservation pointing at it (the only fulfilled_consistency check covers status='fulfilled', not 'ready', and not the copy side). So the orphan is never caught.

Net: a concrete interleaving leaves a physical copy stranded in `reserved` with no reservation referencing it — the same stranded-inventory corruption as circ-1, proving the remediation's copy-CAS is insufficient. Severity high (real data corruption needing manual operator repair), but blast radius is limited and timing-probabilistic (not attacker-controllable, no money/cross-tenant impact), matching the finding's stated severity. The proposed fix (reservation CAS on status='queued' with copy-release on count===0, or a per-book advisory xact lock across all three paths) is correct.
exploit:
Cross-process race between the cron expiry sweep (worker process) and a concurrent returnLoan (API process) on the same book title.

Setup: Book B has copy X held for an expiring `ready` reservation R_exp (X status=reserved), and copy Y on an active loan L. Queue head is reservation N (status=queued, queuePosition=1).

Interleaving (A = expiry job expireOneTenant, B = returnLoan(L)):
- A line 102: updateMany R_exp ready->expired (locks R_exp).
- A line 112: copy X reserved->available.
- A line 119: SELECT next = N (status=queued)  [no lock].
- A line 128: SELECT first available copy = X  [no lock].
- A line 139-142: CAS claim X available->reserved, count=1 (locks X).
- A line 149-161: UPDATE N by PK -> ready, fulfilledByCopyId=X, queuePosition=null (locks N).
- B line 404: SELECT head WHERE status='queued' -> N (B's snapshot still shows N queued because A hasn't committed).
- B line 416: UPDATE N by PK -> BLOCKS on A's row lock.
- A commits. State: X=reserved, N=ready/copyX.
- B line 416 unblocks, re-reads N (now ready/copyX); because the UPDATE has NO status predicate it UNCONDITIONALLY overwrites N -> ready, fulfilledByCopyId=Y, queuePosition=null.
- B line 462: copy Y on_loan->reserved (nextCopyStatus='reserved'), count=1.
- B commits.

Final corrupted state: N.fulfilledByCopyId = Y. Copy Y = reserved (correct, N points to it). Copy X = reserved but NO reservation points at it -> orphaned inventory stuck in `reserved`, invisible to the queue, requiring manual operator repair. The remediation's copy-CAS prevented two reservations from claiming the SAME copy but did not prevent the same reservation N from being promoted twice against two DIFFERENT copies.

Fix that defeats the repro: guard the promotion with `tx.reservation.updateMany({ where: { id: next.id, status: 'queued' }, data: {...} })` and, when count===0, release the just-claimed copy back to 'available' before returning — then B's re-evaluated UPDATE matches 0 rows, aborts the promotion, and frees copy Y instead of orphaning X. Apply the same guard to returnLoan:416 and promoteNextHoldInTx:493, or take `pg_advisory_xact_lock(reservation:<bookId>)` at the top of all three transactions so every promotion for a book serializes.

title: Save-time ReDoS guard is missing on field-definition UPDATE and on ALL collection-field create/update paths
description: grep confirms the ONLY call sites of patternLooksCatastrophic are field-types.ts (match-time) and field-definitions.service.ts (create, line 127). field-definitions.service.update sets `if (input.validationJson !== undefined) data.validationJson = input.validationJson;` (line 243) with NO patternLooksCatastrophic and NO `new RegExp()` compile check — an admin can PATCH a clean field's validationJson to a catastrophic pattern. collections.service.createField persists validationJson (lines 285, 300) and updateField (line 339) with NO pattern guard and NO compile check at all. collections.dto.ts:93,120 accepts validationJson as a free-form `Record<string, unknown>`, so `pattern` flows straight through. collection-records.service.ts:90-91,129-130 loads these stored fields via loadActiveFieldsForValidation and runs validateRecordOrThrow -> validateField, so the ONLY backstop for collection-field patterns is the match-time guard, which CAT-001 proves bypassable.
impact: The save-time defense the commit advertised is hollow for the majority of pattern-storing routes (field-def PATCH, all collection-field create/update). Combined with CAT-001 this is a reliably reachable full-process freeze. A malformed (non-compiling) pattern saved via these paths is also never caught until match time.
fix: Extract save-time validation (patternLooksCatastrophic + new RegExp compile) into a shared helper and call it from field-definitions.update, collections.createField, and collections.updateField whenever validationJson.pattern is a non-empty string. Add tests covering each route.

title: Collection / collection-field schema editing has NO role guard — any tenant user (incl. volunteer) can edit the data model
description: CollectionsController is `@UseGuards(TenantGuard)` only (line 40) and NONE of create/update/archive/addField/updateField/archiveField carry `@Roles` (lines 54,66,82,89,108,127). The directly-analogous FieldDefinitionsController is `@UseGuards(TenantGuard, RolesGuard)` and guards every mutation with `@Roles('owner','admin')`. roles.decorator.ts:6-11 states 'control the library' actions use `@Roles('owner','admin')`; defining new entity types and editing field schemas (including planting validation patterns) is squarely a control-the-library action. RolesGuard (tenancy/roles.guard.ts) is functional and checks current DB role. Because CollectionsController declares no roles metadata, even adding RolesGuard alone wouldn't restrict it — the @Roles decorator is required.
impact: Privilege escalation over the data model: a low-privilege volunteer can create/rename/archive whole collections, add required fields (instantly affecting all writers), and plant validation patterns. Via CAT-001/CAT-002 the lowest-privilege role can also plant a process-freezing regex. Inconsistent with the field-definitions authz model.
fix: Add `@UseGuards(TenantGuard, RolesGuard)` to CollectionsController and `@Roles('owner','admin')` on every mutating handler (create, update, archive, addField, updateField, archiveField), matching FieldDefinitionsController. Leave the GET handlers open.
skepticReasoning:
CONFIRMED. The finding holds under direct inspection of the code and every relevant guard/call-site.

1) CollectionsController is guarded by TenantGuard ONLY (apps/api/src/customization/collections.controller.ts:40 `@UseGuards(TenantGuard)`), and none of its six mutating handlers carry `@Roles`: create (line 54), update (line 66), archive (line 82), addField (line 89), updateField (line 108), archiveField (line 127).

2) TenantGuard (apps/api/src/tenancy/tenant.guard.ts:24-55) performs NO role check. It only verifies: tenant resolved from URL, caller signed in, and `req.session.tid === req.tenant.id`. Any authenticated tenant member passes — including the lowest role.

3) The UserRole enum (packages/db-control/prisma/schema.prisma:41-46) defines owner > admin > librarian > volunteer ("limited rights"). A volunteer is a legitimate signed-in tenant member and thus clears TenantGuard.

4) The service layer has no compensating control: grep of collections.service.ts shows the six mutation methods (create:94, update:138, archive:198, createField:227, updateField:309, archiveField:351) contain zero occurrences of `role`/`Forbidden`/`Roles`. Authorization is purely route-level, and it is absent.

5) The asymmetry is real and deliberate elsewhere: the directly analogous FieldDefinitionsController IS `@UseGuards(TenantGuard, RolesGuard)` (field-definitions.controller.ts:35) with `@Roles('owner','admin')` on create (50), update (71), archive (92). roles.decorator.ts documents that 'control the library' actions use `@Roles('owner','admin')`; defining/renaming/archiving entity types and editing field schemas is squarely such an action.

6) RolesGuard (apps/api/src/tenancy/roles.guard.ts) checks the CURRENT DB role and is functional — but it early-returns `true` when no `@Roles` metadata is present (`if (!roles || roles.length === 0) return true`). So merely adding RolesGuard to the controller would NOT restrict anything; the `@Roles` decorator on each handler is required, exactly as the proposed fix states.

7) DTO confirms the data-model damage surface: CreateCollectionFieldDto.validationJson / UpdateCollectionFieldDto.validationJson are free-form `@IsObject()` (collections.dto.ts:91-93, 118-120), so a low-privilege user can plant arbitrary validation config (including a regex pattern) that affects all subsequent record writes. `required` is also settable, instantly affecting all writers.

8) The controller is live: it is registered in CustomizationModule.controllers (customization.module.ts:22).

Net: a volunteer-tier (or any) tenant member can create/rename/archive collections and add/edit/archive fields and validation rules. This is broken access control / privilege escalation over the tenant data model. Blast radius is confined to the user's own tenant (TenantGuard still blocks cross-tenant), it requires authentication, and it does not by itself cause direct money loss — so HIGH (not critical) is the honest severity. Not refuted by any guard, middleware, or service-layer check.
exploit:
Preconditions: attacker holds a valid session as a `volunteer` (lowest role, "limited rights") in tenant with slug `acme`. This is a normal, intended account type.

Repro 1 — create a whole new entity type (collection):
  POST /t/acme/data-model/collections
  Cookie: <volunteer session>
  { "slug": "secret-donors", "singularLabelJson": {"en":"Donor"}, "pluralLabelJson": {"en":"Donors"} }
  -> 200/201. TenantGuard passes (member of acme); no @Roles to block. svc.create runs with no role check.

Repro 2 — add a REQUIRED field to an existing collection, instantly forcing all writers to supply it:
  POST /t/acme/data-model/collections/books-custom/fields
  { "fieldKey": "approval_code", "labelJson": {"en":"Approval"}, "type": "text", "required": true }
  -> succeeds; every subsequent record write must now satisfy the new required field.

Repro 3 — plant a validation rule (e.g. a pathological regex) via the same low-priv call:
  PATCH /t/acme/data-model/collections/books-custom/fields/approval_code
  { "validationJson": { "pattern": "^(a+)+$" } }
  -> succeeds (validationJson is free-form @IsObject; no role gate). Future writes against this field run that pattern.

Repro 4 — archive (effectively disable) a collection or field:
  DELETE /t/acme/data-model/collections/books-custom
  DELETE /t/acme/data-model/collections/books-custom/fields/title
  -> both succeed for a volunteer.

Contrast / proof of intended model: the same operations on Layer-1 entity fields are correctly blocked:
  POST /t/acme/data-model/fields/book  (FieldDefinitionsController, @Roles('owner','admin'))
  as a volunteer -> 403 "This action is restricted to library admins."

Fix: add `@UseGuards(TenantGuard, RolesGuard)` to CollectionsController and `@Roles('owner','admin')` on create/update/archive/addField/updateField/archiveField; leave the two GET handlers open. (Adding RolesGuard without the @Roles decorators is a no-op because RolesGuard returns true when no roles metadata is present.)

title: PATCH on collection records / built-in customFields still executes the bypassable ReDoS regex for any provided value (no partial exemption)
description: validateRecord's `partial` mode (used by all PATCH endpoints, e.g. collection-records.service.ts:129-130 with `{ partial: true }`) only relaxes the required check via `{ ...def, required: false }` (dynamic-validator.ts:55). For any field the client DOES supply, it still calls validateField (line 51-57), which runs the stored pattern through `new RegExp().test()` (field-types.ts:148-150). So the catastrophic-backtracking explosion from CAT-001 is just as reachable on PATCH as on POST — a single PATCH that includes the trigger value freezes the process. This widens the CAT-001 attack surface to every update endpoint that carries custom fields (books, members, copies, loans, reservations, collection records), not just creates.
impact: Confirms the ReDoS is reachable on both create and update paths across every entity with custom fields, making the process-freeze trivially triggerable by any tenant user with write access who can also (per CAT-002/CAT-003) plant the pattern.
fix: Same root fix as CAT-001 (worker-thread timeout or RE2). No separate guard needed once the engine-level fix lands; flagged to document the full blast radius across create AND update across all custom-field-bearing entities.

title: Stripe retry sweep replays the captured payload with no event-ordering guard → stale event overwrites newer subscription state
description: The sweep deserializes `row.payloadJson as unknown as StripeWebhookEvent` (stripe-retry.job.ts:67) and re-runs the handler, which applies the captured payload as absolute truth: `syncStripeSubscription` overwrites planId/status/currentPeriodStart/currentPeriodEnd/cancelAtPeriodEnd/canceledAt from the payload (billing.service.ts:475-493). The schema model StripeWebhookEvent has only `receivedAt/processedAt/error` and NO Stripe `created`/version/ordering field (schema.prisma:636-648 — confirmed: `id,type,payloadJson,receivedAt,processedAt,error` only). Worse, this needs no concurrency: errored event A stays in the table (error!=null, processedAt=null); Stripe delivers newer B which succeeds and sets current state; the next 5-min sweep still selects A (matches `error: { not: null }`, stripe-retry.job.ts:44) and replays A's old payload, clobbering B. The remediation that broadened the query to also pull never-processed stale rows (`receivedAt < staleBefore`) enlarges the replay surface.
impact: A tenant's local subscription row (plan, status, billing period, cancelAtPeriodEnd, graceUntil) can be reverted to an older Stripe state — wrong plan entitlements, wrong grace window, or a resurrected cancellation — persisting until the next correct webhook. This is an entitlement/money-state corruption, achievable even single-threaded.
fix: Persist the event's Stripe `created` timestamp on the row and refuse to apply an event older than the last successfully-applied one for that subscription/customer. At minimum, before re-dispatching in the sweep, re-fetch the live object from Stripe (driver.retrieveSubscription) instead of replaying the captured payload.

title: Unauthenticated /metrics exposes platform-wide operational intelligence via /lbr-api/metrics
description: health.controller.ts:22 `@Controller()` with NO class-level guard; line 61 `@Get('metrics')` has no @UseGuards. grep for UseGuards/InternalGuard on this file returns nothing. The app-wide middleware (app.module.ts:109-118 SessionMiddleware/TenantMiddleware/etc on '*') are no-ops with no session/tenant, so /metrics is reachable unauthenticated. capacityGauges() (lines 87-142) returns libriant_tenants_total{status} (customer census), libriant_storage_used_bytes, libriant_pg_connections/_max, libriant_pg_cache_hit_ratio, libriant_redis_used_memory_bytes. In the Caddyfile, the only matcher touching /metrics is `@is_probe path /healthz /readyz /metrics` (line 59) inside (maintenance_check); `path /metrics` matches only the literal path, NOT the browser-facing `/lbr-api/metrics`. `handle_path /lbr-api/* { reverse_proxy api:3001 }` (lines 139-151) strips the prefix and forwards `/metrics` straight to the unguarded API route. The public :116 matcher `@probe path /healthz /readyz` doesn't even list /metrics. The code comment at health.controller.ts:55 ('`/metrics` is internal-only (Caddy short-circuits the public path)') is false.
impact: Any unauthenticated internet client hitting GET https://libriant.com/lbr-api/metrics gets live tenant/customer counts by status, total stored bytes (growth trend over time via repeated scrapes), and infra headroom (PG connection saturation, Redis memory) — competitive intelligence plus attacker recon (watch pg_connections climb to time a connection-exhaustion DoS). The misleading comment makes an operator believe it is protected.
fix: Gate the API /metrics route behind an internal-only guard / shared-secret header check, OR have Caddy explicitly block `/lbr-api/metrics` (and `/lbr-api/healthz|readyz`) with a 404 so only Prometheus on the internal docker network can reach api:3001/metrics. Fix or delete the false comment at health.controller.ts:55.

title: SMTP driver has no connection/socket/greeting timeout — hung mail server stalls email workers and blocks shutdown
description: smtp-driver.ts:28 `this.transporter = nodemailer.createTransport(env.smtpUrl)` — built purely from the URL string with no `connectionTimeout`/`socketTimeout`/`greetingTimeout`/`pool` options. `send()` (line 42) awaits `this.transporter.sendMail({...})` with no per-message timeout/abort. nodemailer SMTP defaults are long (socketTimeout 600000ms, connectionTimeout 120000ms). email-worker.ts:81 runs the consumer at `concurrency: 5`. By contrast the remediation did add explicit timeouts elsewhere (Stripe client, OpenLibrary AbortController), so SMTP was missed.
impact: An SMTP incident (provider outage, blackhole, TLS stall) pins all 5 email-worker job slots for minutes each, halting all outbound mail (password resets, hold-ready, overdue). During shutdown, email-worker.stop()→worker.close() (email-worker.ts:97-100) waits for these stuck in-flight sends; combined with REL-03 (no shutdown deadline / no stop_grace_period) a deploy hangs until Docker SIGKILL, leaving outbox rows stuck in `sending`.
fix: Pass nodemailer options to createTransport: `connectionTimeout: 10_000, greetingTimeout: 10_000, socketTimeout: 20_000` (and consider `pool: true, maxConnections`). Optionally wrap sendMail in a Promise.race against an abort so one send can never exceed a hard ceiling.
skepticReasoning:
CONFIRMED. I read the real code and the mitigating layers (BullMQ worker internals, shutdown path) and a concrete failure path genuinely exists.

PREMISE VERIFIED:
- apps/api/src/email/drivers/smtp-driver.ts:28 — `this.transporter = nodemailer.createTransport(env.smtpUrl)`. The transport is built from the URL string ONLY; there is no options object, so no connectionTimeout/socketTimeout/greetingTimeout/pool. A repo-wide grep for those keys returns zero matches outside node_modules.
- send() (smtp-driver.ts:42-49) plainly `await this.transporter.sendMail({...})` with no Promise.race/AbortController/per-message ceiling.
- nodemailer pinned at 8.0.9; its SMTP defaults are long: CONNECTION_TIMEOUT 120000ms, SOCKET_TIMEOUT 600000ms (10 min), GREETING_TIMEOUT 30000ms (node_modules/.pnpm/nodemailer@8.0.9/.../smtp-connection/index.js:14-16).
- email-worker.ts:81 runs the consumer at `concurrency: 5`.

MITIGATIONS CHECKED AND DISPROVED:
- BullMQ does NOT abort a hung job handler. Worker defaults (worker.js:34) are lockDuration:30000 / stalledInterval:30000 / maxStalledCount:1 — these only govern lock renewal and *stalled-job re-queue detection*, they do not cancel the running `await driver.send()` promise. No per-job execution timeout is configured. So a hung send keeps inFlight++ (email-worker.ts:73) and holds its slot for the full nodemailer timeout window.
- Shutdown has no deadline. worker.ts:175-207 `shutdown()` does `await Promise.all([... emailWorker.stop() ...])` then `process.exit(0)`. email-worker.ts:97-100 stop() = `await worker.close()` (default force=false). BullMQ close(false) calls `whenCurrentJobsFinished(false)` (worker.js:761,778) which BLOCKS until in-flight jobs finish. A hung sendMail therefore blocks close → blocks Promise.all → blocks process.exit. There is no overall timeout racing the Promise.all, so the deploy hangs until the orchestrator SIGKILLs the container.

CONSEQUENCE: During an SMTP incident (provider outage, blackhole that accepts SYN then stalls, TLS handshake stall, LB holding the socket), each of the 5 worker slots is pinned for the relevant nodemailer timeout — up to ~2 min (connectionTimeout) or ~10 min (socketTimeout) per stuck send — collapsing all outbound mail throughput (password resets, hold-ready, due-soon, overdue). A redeploy during that window hangs to SIGKILL, and any rows flipped to `status:'sending'` (email-worker.ts:117-120) before the SIGKILL are left stuck in `sending` with no recovery sweep visible in processOne.

HONEST SEVERITY CALIBRATION: This is availability/reliability, not data-loss or security/cross-tenant — so not critical. But it pins ALL email throughput during a dependency incident and turns a routine deploy into a hung-until-SIGKILL event with orphaned `sending` rows. The remediation explicitly added timeouts to the Stripe client and an AbortController to OpenLibrary, so SMTP being left on multi-minute defaults is a genuine gap, not an intentional design choice. High is the right level.
exploit:
Repro (no attacker needed — any SMTP dependency incident):
1. Point SMTP_URL at a host that accepts the TCP connection then stalls (e.g. a blackhole: `iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 25 -j DROP` after SYN, or a netcat that connects but never sends the 220 greeting / never ACKs DATA). A real-world equivalent is a provider outage or LB holding the socket open.
2. Enqueue >5 emails. All 5 email-worker slots enter `await this.transporter.sendMail(...)` and block. Because greetingTimeout is 30s but socketTimeout is 600000ms, a stall mid-conversation (after greeting, during DATA) holds each slot up to 10 minutes. inFlight() stays at 5; no further mail is processed.
3. While stuck, send SIGTERM (simulating a deploy). worker.ts shutdown() awaits Promise.all([emailWorker.stop()...]); emailWorker.stop() → worker.close(false) → whenCurrentJobsFinished(false) blocks on the 5 hung sends. process.exit(0) never runs. The container hangs until the orchestrator's SIGKILL. Any outbox rows already flipped to status:'sending' (email-worker.ts:119) are orphaned.

Fix: pass options to createTransport, e.g. `nodemailer.createTransport(env.smtpUrl, { connectionTimeout: 10_000, greetingTimeout: 10_000, socketTimeout: 20_000 })` (optionally pool:true,maxConnections); and add an overall shutdown deadline in worker.ts (race the Promise.all against a setTimeout before process.exit) so a stuck send can never block a deploy past N seconds.

title: Worker graceful shutdown has no deadline; container healthcheck probes /healthz (always-200) not /readyz; no stop_grace_period
description: worker.ts:175-207 shutdown(): `server.close()` then `await Promise.all([...stop()])` with NO overall timeout, then `await wait(1000)`, then `process.exit(0)`. Each worker's stop() does `worker.close()` (BullMQ graceful: waits for the active job). Import/maintenance/export run heavy jobs (full-DB export+zip, VACUUM, migrations). docker-compose.prod.yml worker service (lines 209-237) sets NO `stop_grace_period`, so Docker's default 10s elapses → SIGKILL mid-job. (2) Worker healthcheck (line 233) probes `/healthz`, which in worker.ts:53-71 returns 200 whenever `!shuttingDown` regardless of whether BullMQ workers attached; `/readyz` (lines 72-84) is the one that checks worker handles but nothing probes it. The five start promises only `console.error` on failure (worker.ts:127-173), so a worker that never connected stays `/healthz`-green forever.
impact: Deploys/restarts hard-kill in-flight imports/exports/maintenance, leaving inconsistent batch rows + orphaned staged files. A worker that fails to attach to Redis reports healthy forever, is never restarted, and silently drains nothing (emails, sweeps, hold-ready notifications all stop) with no alert.
fix: Point the worker healthcheck at `/readyz`; add `stop_grace_period` (e.g. 60s) to the worker service; wrap shutdown's Promise.all in Promise.race against a hard timeout before process.exit. Gate /readyz on all five workers (see REL-04) and ideally on a live Redis ping.

title: Backup/restore only cover the local Postgres container — relocated tenant DBs are silently excluded from DR
description: backup.sh:46-48 dumps ONLY the local container: `docker compose -f "$COMPOSE_FILE" -p "$COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME" exec -T postgres pg_dumpall -U libriant --clean --if-exists | gzip -9 > "$dest/postgres.sql.gz"`. The header at backup.sh:5 claims it captures `pg_dumpall of the control + every per-tenant DB`. But the architecture drives every tenant by its own db_url: tenant-migrate.ts:128 runs `prisma migrate deploy` with `env: { ...process.env, TENANT_DATABASE_URL: t.dbUrl }` per tenant, and tenant-relocate.ts:30 documents `--to-db-url='postgresql://lib:pw@cell-02.lan:5432/'` then writes it back at tenant-relocate.ts:161 `data: { dbUrl: newDbUrl, cellId: newCellId }`. fleet.yml is an explicit multi-host list (`hosts:` with a commented `CyberSystema-2` template, lines 32-39). restore.sh:83-95 only iterates tenant DBs found in the local instance (`SELECT datname FROM pg_database WHERE datname LIKE 'tenant_%'`). There is NO per-db_url / per-host dump loop anywhere in backup.sh or restore.sh. A tenant relocated to a second cell is dumped by neither.
impact: The first time a tenant is relocated off the local box (a documented, first-class operation), that library's entire DB silently drops out of the nightly backup and cannot be restored from the artifact — total silent data-loss exposure for that tenant, masked by a comment that asserts full coverage. Latent today because fleet.yml is single-cell and no relocation has occurred, hence high (conditional) rather than critical.
fix: Drive backups from the control plane: enumerate `tenants.db_url`, group by host, run `pg_dump` per database against each distinct host (mirroring tenant-migrate's fan-out) plus a separate control-DB dump. If multi-host is deferred, add a hard guard in backup.sh that queries the control DB and ABORTS non-zero when any tenant db_url host != the local Postgres host, and correct the backup.sh:5 comment to state the single-host assumption.

title: ReDoS guard is bypassable — admin-authored regex still freezes the whole API event loop
description: patternLooksCatastrophic (field-types.ts:48-59) only catches single-level nesting: `/\([^)]*[*+][^)]*\)\s*[*+]/` — `[^)]*` cannot cross a nested `)`, and there is no alternation or `{n,m}{n,m}` check. I ran the exact heuristic from source against the reviewer's patterns: `(([a-z])+)+`, `^(([a-z])+.)+[A-Z]([a-z])+$`, `(a|a)*`, `(a|ab)*`, `((ab)*)*`, `a{1,1000}{1,1000}` ALL return false (allowed); only flat `(a+)+`/`(.*)*`/`(a+)*` are caught. I then ran `/^(([a-z])+.)+[A-Z]([a-z])+$/.test('a'.repeat(40))` in Node: pattern length 27 (passes save guard at field-definitions.service.ts:127 and match guard at field-types.ts:139), input 40 chars (far below REGEX_INPUT_CAP=4000) — the call blocked the process for 10,814 ms. validateField runs synchronously on the request path via loadActiveForValidation in books/members/copies/loans/reservations services and collection records.
impact: A tenant admin saves a benign-looking <200-char pattern that passes both save-time and match-time heuristics, then every matching record write freezes the single-threaded Node event loop for ~10s+ (longer with longer input up to the 4000 cap), stalling the shared API for ALL tenants on the instance. The 'fixed' ReDoS critical remains exploitable with cross-tenant blast radius. WORSE for collection fields: collections.service.ts createField/updateField never call patternLooksCatastrophic or even RegExp() at save time (no save-time guard at all — verified grep shows no pattern check), so the only defense for collection-record validation is the same bypassable match-time heuristic.
fix: Do not rely on a regex heuristic. Run admin-authored regex in a worker thread with a hard wall-clock timeout, or use a linear-time engine (node-re2) for admin patterns. At minimum, extend the heuristic to reject any quantified group containing a quantifier at ANY nesting depth and any alternation inside a quantified group and `{n,m}{n,m}`, treat uncertain patterns as rejected, and add the bypass patterns above as regression tests. Also add the save-time guard to collections.service.ts createField/updateField, which currently has none.

title: Collection fields never reject a catastrophic/invalid regex pattern at save time (no save-time ReDoS or compile guard)
description: Built-in entity fields validate validationJson.pattern at save time in field-definitions.service.ts:125-137 (rejects patternLooksCatastrophic AND non-compiling patterns). The parallel collection-field path does NOT: collections.service.ts createField (227-307) and updateField (309-349) only call validateOptions for select types and persist validationJson directly (lines 285,300,339) with no patternLooksCatastrophic check and no `new RegExp(pattern)` compile check. So an admin can persist a catastrophic OR syntactically-invalid regex on a collection field. The only runtime defense for collection-record writes is the same match-time heuristic in field-types.ts:139 that REM-1 proves is bypassable, and an invalid (non-compiling) pattern is silently caught at match time (field-types.ts:151) turning every collection-record write into a confusing 400.
impact: Combined with REM-1, collection records are even more exposed than built-in entities: a catastrophic pattern that the heuristic WOULD catch still persists (only rejected at match time), and a bypass pattern freezes the shared event loop on every collection-record write. A non-compiling pattern bricks all writes to that collection with an opaque 'invalid pattern' error.
fix: Apply the same save-time guard used in field-definitions.service.ts:125-137 (reject patternLooksCatastrophic + reject non-compiling RegExp) inside collections.service.ts createField and updateField before persisting validationJson, and prefer a worker-thread/RE2 execution model per REM-1.

title: `print --format env` dumps all plaintext secrets with no --reveal, no --yes, no confirmation (masking bypass)
description: The print handler gates table behind a reveal-confirm (1129-1130 `if (reveal && !values.yes && stdin.isTTY)`), pwmanager behind `--reveal` (1132-1136), and printJson masks unless reveal (1226). But the env branch is unconditional: lines 1140-1141 `else if (fmt === 'env') { for (const l of model.lines) console.log(l.raw); }` — no reveal/yes/TTY check. The env format is undocumented: the usage header (30-38) and print examples only mention table/pwmanager/json.
impact: `pnpm secrets print --format env` prints every raw line — SESSION_SECRET, ADMIN_SESSION_SECRET, MFA_MASTER_KEY, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, STRIPE_API_KEY, SMTP_URL — in cleartext to stdout in any context (CI, redirect, scrollback, shell history), contradicting the tool's masked-unless-revealed contract.
fix: Gate `--format env` behind the same `--reveal (+ --yes/confirm)` path as the other reveal-capable formats, or remove it.

title: ./.env.prod (the tool's default target) and the .tmp-<pid> write files are NOT gitignored — plaintext secrets can be committed
description: Verified with git: `git check-ignore .env.prod` → exit 1 (NOT IGNORED); `git check-ignore .env.prod.tmp-123` → exit 1 (NOT IGNORED); whereas `git check-ignore .env.local` → IGNORED. .gitignore covers `.env`, `.env.local`, `.env.*.local` but not `.env.prod`. resolveDefaultFile() probes `./.env.prod` (secrets.ts:1097), `--dev` targets `./.env.local` (1203), the repo ships `.env.prod.example`, and saveModel writes a transient `${model.path}.tmp-${process.pid}` (secrets.ts:544) which is likewise untracked-but-not-ignored. The `pnpm secrets` script exists (package.json:37 `"secrets": "tsx scripts/secrets.ts"`).
impact: An operator running `pnpm secrets` in a checkout produces a real plaintext `.env.prod` that `git add .` stages and a commit/push publishes — leaking every production credential. A crash between write and rename leaves a `.tmp-<pid>` plaintext file equally uncovered.
fix: Add `.env.prod`, `.env.prod.tmp-*`, and `*.tmp-[0-9]*` to .gitignore. Optionally have saveModel refuse to write inside a git work tree unless forced.

title: Manually-set POSTGRES_PASSWORD has no URL-safety validation; isBareword accepts @ : / which corrupt or crash the DB connection URL
description: POSTGRES_PASSWORD def has NO `validate` (secrets.ts:171-188, unlike MFA_MASTER_KEY at 165). isBareword (519) is `/^[A-Za-z0-9_.:/@%+=-]*$/` — verified it accepts `a/b`, `p@ssword`, `pa:ss` (all true). The value is interpolated into `postgresql://libriant:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@postgres:5432/...` (docker-compose.prod.yml:36,71) and parsed with `new URL(this.env.pgSuperuserUrl)` at tenant-provisioning.service.ts:106 (urlForDb) — also used in createDatabase/teardown (84,112). Verified: `new URL('postgresql://libriant:a/b@postgres:5432/...')` THROWS 'Invalid URL'. A subtler case: `p@host` (single trailing @) misparses — password becomes 'p', host becomes 'host' (verified). `p@ssword`/`pa:ss` percent-encode in u.password (p%40ssword / pa%3Ass) which Postgres receives wrong. Manual `set`/interactive paths only run serializeKV's single-quote check, not URL safety.
impact: An operator overriding POSTGRES_PASSWORD with `/` (or a trailing `@`) writes a value the tool calls valid, which then throws 'Invalid URL' inside tenant provisioning (every new-tenant DB create/teardown fails) or misparses the connection string (auth fails / wrong host) — a hard-to-diagnose outage. Note severity is bounded by this being a manual-override-only path (auto-gen is pure URL-safe hex).
fix: Add a `validate` to POSTGRES_PASSWORD rejecting any non-URL-userinfo-safe char (or require the generated hex shape). Apply the same URL-safety check to SMTP_URL credentials embedded in the URL.

title: Mobile nav drawer has no focus trap, no focus management, and background is not inert
description: The drawer is a plain `<aside id="lbr-tenant-sidebar" className={`lbr-shell__sidebar${menuOpen ? ' is-open' : ''}`}>` (SidebarNav.tsx:135; AdminSidebar.tsx:109). It carries NO role="dialog" and NO aria-modal — a source-wide grep for `aria-modal|role="dialog"|inert` returns zero hits anywhere in apps/web or packages/ui/src. The only on-open behavior is the effect at SidebarNav.tsx:55-67 / AdminSidebar.tsx:26-38, which adds an Escape keydown listener and sets `document.body.style.overflow='hidden'` — it never moves focus into the drawer, never traps Tab, and never restores focus to the hamburger on close. The shell's `<main className="lbr-shell__main">` (layout.tsx:179) is a sibling of the sidebar and is never marked inert/aria-hidden when the drawer opens. Meanwhile the drawer IS visually modal: a `.lbr-shell__scrim` with `background: rgba(15,23,42,0.5)` (styles.css:638) and scroll lock cover the page. HelpDrawer.tsx:15-46 deliberately uses a native `<dialog>`+`showModal()` precisely to get focus trap, Esc, and focus-return for free, so this is a regression from the codebase's own established accessible pattern, applied to the PRIMARY mobile navigation.
impact: On narrow/mobile viewports a keyboard or screen-reader user can Tab straight out of the visually-modal, scroll-locked drawer into hidden background content (which remains in the DOM and focusable), and focus is not returned to the trigger on close. WCAG 2.4.3 (Focus Order) and 4.1.2/1.3.1 failures on the app's main navigation.
fix: Reuse the native-<dialog>/showModal() pattern from HelpDrawer.tsx for the nav drawer (free focus trap + Esc + focus return), or add explicit management: on open move focus to the first nav link and trap Tab/Shift+Tab within the aside, set role="dialog" aria-modal="true", mark the rest of the shell inert/aria-hidden while open, and restore focus to the hamburger on close.

title: Hard-deleting a tenant does not invalidate the TenantResolver Redis cache or evict the per-tenant Prisma client
description: remove() (admin-tenants.controller.ts:171-181) calls provisioning.teardown, purgeStorage, `controlDb.tenant.delete`, then ONLY `this.effectivePlan.invalidate(tenant.id)`. It never calls resolver.invalidate(...) nor tenantPrisma.forget(...). The controller's constructor (lines 41-44) injects only TenantProvisioningService + EffectivePlanService — neither TenantResolverService nor TenantPrismaService is injected, so it structurally cannot bust those caches. The resolver caches the FULL TenantContext including `status` and `dbUrl` (tenantSelect at tenant-resolver.service.ts:117-127, written for `this.ttlSec` = tenantCacheTtlSec default 300s, env.ts:162). `forget()` exists (tenant-prisma.service.ts:79) but a grep shows NO production call site anywhere. The established discipline is proven elsewhere: admin-tenant-tags.controller.ts:72 and scripts/tenant-relocate.ts:177 both bust the resolver cache after a tenant-row change; hard-delete is the one mutation that skips it.
impact: For up to 5 minutes after an irreversible hard-delete, TenantMiddleware resolves the slug to a stale `active` context (tenant.middleware.ts:67-84), a still-valid session passes TenantGuard, and services call getClient(ctx) against the DROPped DB — connection-error 500s instead of a clean 404/410. The dead Prisma client (pointing at a dropped database) lingers in the LRU until its 30-min idle TTL, holding broken connections. No cross-tenant data exposure (cuid DB names aren't reused), but a real correctness/availability + resource-leak gap.
fix: Inject TenantResolverService + TenantPrismaService into AdminTenantsController and, after deleting the control row, call `await resolver.invalidate({ slug: tenant.slug, customSubdomain: tenant.customSubdomain })` and `tenantPrisma.forget(tenant.id)`. The Redis DEL covers all API processes; for the in-process Prisma LRU, the multi-process case still relies on idle eviction unless a forget pub/sub is added. Mirror the resolver DEL in the CLI teardown path.

title: Login lockout bypass via concurrent requests (non-atomic failedLogins read-modify-write)
description: login() selects user.failedLogins once at the top (login.service.ts:84) and passes that snapshot to recordFailure (line 107), which writes an ABSOLUTE value `failedLogins: nextCount` where nextCount = currentFailed+1 (lines 161,166) — not Prisma's `{ increment: 1 }`. Concurrent failed attempts all read the same stale count and all write the same value (lost updates). admin-auth.service.ts:62-71 has the identical pattern (`nextAttempts = admin.failedAttempts + 1` then a plain set).
impact: A burst of N parallel wrong-password guesses advances the counter by only 1, so the lockout never trips from concurrency. Effective guesses are then bounded only by the per-IP cap (20/5min) rather than maxFailedLogins (5), materially weakening brute-force / credential-stuffing defense. Bounded blast radius (the per-IP limiter still applies), hence medium.
fix: Use an atomic update: `data: { failedLogins: { increment: 1 } }` and read the returned row to decide locking, or perform the increment + lock decision in a single UPDATE ... RETURNING / row-locked transaction. Apply to both login.service.ts and admin-auth.service.ts.

title: Rate-limiter INCR and EXPIRE are not atomic — a stranded TTL-less key can wedge a bucket (incl. global signup)
description: hit() does `const count = await this.redis.client.incr(redisKey)` then `if (count === 1) { await this.redis.client.expire(redisKey, windowSec); }` (rate-limit.service.ts:45-48) — two separate round-trips, not a MULTI/Lua. If the process/connection dies or the expire errors after a successful first incr, the key persists with no TTL. There is no defensive re-arm when ttl == -1. The signup:global bucket is a single shared key with limit 60 (auth.controller.ts:44 RL.signupGlobal, used at line 97).
impact: A transient Redis/instance hiccup between incr and expire on the first hit leaves a TTL-less counter that never resets; for signup:global this blocks ALL platform signups until an operator manually DELs the key. Severity tempered to medium because prod Redis runs with `--maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru` + appendonly (docker-compose.prod.yml:289), so the key is not strictly immortal (LRU eviction / process exit windows exist) — but the latent self-inflicted signup outage is real and was introduced by the remediation.
fix: Make increment+expire atomic via a tiny Lua script (INCR then `if res==1 then PEXPIRE end`) or `SET key 0 EX win NX` then INCR. Defensively, when reading ttl and it is -1, re-arm EXPIRE.

title: Global signup cap is itself a cheap platform-wide signup-DoS lever
description: signup throttles on two buckets: `signup:ip:${ip}` (RL.signupPerIp = 5/600s) and a single cross-tenant `signup:global` key (RL.signupGlobal = 60/600s) (auth.controller.ts:43-44,96-97). The global key is shared by every client, so any actor spreading 60 requests across ~12 IPs (each ≤5, under the per-IP cap) saturates it and blocks every legitimate signup platform-wide for the rest of the 10-min window. No CAPTCHA/proof-of-work exists (grep for captcha|turnstile|recaptcha|hcaptcha|proof-of-work returns nothing).
impact: A modest IP pool / botnet can deny all new-customer signups platform-wide at near-zero cost — a direct onboarding/revenue outage. Compounded by AUTH-04 (a stranded global key makes it persistent). Medium: hard-reject converts an expensive provisioning DoS into a trivial blackout DoS, but only signups are affected, not existing tenants.
fix: Replace the blunt hard global counter with provisioning-side admission control (concurrency limiter/queue on DB+storage provisioning, or per-cell capacity gating). If a global cap is kept, make it advisory (shed/queue) rather than hard-reject, and require CAPTCHA/PoW before a request counts.

title: RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED env escape hatch silently disables ALL rate limits with no production guard
description: hit() returns `{ allowed: true, count: 0, retryAfterSec: 0 }` whenever `process.env.RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED === 'true'` (rate-limit.service.ts:40-42), regardless of NODE_ENV. The only references are this check and apps/api/test/integration/setup.ts:15 (`process.env.RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED ||= 'true'`). main.ts bootstrap (lines 10-11) calls loadEnv() but has no guard rejecting RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED in production (grep of main.ts for production|NODE_ENV|RATE_LIMIT returns nothing).
impact: A stray/copied env var in a prod compose or CI-promoted env file no-ops every limiter the remediation added (signup per-IP, signup global, login per-IP, password-reset per-IP/per-target, admin login, support redeem) with no boot warning or failure — re-opening the exact signup-DoS and email-bomb/brute-force vectors the remediation closed.
fix: Honor the flag only when nodeEnv !== 'production' (ideally only 'test'); log a loud warning at boot if set; refuse to boot in production if it is 'true'.

title: Password-reset token is not consumed atomically — a possessed token is usable in a concurrency race
description: complete() does `const raw = await this.redis.client.get(key)` (line 120), then `await this.passwords.hash(...)` (~250ms bcrypt, line 129), then `updateMany` (line 130), and only DELs the token at the very end (line 134). Read and delete are not atomic, so two requests presenting the same token both pass the GET and both proceed through the ~250ms+ window. The comment 'Tokens are one-time-use (DEL on success)' (line 116) overstates the guarantee.
impact: An attacker who obtains a valid reset token (referer/proxy/log leakage) can race the legitimate user to set the password, or replay the token before deletion. The single-use property does not hold under concurrency. Medium: exploitation still requires possessing a valid token, and updateMany is idempotent on the same row, but the intended guarantee is violated and bcrypt is burned twice.
fix: Claim the token atomically BEFORE doing work: use Redis GETDEL (ioredis supports it; the codebase already uses SET ... NX in mfa.service.ts:108) or a small Lua check-and-delete, and only hash+update if the claim succeeded.

title: MFA enrollment uses an in-process static Map for the pending secret — lost on restart/deploy and broken under multi-instance
description: `private static readonly pending = new Map<string, string>()` (mfa.controller.ts:39) holds the not-yet-confirmed TOTP secret between POST /admin/mfa/setup (`MfaController.pending.set(session.sub, secret)`, line 61) and POST /admin/mfa/verify (`MfaController.pending.get(session.sub)`, line 69). It is process-local heap state. docker-compose.prod.yml defines a single `api` service with no `deploy.replicas`/`scale` (grep returns none), so it works today, but any restart/redeploy between setup and verify drops the secret (verify throws 'No MFA setup in progress', line 71-73), and scaling api to >1 replica breaks enrollment non-deterministically.
impact: MFA enrollment — the prerequisite for the support-redeem hard-MFA rule (admin-support.controller.ts:101) and any future mandatory-MFA gate (AUTH-06) — is fragile: silently fails after deploys and as soon as the API is horizontally scaled, with a confusing error and no clear remediation.
fix: Store the pending secret in Redis keyed by admin id with a short TTL (~10 min) — the shared-state pattern already used by RateLimitService and MfaService.verifyTokenOnce. Remove the static Map.

title: Staff temp passwords are 4-digit numeric (≈13 bits) on predictable usernames — brute-forceable pre-first-login credential
description: Both staff create() and resetPassword() generate the initial/reset password as `String(randomInt(1000, 10000))` — a 4-digit PIN with only 9000 possible values (~13 bits of entropy) (staff.service.ts:49 and :100). The account is created with status:'active' and mustChangeCredentials:true, but it is fully usable for /auth/login with that PIN until the holder voluntarily completes setup. Usernames are sequential and predictable (`staff_N`, generated by nextUsername, see staff.service.ts:79,83), and login accepts username as the identifier (login.service.ts:75). So an unauthenticated attacker who knows the tenant slug can target staff_1, staff_2, ... and brute-force a 4-digit PIN.
impact: 9000-value keyspace is well within reach of an online attack: the per-IP login cap is 20/5min (auth.controller.ts:45) and account lockout is 5/15min, but lockout self-resets and is further weakened by the AUTH-03 concurrency race; an attacker rotating across staff_N accounts and IPs can plausibly land a staff login (librarian/volunteer role) on a tenant. Worse, the one-time PIN is displayed to the admin to hand over out-of-band, so any shoulder-surf/screenshot/log leak before first login is trivially replayable. This grants tenant-scoped staff access (catalog/circulation actions).
fix: Generate a high-entropy temporary password (e.g. crypto.randomBytes → 10+ char base32, or a 6-8 word passphrase) instead of a 4-digit PIN. If a short human-typable code is a UX requirement, pair it with a short server-side TTL and a strict per-account attempt cap that does not self-reset, and force the change before any other action is permitted.

title: Password brute-force lockout counter reset before the MFA check — failed-TOTP logins never lock and reset the counter on every password-correct attempt
description: On password success `verify()` immediately runs `controlDb.adminUser.update({ data: { failedAttempts: 0, lockedUntil: null, status: 'active', lastLoginAt: new Date() } })` and returns (admin-auth.service.ts:80-91). The MFA/TOTP gate runs only afterward in the controller (admin-auth.controller.ts:88-106), and a cookie is issued only past it (line 108). So a caller with the correct password but wrong/absent TOTP resets the per-account counter every time, so the `maxFailedLogins` lockout (admin-auth.service.ts:62-71) can never accumulate against TOTP guessing; and `lastLoginAt` is stamped + any prior lockout cleared on an incomplete login where no session is issued. TOTP guessing is still bounded by `verifyTokenOnce` single-use burn (mfa.service.ts:103-114) and the coarse 20/300s/IP edge limiter (admin-auth.controller.ts:54,72-82), but the per-account permanent-lockout invariant is defeated for the second factor.
impact: Defeats the per-account brute-force lockout for the MFA second factor whenever the password is known/guessed, and corrupts lastLoginAt/lockout audit state on incomplete logins. Lowers the cost of online TOTP brute force and weakens the permanent-lockout remediation. Medium because the IP edge limiter and 6-digit single-use TOTP still make online guessing slow.
fix: Only reset counters / stamp lastLoginAt / clear lockout AFTER the full login (password AND, when enabled, TOTP) succeeds. Treat a wrong TOTP as a failed attempt that increments `failedAttempts` and can trip the lockout, exactly like a wrong password.

title: Support-key redemption is a check-then-act race — two concurrent redeems of the same code both pass verification
description: `verifyAndConsume` only READS pending candidates and bcrypt-compares; it never marks the key consumed (support-key.service.ts:140-147). The key flip to 'redeemed' happens later in a separate `open` transaction via `tx.supportKey.update({ where: { id: input.keyId }, data: { status:'redeemed', ... } })` — an UNCONDITIONAL update with no `status:'pending'` guard (support-session.service.ts:55-64). Two near-simultaneous redeems of the same code each pass verify (both see pending) and both reach `open`. The orphan-cleanup `updateMany({ where: { endedAt:null, OR:[tenantId, adminId] } })` (support-session.service.ts:38-41) runs at the top of each transaction; under concurrent execution both updateMany calls can run before either `create`, so neither sees the other's row and both sessions are created. The two `recordAttempt`/notification side effects in the controller also fire twice.
impact: The 'single-use support key' invariant is not enforced under concurrency: one code can mint more than one SupportSession and is logged/notified as two events. Blast radius limited (still needs the plaintext code + each redeemer's own MFA), but it breaks a stated security invariant and can spawn a duplicate/orphaned session.
fix: Make consumption atomic inside the `open` transaction: `const c = await tx.supportKey.updateMany({ where: { id: keyId, status: 'pending' }, data: { status: 'redeemed', ... } }); if (c.count === 0) throw ...` so the race loser fails cleanly. Or fold verify+consume into one conditional transaction.

title: invoice.payment_succeeded/failed unconditionally mutate subscription status for ANY invoice on the customer (ignore subscription/status/amount)
description: handleStripeInvoicePaid (533-540) only does `findFirst({where:{stripeCustomerId: payload.customer}})` then `recordPaymentSuccess(tenantId)`, which blindly runs `subscription.update ... data: { status: 'active', graceUntil: null }` (419-422). It never reads `payload.subscription`, `payload.status`, or `payload.amount_paid` — all present on StripeInvoiceShape (stripe-driver.ts:80-82). Mirror: handleStripeInvoiceFailed (542-548) → recordPaymentFailure (406-414) arms `status:'past_due', graceUntil: now+N` for ANY failed invoice on the customer (incl. one-off/unrelated). Out-of-order or sweep-retried delivery of an old payment_succeeded after handleStripeSubscriptionDeleted (516-529, which sets status:'canceled', planId:starter, stripeSubscriptionId:null) flips status back to 'active' on the free plan.
impact: Subscription.status can disagree with reality: 'active' label on a canceled/free plan with null stripeSubscriptionId, or 'past_due'+grace from an unrelated/one-off invoice. Blast radius is bounded because EffectivePlanService (effective-plan.service.ts:148-159) keys feature access off planId + (status IN active/trialing OR past_due within grace) — after a deletion the planId is already 'starter', so features resolve to Starter not the old paid plan. But the mirror failed-invoice path can ARM a fresh grace window (now+N days) on a tenant who should have no access, granting unearned paid-feature time, and snapshot/admin status views become unreliable.
fix: In handleStripeInvoicePaid/Failed, skip when `payload.subscription` is null and when the local row's stripeSubscriptionId is null or differs from `payload.subscription`. Drive status from customer.subscription.updated events; treat invoice events only as grace-window signals for the subscription they actually belong to.

title: Grace window is re-armed to now+N days on every past_due redelivery, letting a perpetually-failing card keep paid features far beyond the intended grace period
description: syncStripeSubscription's past_due branch sets `graceUntil: localStatus === 'past_due' ? new Date(Date.now() + loadEnv().billingGracePeriodDays * MS_PER_DAY) : null` (lines 488-491). Stripe emits a `customer.subscription.updated` event on each dunning/retry cycle while a subscription stays `past_due`. Because graceUntil is recomputed as `now + N days` on EVERY such delivery (rather than anchored to the FIRST failure or to the invoice's period end), each redelivery slides the grace deadline forward another full N days. EffectivePlanService (effective-plan.service.ts:158) grants full paid-plan feature access for any `status='past_due' AND graceUntil > NOW()`. recordPaymentFailure (line 408) has the same now-relative recompute. There are no tests covering grace behavior (no matches for graceUntil/grace in billing/*.spec.ts or jobs/*.spec.ts).
impact: A tenant whose card keeps declining receives a fresh N-day grace window on each Stripe dunning retry, so they retain paid features indefinitely instead of for a single N-day window. Combined with BILL-2 (handleStripeInvoiceFailed also re-arming grace for any failed invoice on the customer), the intended hard grace cutoff effectively never fires for a chronically-failing payer. Real revenue/access leakage, bounded blast radius (per-tenant, paid-feature access only).
fix: Anchor graceUntil to the first failure, not 'now': only set it when transitioning into past_due (e.g. `graceUntil ??= now + N days`, or compute from the invoice's `period_end`/first-failure timestamp). Skip re-arming when the row is already past_due with a graceUntil in the future. Add tests for repeated past_due deliveries.

title: storageMaxUploadBytes is Number()-parsed with no finite guard — the claimed 'NaN-disables-limit fix' does not exist; a misconfigured env var disables/breaks the upload size cap
description: env.ts:214: `storageMaxUploadBytes: Number(optional('STORAGE_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES', String(25 * 1024 * 1024)))` — no Number.isFinite/isNaN guard. `git show 151f579 --name-only` confirms env.ts was NOT in the remediation commit ('NO env.ts in commit 151f579'). The value feeds FileInterceptor limits in 4 live controllers (storage-demo.controller.ts:66, branding.controller.ts:55, covers.controller.ts:39, photos.controller.ts:39). Verified busboy@1.6.0 multipart.js:254-256 gates on `typeof limits.fileSize === 'number'` (NaN passes, so fileSizeLimit=NaN) and enforces via `if (fileSize === fileSizeLimit)` at line 476 (NaN never equals NaN → cap never fires). Verified multer@2.1.1 index.js:17 defaults to `memoryStorage()` (no dest/storage configured anywhere — grep found none), so the whole body buffers into RAM. On the installed Node v26.0.0 I confirmed `Buffer.allocUnsafe(NaN)` throws `RangeError: ... Received NaN` (busboy multipart.js:469 hits this when isDataSafe is false), so the practical outcome here is broken uploads (500); on the isDataSafe=true branch (`data.slice(start, NaN)`) the cap is silently disabled instead.
impact: A single non-numeric env typo (e.g. STORAGE_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES=25MB) either silently removes the per-request upload ceiling (unbounded in-memory buffering → memory-exhaustion DoS) or breaks every upload with an opaque 500 — with no boot-time signal because env loads without validation.
fix: Validate at boot: `const n = Number(...); if (!Number.isFinite(n) || n <= 0) throw new Error('STORAGE_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES must be a positive integer of bytes')`. Apply the same finite-positive (and Number.isInteger) guard to the other Number(optional(...)) limit values.

title: Per-plan storage quota check is a read-then-write TOCTOU race — concurrent uploads evade max_storage_mb
description: put() reads usage via `currentUsedBytes` (line 68 → findUnique select at lines 174-179), compares `currentBytes + newSize > limitBytes` (line 70), writes the file (line 87), then increments via `{ increment: stored.sizeBytes }` (lines 92-96) — three separate statements with NO `$transaction`, advisory lock, FOR UPDATE, or conditional update (grep of storage.service.ts confirms none). All 4 callers (branding/covers/photos/storage-demo controllers) call put() without any wrapping tx. The Prisma increment is atomic but the DECISION at line 70 is not serialized with it, so N concurrent uploads near the limit each read the same pre-write currentBytes, each pass, each write + increment. QuotaInterceptor is NOT on any storage route (it's only on books/members/staff entity-count routes) — confirmed via grep, so there is no second enforcement layer.
impact: A tenant can exceed paid storage by up to (concurrency × per-request bytes) via parallel uploads; the plan storage limit is advisory under concurrency. Bounded blast radius but real resource/money leakage.
fix: Make the reservation atomic: conditional UPDATE `SET storageUsedBytes = storageUsedBytes + $bytes WHERE id = $id AND storageUsedBytes + $bytes <= $limitBytes`, reject if 0 rows updated; write to disk only after the counter reservation succeeds and roll the counter back if the disk write fails.

title: Authenticated storage download/signed-url endpoints have no role guard — but more importantly the whole StorageDemoController exposes per-ref CRUD with only tenant-membership checks
description: Beyond the destructive routes in STG-01, the GET download (lines 88-101) and GET signed-url (lines 115-138) handlers are also only `@UseGuards(TenantGuard)` with no `@Roles`. Any tenant staff (volunteer included) can mint a signed download URL for ANY ref including `members/<photo>` and `attachments/<file>` and `branding/<logo>` by guessing/enumerating refs, then share that public `/_files/signed?token=...` URL externally (the token IS the bearer, no further auth). Combined with the fact that refs are predictable-ish (`covers/<cuid>.jpg`) and the signed endpoint is fully public, this widens the read surface: a low-privilege staff member can exfiltrate member PII photos and attachments and hand out long-lived (up to 24h) public links. This is a read-side analogue of STG-01 that the original finding set did not call out.
impact: Low-privilege staff can generate publicly-shareable signed URLs (up to 24h TTL) for member photos / attachments / branding of their own tenant, enabling PII exfiltration outside the app's auth boundary.
fix: Gate signed-url minting (and ideally download) behind at least `@Roles('owner','admin','librarian')`, and consider scoping which resourceTypes a given role may mint links for (e.g. block volunteers from members/attachments). Keep signed-URL TTLs short for sensitive resource types.

title: Crashed/killed import is permanently stuck in committing/validating — undeletable, un-restartable, staging leaked; promised recovery sweep does not exist
description: Confirmed NO import recovery sweep exists: jobs/registry.ts:22-71 lists 8 scheduled jobs (support-session-expiry, reservation-pickup-expiry, stripe-webhook-retry, fine-accrual, export-file-cleanup, announcement-publish, book-metadata-refresh, member-notifications) — none reconcile stuck import batches; worker.ts:148 only calls startImportWorker. BullMQ is attempts:1 (import-queue.service.ts:35), so a crashed job is not re-run. A stuck 'committing' batch is rejected by requireRunnable (import.service.ts:322 `if (!['uploaded','validated'].includes(batch.status))`) so it cannot be re-run/remapped. HOWEVER the finding's core 'undeletable + staging leaked + manual DB surgery' claim is FALSE: cancel() (import.service.ts:215-220) has NO status guard and unconditionally flips ANY batch to 'canceled'; remove() (import.service.ts:227-230) only blocks 'validating'/'committing' and then calls deleteStaged(batch.stagingPath). So the operator can cancel-then-delete a stuck batch entirely through the API, clearing the staging file — no DB surgery needed.
impact: After a worker crash a batch is stuck in 'committing'/'validating' and cannot be re-run or remapped, and there is no automatic reconciliation, so the UI shows a perpetually 'running' import until an operator manually cancels+deletes it. Partially-written rows from a half-done commit remain in the tenant DB. Real availability/UX gap, but recoverable via the existing cancel→delete path; not a permanent stuck/undeletable outage.
fix: Add a startup/periodic sweep that resets 'validating'/'committing' batches with no live BullMQ job (or past a TTL) to 'failed' and clears staging, as the worker docstring (import-worker.ts:11-12) already promises; allow re-run after that reset.

title: errors.csv export omits spreadsheet formula-injection neutralization applied everywhere else
description: csvCell (import.service.ts:383-386) does ONLY RFC-4180 quoting: `if (/[",\r\n]/.test(value)) return ...; return value;` — no leading =,+,-,@,tab/CR neutralization. The sibling export pipeline DOES neutralize: export-processors.ts neutralizeFormula `/^[=+\-@\t\r]/.test(s) ? `'${s}` : s` applied inside toCsv esc(). The errors.csv rows (import.service.ts:209) emit r.field, r.code and r.message; r.message embeds raw uploaded cell content via transforms (transforms.ts:48 `not a yes/no value: "${raw}"`, :147 `unrecognized date: "${raw}"`, :178 `not a valid ISBN-13: "${raw}"`) and the field/code columns are largely fixed labels. The label prefix (row-mapper.ts: `${def.label}: ${result.reason}.`) blunts message payloads, but a raw value carrying a leading delimiter still surfaces, and crafted multi-line/raw content can yield a cell starting with =,+,-,@.
impact: A librarian opening import-errors.csv in Excel/Sheets can be exposed to attacker-influenced formula content — the same injection class the remediation explicitly closed on data exports but missed on the import errors.csv path. Lower likelihood than a raw data export due to the label prefix, but the gap is real.
fix: Reuse export-processors' neutralizeFormula inside csvCell (import.service.ts:383): apostrophe-prefix any cell whose first char is = + - @ tab or CR before RFC-4180 quoting.

title: Authors find-or-created outside the book write transaction → orphan author rows on row failure
description: writeBook resolves authors BEFORE writing the book: import-engine.ts:289 `for (const name of authorNames) authorIds.push(await this.findOrCreateAuthor(name))`, and findOrCreateAuthor creates rows on the bare client (import-engine.ts:643-648 `await this.ctx.client.author.create(...)`, then caches at :647) — NOT inside the book's $transaction (existing-book tx at :319-327) or the new-book create (:330-336). processRow catches a book-write failure (import-engine.ts:166-170) and yields 'error', but the already-created Author rows are not rolled back and stay cached for reuse. writeBook only runs at commit time (commitBook returns before writeBook when dryRun, import-engine.ts:273), so this is a commit-time corruption, not a validate-time one.
impact: A dirty/partially-failing catalogue commit leaves orphan Author rows (no book) in the tenant DB that clutter author pickers/search and accumulate across re-runs. Silent data pollution, limited blast radius (no cross-tenant, no money), recoverable but never auto-cleaned.
fix: Resolve/create authors inside the same $transaction as the book write using the tx client (move findOrCreateAuthor into the transaction), so a row failure rolls back the new author; and invalidate the authorCache entry if the enclosing transaction fails.

title: Loan import bypasses the one-active-loan-per-copy invariant; no DB constraint backs it
description: commitLoan creates the loan then, for active status, blindly flips the copy: import-engine.ts:522-528 `const created = await this.ctx.client.$transaction(async (tx) => { const loan = await tx.loan.create({ data, ... }); if (status === 'active') { await tx.bookCopy.update({ where: { id: copyId }, data: { status: 'on_loan' } }); } ... })` — no check that the copy is available or that no other active loan exists. The manual path enforces this (loans.service.ts:174-183 per-member cap + loans.service.ts:186 expectedCopyStatus requiring 'available'). The tenant schema Loan model has only `@@index([copyId])` and `@@index([memberId, status])` (schema.prisma:381-382) — no partial unique index on (copyId) WHERE status='active'. So two active loan rows for one barcode, or an active loan against a copy already on loan to another member, both succeed.
impact: A migration can create multiple concurrent active loans for one physical copy and silently overwrite the copy's on_loan owner, corrupting circulation state (returns, holds, availability) that the rest of the app assumes is single-active. Data integrity bug confined to imports; no cross-tenant or money loss.
fix: In commitLoan, when status==='active', verify no existing active loan on the copy / that the copy is available and emit a row error otherwise; back it with a Postgres partial unique index on Loan(copyId) WHERE status='active'.

title: Upload preview tokenizes the entire file synchronously on the API event loop
description: createBatch runs in the API request and calls parseByFormat(format, input.file.buffer, { maxRows: PREVIEW_ROWS=20, ... }) (import.service.ts:48-54). For CSV that is parseDelimited→tokenize(text, delimiter) over the FULL decoded text (csv-parser.ts:131-132); tokenize (csv-parser.ts:28-90) has no maxRows early-exit and builds the entire matrix; maxRows is only honored afterward in buildTableFromMatrix (tabular.ts:69). FileInterceptor is configured with only `{ limits: { fileSize: IMPORT_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES } }` and NO storage option (import.controller.ts:70), so multer defaults to memoryStorage — the whole <=64MB upload is buffered in API RAM, then fully tokenized synchronously, blocking the Node event loop.
impact: A single large CSV upload stalls all API requests (every tenant) during synchronous tokenization, and concurrent large uploads buffer multiple 64MB blobs in the API process. Authenticated, but a low-effort way for one tenant to degrade the shared API.
fix: For preview, early-exit the tokenizer at PREVIEW_ROWS (or parse only the first N KB) instead of the whole file; consider disk-backed multer storage + streaming so the full 64MB never sits in API memory; offload large parsing to the worker.

title: readTables loads entire database into memory with no statement/connection timeout, OOMing and wedging the concurrency-1 export worker
description: readTables() opens `new PgClient({ connectionString: dbUrl })` (line 201) with NO connectionTimeoutMillis / query_timeout / statement_timeout, runs `SELECT * FROM "${name}"` (line 213) for every public table and buffers all rows (`res.rows`, line 214) into `out`. For json/xlsx/csv every table's full result set is materialized then serialized in memory (produceSingleFile lines 117-124, addTargetToArchive lines 137-155). For scope 'all', resolveTargets iterates control + every non-archived tenant DB (lines 179-187). The worker runs concurrency:1 (export-worker.ts:38) and attempts:1 (export-queue.service.ts:21). So a large DB OOMs the worker, and a hung/slow DB blocks the single SELECT forever, stalling all queued exports. The 16MB stdout sub-claim is moot because pg_dump writes to --file.
impact: An owner/admin export of a normal-sized library can OOM-kill the export worker, and a slow/hung tenant DB can deadlock the single-slot export queue platform-wide. Real but bounded to authenticated callers.
fix: Set statement_timeout + connectionTimeoutMillis on the PgClient; stream rows with a server-side cursor (pg-cursor) and write CSV/JSON incrementally to disk instead of buffering whole tables; bound total export size and defer/reject when exceeded. The 16MB maxBuffer concern is unnecessary (dump goes to --file).

title: Crashed/failed exports leak orphaned files and stick at status='running' forever; cleanup never reclaims them
description: generate() writes output to `${job.id}.zip`/`${job.id}.${format}` (lines 75,82) and temp `${jobId}-${target.label}.sql` files (line 159) that are only rm'd at lines 101-102 AFTER `archive.finalize()` + `closed` succeed — there is no try/finally, so any throw in addTargetToArchive/dumpSql/readTables leaves the temp .sql and the half-written zip on disk. The failure catch (lines 42-48) only updates the DB row to status:'failed' and never deletes partial files. filePath is set ONLY on the success branch (line 40), so failed jobs have filePath=null. export-cleanup.job.ts selects only `{ expiresAt: { lt: now }, filePath: { not: null } }` (lines 19-22) — failed jobs (filePath=null) are never swept, so their orphaned files persist forever. If the worker dies between status:'running' (line 26) and a terminal update, attempts:1 (export-queue.service.ts:21) means no retry and no stalled-job reconciler exists, so the row stays 'running' permanently and the UI shows a perpetual in-progress export.
impact: Unbounded disk growth from orphaned dump/temp/zip files on the shared storage volume; users see exports frozen at 'running' with no auto-recovery and no signal that they failed.
fix: Wrap temp-file cleanup in try/finally so it runs on the error path; in the catch block rm the partial output path(s); have the cleanup sweep also delete on-disk `${jobId}.*` for failed/stale jobs regardless of filePath and reset rows stuck in running/queued past a timeout to failed.

title: control/all-scope export dumps password hashes, encrypted TOTP secrets, per-tenant DB credentials and reset tokens to an unencrypted 24h file
description: readTables() does `SELECT * FROM "${name}"` for every public table (line 213) with no column denylist, and resolveTargets returns the control DB for scope 'control'/'all' (lines 176-187). The control schema holds User.passwordHash (schema.prisma:323), the AES-GCM TOTP cipher User.mfaSecretCipher/mfaNonce/mfaKeyId (324-327), the one-shot onboarding token (329), and TenantDbCredential.encryptedPwd (the 'Sensitive per-tenant DB role secret', 277-284). cellValue()/jsonValue() base64-encode Bytes columns, so the ciphertext is exported verbatim. These land in storageRoot/_exports as a plaintext file with EXPORT_TTL_HOURS TTL and no at-rest encryption, downloadable by an owner-admin. Note: these are bcrypt hashes / AES-GCM ciphertext (the AES key is not in the DB), and only owner-admins (platform operators) can request control/all scope (admin-export.controller.ts guarded by AdminAuthGuard) — so this is a secrets-at-rest / least-privilege concern, not direct plaintext exposure; medium leaning low.
impact: A leaked or over-broadly-shared admin export bundle exposes all user/admin password hashes (offline crackable), encrypted TOTP secrets, encrypted per-tenant DB role secrets, and onboarding tokens — material for offline attack and lateral movement, plus a PII/compliance concern.
fix: Maintain a denylist of sensitive columns/tables (passwordHash, mfaSecretCipher/nonce/keyId, *token*, TenantDbCredential.encryptedPwd, support session tokens) and redact/omit them from control-plane exports, or gate behind an explicit 'include secrets' confirmation. At minimum encrypt export artifacts at rest and shorten the TTL for control/all-scope dumps.

title: control/all SQL export passes superuser URL as pg_dump argv too (same leak as EXP-001 on the admin path)
description: For scope 'control'/'all' with format 'sql', addTargetToArchive() calls dumpSql(target.dbUrl, tmp) where target.dbUrl is env.pgSuperuserUrl itself (resolveTargets lines 176-186), again passing the full superuser connection string as a pg_dump argv element (line 194). On a non-ENOENT pg_dump failure the credential lands in job.error (lines 46,13) and is shown on GET /admin/exports via publicExportJob (admin-export.controller.ts:36). This is the same root cause as EXP-001; the exposure here is only to platform owner-admins (who already hold high trust), so it is not a privilege escalation — but it is the same un-redacted secret-in-error sink and the argv fix should cover both the tenant and control/all paths.
impact: Superuser credential can appear in admin-visible export error text on the control/all path; not a cross-tenant escalation (admin already privileged) but the same insecure pattern that must be fixed alongside EXP-001.
fix: Apply the same pg_dump fix (PG* env / PGPASSFILE, never argv) and oneLine() URL-userinfo scrubbing to all dumpSql call sites; redact job.error before persistence regardless of requester kind.

title: backup.sh / restore.sh default COMPOSE_FILE points at a non-existent path; out-of-the-box runs find no postgres service
description: backup.sh:25 and restore.sh:26 default `COMPOSE_FILE="${COMPOSE_FILE:-/srv/libriant/deploy/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml}"`. There is no `deploy/` directory in the repo (verified `ls deploy` → not found; no `*/deploy/compose*` match). The deployed layout is `/srv/libriant/app/infra/compose/...` per .github/workflows/deploy.yml:203 (`cd /srv/libriant/app`) and :215 (`-f infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml -f infra/compose/docker-compose.volume.yml`). The prod stack is split across TWO compose files (prod + volume), but the script defaults reference only one. The in-file cron comment backup.sh:14 also points at the wrong path `/srv/libriant/deploy/scripts/backup.sh`. Without an explicit override, `docker compose -f .../deploy/compose/... exec` errors 'no configuration file provided'.
impact: A backup wired using the script's own header-comment cron, or run without overriding COMPOSE_FILE, produces no backup and exits non-zero. If unmonitored, the system silently has no backups — undermining the DR posture (heartbeat/off-site warnings only help if the script can run). Mitigated for operators who follow deployment-hetzner.md:494-503 (which passes the correct COMPOSE_FILE), so it is medium, not high.
fix: Default COMPOSE_FILE to the real path (`/srv/libriant/app/infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml`) and include the volume compose file too, or auto-detect via `${LIBRIANT_APP_DIR:-/srv/libriant/app}`. Fix the cron comment at backup.sh:14.

title: tenant-relocate --drop-source host guard ignores port normalization — can permit dropping the live DB on the same server
description: The guard compares only host: line 247 `const currentHost = new URL(tenant.dbUrl).host;`, line 248 `const sourceHost = new URL(sourceUrl).host;`, line 249 `if (sourceHost === currentHost)`. Empirically verified that `postgresql://` is a NON-special URL scheme, so the default port 5432 is NOT normalized away: `new URL('postgresql://u:p@db/x').host === 'db'` but `new URL('postgresql://u:p@db:5432/x').host === 'db:5432'` — unequal for the same server. sourceUrl comes verbatim from `beforeJson.dbUrl` recorded at line 170; currentHost from `tenant.dbUrl` (= newDbUrl built via urlForDb from operator's --to-db-url). The same-host pre-check at line 97 is also string-equality (`if (newDbUrl === tenant.dbUrl)`) so it too is defeated by differing port notation. dbName is `dbNameForTenant(tenant.id)` (host-independent), so when source and current address the same server with differing :5432 notation, the guard passes and lines 267-276 run `DROP DATABASE "tenant_X"` against the server the tenant currently lives on.
impact: Residual data-loss footgun in the 'fixed' critical: under inconsistent default-port notation between recorded source and current dbUrls (common when operators omit :5432), `--drop-source --yes` can drop the tenant's live database. Narrower than the original bug (requires same server + differing port notation) but catastrophic when triggered.
fix: Canonicalize both URLs before comparing: resolve the default port (treat empty port as 5432) and compare (host, normalized-port) — and additionally refuse the drop whenever the resolved (server, dbName) tuple equals the tenant's current live (server, dbName).

title: storage-migrate.ts read_only window never auto-expires and leaks open when the post-rsync transaction fails
description: openReadOnly (lines 219-231) creates a per-tenant `read_only` SystemModeEvent with NO `endsAt` (unlike tenant-relocate, whose failure path bounds the window to +30min at tenant-relocate.ts:195-198). In storage-migrate the catch block (lines 153-156) only logs and rethrows — it neither closes the event nor sets endsAt nor busts the system-mode cache. Combined with STOR-001 (the transaction ALWAYS throws on a real run due to undeclared `toSize`), and with any genuine rsync/verify failure, the tenant is left in `read_only` indefinitely with no auto-expiry. Even on the success path, closeEvent (line 233) sets endedAt but does NOT bust the system-mode Redis cache (contrast tenant-relocate's closeEvent at lines 300-308 which calls bustSystemModeCache), so the window lingers up to the 30s cache TTL — minor on success, but the failure case is the real problem.
impact: After a failed (or, due to STOR-001, EVERY) storage migration, the tenant rejects all writes (503/maintenance) until an admin manually finds and closes the SystemModeEvent. There is no auto-expiry safety net, so an unattended migration can strand a library read-only for an unbounded time.
fix: Mirror tenant-relocate's hardening: on the catch path bound the window (`endsAt = now + 30min`) and bust the system-mode cache; or close it. Give openReadOnly an endsAt as a backstop. Make closeEvent bust the per-tenant system_mode cache key on success too.

title: Deploy gate (verify) omits integration, db-migration, and tenant-smoke tests — a broken migration ships
description: deploy.yml `verify` (lines 44-74) runs only translation/asset checks, typecheck, eslint, prettier, and `pnpm --filter @libriant/api exec vitest run --project unit` (line 74). `build: needs: verify` (line 81) — the entire deploy hangs off this one job. The real-DB jobs `integration-tests` (ci.yml:80-154, runs `--project integration` against live Postgres+Redis after `pnpm db:migrate:deploy`) and `db-migration` (ci.yml:156-271: control+tenant `prisma migrate deploy`, seed idempotency, the `1,15,5,75` row-count drift assertion at lines 238/255, and `pnpm tenant:smoke` line 268) exist ONLY in ci.yml. Both ci.yml (line 4-5 `push: branches: [main]`) and deploy.yml (lines 11-12) trigger on push to main, but deploy.yml has NO `workflow_run` dependency on ci.yml — they are independent workflows. So a migration/seed defect with green typecheck/lint/unit DEPLOYS (running the migration via the gating `migrate` service) while ci.yml separately turns red.
impact: A schema/seed/migration defect reaches production unblocked. prod-bootstrap.sh runs db:migrate:deploy as a hard prerequisite (compose migrate service, service_completed_successfully), so a bad migration can wedge the whole stack on deploy.
fix: Add the db-migration + tenant-smoke (and ideally integration) jobs to the deploy `verify` gate's prerequisites, or make deploy a `workflow_run` gated on ci.yml conclusion == success. At minimum run `db:migrate:deploy` + tenant migrate against an ephemeral Postgres inside verify.
