title: No NaN/range validation on any numeric env var, despite the "valid or fail loudly" contract
description: Every numeric is `Number(optional(...))` with no guard (env.ts: port 147, tenantCacheTtlSec 162, tenantClientCacheSize 163, tenantClientIdleMs 164, sessionTtlSec 166, adminSessionTtlSec 171, supportSessionTtlSec 189, supportKeyTtlSec 190, bcryptCost 200, maxFailedLogins 201, loginLockoutMs 202, storageSignedTtlSec 213, storageMaxUploadBytes 214, billingGracePeriodDays 240, emailMaxAttempts 255). grep for isNaN/isFinite/Number.isInteger in config+main returns nothing; no zod/joi/class-validator. The docstring lines 1-4 claim 'present + valid, or boot fails loudly.' SILENT degradations I confirmed: (1) `MAX_FAILED_LOGINS=abc` -> NaN: login.service.ts:162 `nextCount >= this.env.maxFailedLogins` is always false -> account lockout SILENTLY DISABLED (brute-force protection off); line 167 `new Date(Date.now()+NaN)` = Invalid Date. (2) `BCRYPT_COST=abc` -> NaN: I tested bcryptjs.hashSync(_, NaN) — it does NOT throw, it silently falls back to cost 10 (GENSALT_DEFAULT_LOG2_ROUNDS), downgrading hashing below the intended 12 (password.service.ts:23). (3) `STORAGE_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES=abc` -> NaN passed to multer `limits.fileSize` (branding/covers/photos/storage-demo controllers) effectively removes the upload ceiling (size comparison vs NaN is always false). Loud-failure cases exist too (TENANT_CLIENT_CACHE_SIZE=abc throws in the lru-cache constructor at tenant-prisma.service.ts:38).
impact: A typo'd security-relevant numeric env var does NOT fail at boot as the contract claims; it silently changes security behavior — lockout disabled, bcrypt cost downgraded to 10, upload size limit removed — none of which surface until exploited.
fix: Add a `num(key, fallback, {min,max})` helper that parses, asserts Number.isFinite (+ range: port 1-65535, bcryptCost 4-31, positive TTLs/limits), and throws `Missing/invalid env var: KEY` like required(). Route every Number(...) (env.ts and worker.ts:41) through it.

title: Loan renewal has no status/version CAS — concurrent renews exceed maxRenewals and double-extend dueAt
description: Confirmed. renew runs OUTSIDE any transaction (uses `client`, not `tx`): reads `loan.renewedCount` (line 556), computes `const remaining = Math.max(0, settings.maxRenewals - loan.renewedCount)` (line 573), validates `periods > remaining` (line 579), then `await client.loan.update({ where: { id: loanId }, data: { dueAt: newDueAt, renewedCount: { increment: periods } } })` (line 603-606). The update is keyed only on `id` — no `renewedCount` predicate, no advisory lock, no tx. The migration only enforces `loans_renewed_count_nonneg CHECK (renewedCount >= 0)` (20260526184041_init/migration.sql:507-509) — there is NO DB CHECK of `renewedCount <= maxRenewals` (maxRenewals is a runtime setting), so two concurrent renews both reading renewedCount=N both pass and both `increment`, landing at N+2*periods, over cap, with dueAt pushed past the ceiling. The queued-hold guard (line 588-596) is also read outside any tx, so a hold placed between check and update is missed.
impact: A loan can be renewed beyond the configured maximum and its due date pushed further than policy allows. Blast radius is a single loan acted on twice near-simultaneously (double-click, two staff stations) — real but limited.
fix: Make renew atomic: wrap in a tx with a loan/member advisory lock, or use a guarded `updateMany({ where: { id: loanId, status: 'active', renewedCount: loan.renewedCount }, data: { renewedCount: { increment: periods }, dueAt: newDueAt } })` and throw ConflictException when count===0 so the loser retries with fresh state.

title: Accrued outstanding fine is never reconciled when overdue fines are disabled before return
description: Confirmed. On return, `shouldCreateFine = settings.overdueFinesEnabled && daysOverdue > 0 && fineAmountCents > 0` (line 383). The entire fine-finalisation block — the find-existing-then-update/create that closes the accrued outstanding fine — is gated behind `if (shouldCreateFine)` (lines 478-502) with NO else branch. If an admin turns overdueFinesEnabled off after the hourly accrual sweep already created an outstanding fine (fine-accrual.job.ts:118-130), then on return shouldCreateFine is false, the block is skipped, and the stale outstanding fine stays open. The accrual job stops touching it because the loan is no longer active (fine-accrual.job.ts:99-103 re-reads loan status and `continue`s when not active). tenant-settings.service.ts update (lines 99-157) only writes the new flag + audits; it performs NO reconciliation of existing outstanding fines, and there is no separate fines/waive module to clean up. So nothing reconciles the stale charge.
impact: Members can be left owing overdue fines the library has since switched off — a billing-correctness/trust issue (not a duplicate charge). Blast radius is loans that were overdue while fines were on and returned after fines were turned off.
fix: On return, always look up the existing outstanding fine for the loan and reconcile it regardless of shouldCreateFine: when shouldCreateFine is false but an outstanding accrued fine exists, waive/zero it (or recompute to the now-correct amount) inside the same transaction. Optionally also reconcile open accrued fines when overdueFinesEnabled is toggled off in tenant-settings.

title: New ReDoS guard ships with zero test coverage
description: grep for patternLooksCatastrophic across *.spec.ts returns NONE. The only customization spec files are dynamic-validator.spec.ts and quota.service.spec.ts; there is no field-types.spec.ts. dynamic-validator.spec.ts:148-156 ('text pattern enforcement') tests only the benign `^[A-Z]{2}-\d+$`. No adversarial test asserts known-catastrophic patterns are rejected — which is exactly why the CAT-001 bypasses shipped unnoticed.
impact: A security control with no tests gives false confidence and will silently regress. Directly contributed to CAT-001 shipping broken.
fix: Add field-types.spec.ts asserting patternLooksCatastrophic(p) === true for an OWASP/real-world evil-regex corpus (incl. the CAT-001 bypasses) and false for legitimate patterns, plus integration tests that field-definition AND collection-field create+update reject them with 400.

title: Stripe retry sweep dispatches without the controller's Redis dedup lock → concurrent double-processing of the same event
description: The sweep loops rows and calls `await dispatch(billing, event)` (stripe-retry.job.ts:69) with no Redis lock — confirmed it builds Redis only for EffectivePlanService (line 54-56) and never touches `stripe:event:<id>`. The live controller guards every dispatch with `this.redis.client.set(EVENT_KEY(event.id),'1','EX',EVENT_TTL_SECONDS,'NX')` (stripe-webhook.controller.ts:90-96) and on failure `await this.redis.client.del(EVENT_KEY(event.id))` (line 120). The sweep query selects `processedAt: null` AND `OR: [{ error: { not: null } }, { receivedAt: { lt: staleBefore } }]` (stripe-retry.job.ts:42-44), so an errored row (error!=null, lock already deleted) qualifies. If Stripe re-delivers that errored event, the controller re-acquires the lock and dispatches while the sweep concurrently dispatches the same row with no lock. The stripe-retry.job.spec.ts never references the lock at all (confirmed — no `stripe:event`/SETNX/del in the spec).
impact: Two concurrent dispatches of the same billing webhook against the control DB. `recordPaymentFailure` recomputes `graceUntil = new Date(Date.now() + grace)` on each call (billing.service.ts:408), so concurrent runs drift the grace deadline; `syncStripeSubscription` double-writes planSelectedAt (billing.service.ts:497-500) and double-invalidates the plan cache. Most absolute-state fields converge, so blast radius is limited to grace-window drift + redundant churn — hence medium, not high.
fix: Have the sweep acquire the same `stripe:event:<id>` SETNX lock (with TTL) before dispatch and skip rows whose lock is held; release after. Or re-check `processedAt IS NULL` inside a control-DB transaction with a row-level `SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`-style claim so controller and sweep cannot both own the event.

title: Worker process has no unhandledRejection/uncaughtException handler — one floating rejection crashes every queue at once
description: worker.ts registers only `process.on('SIGTERM', shutdown)` and `process.on('SIGINT', shutdown)` (worker.ts:209-210). A repo-wide grep for `unhandledRejection`/`uncaughtException` in apps/api/src returns zero matches (confirmed). The process hosts five queues (email-outbox, scheduled, import, maintenance, export). Floating promises exist: TenantPrismaService `dispose` fires `entry.client.$disconnect().then().catch()` un-awaited (tenant-prisma.service.ts:44-53). On modern Node the default for an unhandled rejection is process termination, so one stray rejection takes down all five consumers with no central logging.
impact: Any single unhandled rejection kills the whole background worker — emails stop, crons stop, imports/exports/maintenance stall — until the orchestrator restarts it, and with no logged cause. Downgraded to medium: the LRU dispose path already attaches a `.catch` (tenant-prisma.service.ts:48), and the most common reject sources (BullMQ worker handlers, per-run jobs) are awaited inside try/catch, so a triggering floating rejection is plausible but not abundant.
fix: Add `process.on('unhandledRejection', …)` and `process.on('uncaughtException', …)` in worker.ts that log with full stack and trigger the graceful `shutdown()` (for uncaughtException) or at least record before exit, so failures are observable and restarts are clean.

title: Each per-tenant sweep builds its own TenantPrismaService LRU — overlapping crons multiply Postgres connections toward max_connections
description: Each job does `new TenantPrismaService()` per run (fine-accrual.job.ts:43, member-notifications.job.ts:134, book-metadata-refresh.job.ts:57, reservation-expiry.job.ts:46), creating an independent LRU `max: env.tenantClientCacheSize` (default 50, env.ts:163) that retains clients for the whole run. The tenant client factory is `new PrismaPg({ connectionString: opts.databaseUrl })` with NO pool `max` and NO `connection_limit` in the URL (db-tenant/src/client.ts:26) — so each cached client holds a node-postgres pool at its library default (10), NOT the `connection_limit=5` the TenantPrismaService comment claims (tenant-prisma.service.ts:27 — comment is false; nothing sets it). The runner uses `concurrency: 4` (scheduled-jobs.runner.ts:95) and fine-accrual + member-notifications are both hourly (registry.ts:41-43, 67-69) with book-metadata 6-hourly, so their ticks align and several per-tenant sweeps run at once, each holding up to min(N_tenants,50) clients with live pools. Teardown is only in `finally` at end of run (fine-accrual.job.ts:56-58), so pools coexist during overlap.
impact: On an aligned hour the worker can approach/exceed Postgres max_connections (default 100): even ~10 tenants × 2-3 overlapping sweeps × pool-of-10 blows past 100, causing `too many clients already` that fails unrelated tenant queries and the API competing for the same Postgres. The wrong `connection_limit=5` comment makes the real footprint 2× worse than the docs imply.
fix: Share one TenantPrismaService across all worker jobs (inject via JobContext like `emails` already is), and/or pin `connection_limit=1` (or a small explicit pool `max`) for the worker's tenant URLs, and/or serialize the heavy per-tenant sweeps on a dedicated low-concurrency lane. Fix the stale `connection_limit=5` comment.

title: support-session-expiry marks the row ended before the (error-swallowed) notification enqueue, so a lost enqueue is never retried
description: The sweep does `updateMany({ data: { endedAt: now, endedReason: 'expired' } })` first (support-session-expiry.job.ts:33-36), then `await notifs.sessionEnded(...)` (line 39). `sessionEnded` routes through `tryEnqueue`, which catches and only logs any failure: `catch (err) { this.logger.warn(...) }` (support-notifications.service.ts:151-159). The sweep's selection filters `endedAt: null` (line 24), so once stamped the row is never re-selected. If the enqueue itself fails (Redis/control-DB blip at enqueue time), the 'session ended' notice is lost with no compensating retry. The idempotency key `support.session.ended:<sessionId>` only dedups delivery once an outbox row exists (support-notifications.service.ts:132) — it does nothing when the row was never created.
impact: A library can be silently not-notified that a Libriant support engineer's debugging window into their tenant closed — an audit/trust gap for a security-sensitive event. Bounded blast radius (only on enqueue failure), hence medium.
fix: Enqueue the notification (or durably record 'notification owed') before/in the same transaction that stamps endedAt, or have the sweep also re-scan recently-ended sessions whose `support.session.ended` outbox row is missing and re-enqueue.

title: Tenant PrismaPg pool has no max set — comment claims connection_limit=5 but it is never applied
description: `makeTenantPrismaClient` does `new PrismaPg({ connectionString: opts.databaseUrl })` (client.ts:26) with no pool `max` and no `connection_limit` query param appended to the URL. The TenantPrismaService docblock asserts 'we keep `connection_limit=5` by default' (tenant-prisma.service.ts:27), but a grep for `connection_limit` across the whole repo finds it ONLY in that comment — it is set nowhere in code, env, or URL construction. node-postgres Pool therefore defaults to its built-in max (10) per cached tenant client. This is the multiplier behind PER-JOB-TENANTPRISMA-CONN-MULTIPLY and also inflates the API process's own footprint, since the API shares the same factory.
impact: Every tenant client holds up to ~10 Postgres connections instead of the documented 5, so both the API and worker reach Postgres max_connections at roughly half the tenant count operators would expect from the comment. Increases the likelihood of `too many clients already` under load.
fix: Set an explicit small pool size — either `new PrismaPg({ connectionString, max: 5 })` (or smaller for the worker) or append `?connection_limit=5` to the tenant DB URL — and make the value env-tunable so worker vs API can differ. Then the docblock matches reality.

title: Demo controller (PlanDemoController) is mounted in production — real unaudited book-create that bypasses the race-safe quota authority and dumps plan internals
description: plans.module.ts:12 `controllers: [PlanDemoController]`; app.module.ts:52 imports `PlansModule` into the root graph with no NODE_ENV gate, so all four routes are live in prod. The controller is guarded by only `@UseGuards(TenantGuard, PlanGuard)` (plan-demo.controller.ts:35) with NO role check — TenantGuard (tenant.guard.ts:46-53) admits ANY signed-in user whose session.tid matches the URL tenant (including a member, not just staff). `createBook` writes a real row via raw `client.book.create({...})` (plan-demo.controller.ts:94-101), gated ONLY by the count-based `QuotaInterceptor` pre-check (quota.interceptor.ts:86-95, whose own doc-comment at :36-39 admits 'two concurrent creates can each pass the check and land at limit+1'). It deliberately skips `QuotaService.enforceWithinTx`, the advisory-lock authority the real path uses (books.service.ts:200-205: `client.$transaction` → `enforceWithinTx` → `tx.book.create`). The real `BooksController.create` also runs `validateDto(CreateBookDto, raw)` + custom-field validation (books.controller.ts:64); the demo path coerces `body` ad hoc (plan-demo.controller.ts:90-92) and skips all of it. `GET plan` / `GET plan/usage` (plan-demo.controller.ts:43-72) return the full EffectivePlan blob (every limit, source layer, override note) to any authenticated tenant user.
impact: Live unintended duplicate write path in prod. With billing enabled it is a working max_books TOCTOU bypass under concurrency (N parallel POST /t/:slug/demo/books all pass the count pre-check and all insert, landing the tenant past its ceiling), reachable by any authenticated tenant user. Also creates Book rows with no DTO/custom-field validation and leaks plan/override internals. Note: when billing is disabled (default), unlimitedPlan() lifts the limit to MAX_SAFE_INTEGER so the quota bypass is inert until billing is turned on — which caps this at medium.
fix: Remove PlanDemoController and its `controllers` entry from PlansModule, or register it only when NODE_ENV !== 'production'. If kept, route demo/books through BooksService.create (so it gets enforceWithinTx + validation) and gate the raw plan-dump endpoints behind owner/admin.

title: Worker /readyz omits maintenance + export workers and never re-checks live Redis connectivity
description: worker.ts:76 `const ready = !shuttingDown && !!emailWorker && !!scheduledJobs && !!importWorker;` — does NOT include `maintenanceWorker` or `exportWorker`, both of which are declared (lines 48-49), started (lines 158-173), and tracked. The `!!emailWorker` etc. checks only assert the start promise resolved once at boot — no liveness re-check. The BullMQ worker connections are created with `maxRetriesPerRequest: null` (email-worker.ts:61, import-worker.ts:236, maintenance-worker.ts:30, export-worker.ts:23, scheduled-jobs.runner.ts:35), so a post-boot Redis drop queues commands forever rather than erroring while the handle stays non-null and /readyz stays green.
impact: Readiness is a boot-time latch, not a liveness signal. A post-boot Redis partition or a dead maintenance/export consumer leaves /readyz at 200; combined with REL-03 (healthcheck on /healthz anyway), nothing detects a silently-stalled worker.
fix: Include maintenanceWorker + exportWorker in the readiness expression, and have /readyz actually ping Redis (or inspect worker.isRunning()/connection.status) instead of relying on handle presence.

title: Redis connection URL (with password) logged in plaintext on every connect/reconnect
description: redis.service.ts:34 `this.client.on('connect', () => this.logger.log(`Connected to Redis at ${env.redisUrl}`))`. env.redisUrl is logged verbatim. ioredis fires `connect` on every (re)connect. The SMTP driver explicitly redacts (smtp-driver.ts:58-60 redactUrl, used at lines 35) — Redis was not given the same treatment. Docker json-file logs retain 50m x 5 files (docker-compose.prod.yml:79-81). NOTE: in the *prod compose* REDIS_URL is currently `redis://redis:6379` with no credentials (docker-compose.prod.yml:37), so this leaks nothing in the default single-host topology; it becomes a live credential leak only when REDIS_URL carries a password (rediss://default:PASSWORD@... for managed/remote Redis). Confirmed real code defect; impact is conditional on credentialed REDIS_URL.
impact: When REDIS_URL carries credentials, the Redis password is written to stdout on every connect/reconnect and persists in Docker logs / any aggregation pipeline. Anyone with log access (or a log-exfil bug) gets Redis auth — which holds rate-limit keys, webhook dedup locks, the announcement cache, and BullMQ job data. In the current credential-less default URL the immediate leak is nil, which is why this is medium not high.
fix: Redact credentials before logging — reuse the redactUrl pattern from smtp-driver.ts, or log only host:port from this.client.options.

title: Prod compose defaults EMAIL_DRIVER to console, defeating env.ts fail-fast and logging reset tokens + member PII
description: env.ts:241-248 defaults emailDriver to 'smtp' for any non-development NODE_ENV (so SmtpEmailDriver throws if SMTP_URL missing — fail fast). docker-compose.prod.yml:66 `EMAIL_DRIVER: ${EMAIL_DRIVER:-console}` always sets the var to at least 'console', so env.ts reads 'console' (line 243 `if (raw === 'console' || raw === 'smtp') return raw;`) and the smtp fail-fast default at line 247 is never reached. console-driver.ts:18 `const preview = input.bodyMarkdown.split('\n').slice(0, 6).join(' ⏎ ')` then logs it (lines 19-21). password-reset.service.ts body (lines 80-92) places the live reset link at line index 5 (`  ${resetLink}`), which IS inside slice(0,6) → the token URL gets logged. Member due-soon/overdue/hold-ready bodies contain member names + book titles, also logged.
impact: A live deploy that forgets EMAIL_DRIVER=smtp (a) sends zero real email with no fail-fast (compose silently injects console) and (b) writes password-reset token URLs (account-takeover material) and member PII into retained Docker logs. The fail-fast safety the env.ts author built is silently disabled by the compose default.
fix: Drop the `:-console` default in prod compose (leave EMAIL_DRIVER unset so env.ts's smtp+fail-fast default applies) or set it to smtp explicitly. At minimum make ConsoleEmailDriver refuse to run, or stop logging the body preview, when NODE_ENV=production.

title: Ack-required announcement emails are deduped tenant-wide — only the first user who opens the app ever gets emailed
description: For an ack-required announcement (`requiresAck: true`) with `deliverEmail: true`, ensureDelivery uses PER-USER delivery rows (scope='user', userId set — announcement-delivery.service.ts:103-107) and addresses the email to that specific user (`to: input.userEmail`, line 109). But the email idempotencyKey is tenant-scoped, NOT user-scoped: `announcement:${announcementId}:tenant:${tenantId}` (line 258). idempotencyKey is `@unique` in schema.prisma:672, and EmailService.enqueue (email.service.ts:97-125) dedupes on it: the first user's fetch creates the outbox row addressed to User A; every subsequent user's fetch enters the markEmail branch (their own per-user delivery row doesn't exist yet), calls enqueue with the SAME tenant-scoped key, hits P2002 (line 116), and gets User A's existing row back with no new email queued (alreadyExisted=true → no queue.add at line 127). So only the first user in the tenant who opens the app ever receives the ack-required announcement email; everyone else gets nothing.
impact: Ack-required announcements are the highest-priority class (critical notices that demand acknowledgement), and email delivery for them is silently broken for all-but-one user per tenant. In-app delivery still works (per-user rows are created), so it is not total loss, but the email channel — the one likely relied on for must-read notices — reaches a single recipient per library. Mis-stated stats too: deliveredEmailAt is set on every user's row even though only one email was sent.
fix: Make the idempotencyKey user-scoped when the delivery is per-user, e.g. `announcement:${announcementId}:tenant:${tenantId}:user:${userId}` (or `:tenant-wide` when userId is null). That preserves the existing tenant-wide dedup for non-ack announcements while giving each ack-required recipient their own dedup key + email.

title: Signup DoS critical re-opens under any Redis outage — limiter fails open with no DB backstop
description: RateLimitService.hit fails OPEN on any Redis error: catch returns `{ allowed: true, count: 0, retryAfterSec: 0 }` (rate-limit.service.ts:56-61), and `RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED==='true'` short-circuits to allowed at line 40. The signup throttle is purely this Redis limiter (auth.controller.ts:94-100, signupPerIp 5/10min + signupGlobal 60/10min). signup.service.ts has NO other limit: cell is picked via `controlDb.cell.findFirst({ where: { acceptsNew: true } })` (signup.service.ts:69) with no tenant-count/capacity check, and the Cell model in packages/db-control/prisma/schema.prisma:207 has only `acceptsNew Boolean` — no capacity/maxTenants column. Provisioning (tenant-provisioning.service.ts) has no count-based cap either. Each signup provisions a physical Postgres DB.
impact: When Redis is unreachable (a common dependency failure) or RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED is set, all signup throttling vanishes and the signup→Postgres-DB-provision DoS the audit flagged is fully re-exposed, allowing unbounded DB provisioning and cell exhaustion — exactly when an attacker may also be hammering Redis.
fix: For the signup path specifically, fail CLOSED or degrade to a DB-backed backstop (e.g. a cell-level tenant-count / signups-per-window cap inside the provisioning transaction, plus a real Cell.capacity column). Login/reset fail-open is defensible; expensive provisioning is not.

title: `gen` subcommand silently emits an empty secret on bad --length/--hex (and crashes on non-numeric --hex)
description: The non-interactive `gen` case does no validation (secrets.ts:1170-1171): `if (values.hex) console.log(genHex(Number(values.hex))); else console.log(genPassword(Number(values.length ?? '20'), false));`, unlike actionGenerate which guards `Number.isFinite(len) && len > 0 ? len : 20` (994-998). Verified at runtime: `genPassword(Number('abc'))`, `Number('0')`, `Number('-5')` all return '' (the for-loop never runs); `genHex(Number('abc'))` throws 'size out of range ... Received NaN'; `genHex(Number('1e9'))` throws 'Cannot create a string longer than 0x1fffffe8 characters'.
impact: `pnpm secrets gen --length l8` (letter ell) prints a blank line; an operator may paste an empty password into a credential field believing it was generated. `--hex <typo>` crashes the tool. A generator that can silently yield an empty secret is a real weakness for a credential tool.
fix: Validate parsed numbers in the `gen` case (reject NaN/<=0, clamp upper bound) as actionGenerate does, and error loudly instead of printing an empty string.

title: getValue (last-wins) vs setValue (first-match) disagree on duplicate keys; `set` reports success while the live value stays stale
description: getValue iterates backwards returning the LAST occurrence (secrets.ts:507 `for (let i = model.lines.length - 1; i >= 0; i--)`). setValue uses `model.lines.find(...)` overwriting the FIRST occurrence (535-536). Verified at runtime on a model with `FOO=first` then `FOO=second`: getValue returns 'second'; after `setValue(FOO, 'NEW')` lines become `['FOO=NEW','FOO=second']` and getValue still returns 'second'. The post-write '✓ KEY updated' message (907) is then false; audit/print/print-json (which all use getValue) show the stale value, and bash sourcing (also last-wins) reads the stale second line.
impact: On any env file with a duplicated key, `set`/`rotate` appear to succeed but the value the app actually loads is unchanged — e.g. an operator 'rotates' STRIPE_API_KEY or a session secret, sees the success line, but production keeps the old credential. Silent and easy to miss.
fix: Make setValue update (or remove-then-append) the LAST occurrence to match getValue and bash semantics, or detect duplicate definitions of a managed key and refuse/warn.

title: Parser ignores `export KEY=` lines and inline `# comments`, causing false MISSING reports and duplicate appends
description: loadModel's regex `/^\s*([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*)\s*=/` (secrets.ts:497) does not match `export FOO=bar` — verified key parses to undefined and getValue returns undefined for an export-prefixed key. Yet `bash -c 'set -a; . file; set +a'` sources both `export BAR=baz` and `KEY=val # comment` correctly, returning BAR=[baz] KEY=[val] (verified). parseValue (483-489) does not strip inline comments — verified `getValue` for `KEY=val # comment` returns 'val # comment' whereas bash returns 'val'. Because getValue returns undefined for export-prefixed keys, statusOf/printAudit flag a present required secret as MISSING, and setValue appends a DUPLICATE line.
impact: If an operator or tool writes export-prefixed or inline-commented lines, `secrets audit` can falsely flag a required secret (e.g. POSTGRES_PASSWORD) as MISSING — and the natural response to a 'MISSING POSTGRES_PASSWORD' is to regenerate it, which (see SEC-02) locks the app out of its DB. Fingerprint/length shown for a commented value is also wrong.
fix: Accept an optional `export\s+` prefix in the line regex, and strip unquoted trailing `# ...` comments in parseValue to match shell sourcing. Add a round-trip test against `set -a; . file`.

title: set KEY with a newline-containing value writes a corrupt multi-line env entry, silently truncating the stored value
description: serializeKV (522-531) only rejects values containing a single quote; a value containing a newline is NOT a bareword (newline isn't in the isBareword charset at 519) so it takes the single-quote path and produces `KEY='a\nb'` with a RAW embedded newline. saveModel then writes that across two physical lines. Verified round-trip: writing `K='a<newline>b'` and reloading yields lines `K='a` (key=K) and `b'` (no key), and getValue('K') returns `'a` — the leading quote is kept and the value is truncated. This is reachable via the CLI `set KEY $'a\nb'` (positionals[2] is passed verbatim to actionSet, secrets.ts:1155 → setValue with no newline check; explicit-value path skips even promptValue's serializeKV try/catch and only runs def.validate at 898-903). The orphan `b'` line also becomes a parseless garbage line in the file.
impact: An operator who pastes/types a credential containing a newline (e.g. a multi-line value copied with a trailing newline into a shell arg, or a pasted PEM-ish string) gets a silently corrupted env file: the intended secret is truncated to its first line with a stray leading quote, and a dangling `<rest>'` line is appended. The success message '✓ KEY updated' still prints. On reload the app reads the wrong/truncated secret, and the orphan line may break other tooling that parses the file.
fix: Reject values containing a newline (or any control char) in serializeKV, and apply that check on the explicit-value `set` path before setValue. Mirror ensure-env.sh which only writes shell-safe values.

title: Body scroll-lock leaks ('hidden') if the viewport crosses to desktop width while the drawer is open
description: The lock effect sets `const prevOverflow = document.body.style.overflow; document.body.style.overflow = 'hidden';` and only restores it in the cleanup that runs when `menuOpen` flips false or on unmount (SidebarNav.tsx:61-66). `menuOpen` is pure JS state, decoupled from viewport width, and a grep for `matchMedia|addEventListener('resize')|window.innerWidth` across apps/web and packages/ui/src returns NOTHING — only the `[pathname]` reset effect (lines 51-53) and the `[menuOpen]` lock effect exist. The hamburger and scrim are `display:none` outside the `@media (max-width:768px)` block (styles.css:578,604), and `.lbr-shell__sidebar.is-open { transform: translateX(0) }` exists ONLY inside that media query (styles.css:632). So if the drawer is opened below 768px and the viewport is then widened to >=768px (tablet rotate, exit split-view, desktop window straddling 768px, dev-tools), `menuOpen` stays true and `body.overflow` stays 'hidden', but the hamburger/scrim are gone and the sidebar reverts to a static grid column — no visible control to close it.
impact: Crossing the 768px breakpoint while the menu is open silently leaves the desktop page unscrollable with no visible affordance to recover except pressing Escape or navigating. Confusing dead-end; narrow trigger conditions.
fix: Add a `matchMedia('(max-width: 768px)')` listener that calls `setMenuOpen(false)` when it stops matching, or gate the scroll-lock on the same media query, so leaving the mobile breakpoint always restores `body.overflow`.

title: Closed mobile nav drawer stays in the tab order and the accessibility tree (off-screen but not hidden)
description: On mobile (`@media (max-width:768px)`) the closed drawer is hidden ONLY by `.lbr-shell__sidebar { position: fixed; ...; transform: translateX(-100%); }` (styles.css:619-626). It is never set to `display:none`, `visibility:hidden`, `hidden`, or `inert`, and the `<aside>` carries no aria-hidden/tabIndex when closed (the only aria-hidden in SidebarNav.tsx/AdminSidebar.tsx are on the decorative SVGs at lines 110/119 and the scrim at line 132). Because `translateX(-100%)` only moves the element off-screen, every nav `<Link>` inside the closed drawer remains in the DOM, keyboard-focusable, and exposed to screen readers. A keyboard user on a phone Tabbing through the visible page will land on the entire invisible, off-screen nav list (catalog/members/loans/settings/etc.), and a screen reader will announce them — with no visible indication of where focus is. This is the closed-state mirror of mob-1 and is also avoided by the HelpDrawer native-<dialog> pattern (a closed <dialog> is display:none by default).
impact: Keyboard and screen-reader users on narrow viewports encounter the full navigation menu twice (once via the hamburger, once as off-screen ghost links) and can focus invisible controls — a WCAG 2.4.3 / 1.3.1 / 2.4.7 (focus visibility) problem affecting every mobile screen in both the tenant and admin shells.
fix: When closed on mobile, remove the drawer from the tab order and a11y tree — e.g. `display:none` / `visibility:hidden` until `.is-open`, or apply `inert`/`aria-hidden="true"` + `tabindex="-1"` on the closed `<aside>` (toggled from menuOpen). Adopting the native-<dialog> approach used by HelpDrawer handles this automatically.

title: TenantResolver caches tenant status (active/suspended/archived) for 5 minutes with no proactive invalidation on status change
description: TenantMiddleware is the only layer that blocks suspended (403) / archived (410) tenants on data routes (tenant.middleware.ts:76-83), reading `ctx.status` which comes from the cached TenantContext (resolved/cached at tenant-resolver.service.ts:73,81 for ttlSec=300s; `status` is in tenantSelect at lines 117-127). resolver.invalidate is only called from auth.controller.ts:105 (signup) and admin-tenant-tags.controller.ts:72 (tag edits) in production. Grep confirms no `controlDb.tenant.update({ data: { status: ... } })` exists anywhere — suspend/archive is not yet implemented as an operation, so the cache-staleness is latent rather than currently exploitable. Severity lowered from medium to low accordingly.
impact: Latent: the day a suspend/archive (or billing past_due -> suspend) operation is wired, it will be silently ineffective for up to 5 minutes (every API process keeps serving member PII, circulation, catalog) unless the new code also issues resolver.invalidate. A manual DB suspend today already exhibits this. Not a currently-reachable breach because no shipped path sets the status.
fix: Make every future tenant-status mutation (suspend/archive/reactivate) call resolver.invalidate({slug, customSubdomain}), like relocate and tenant-tags already do. Better: don't cache `status` in the resolver context at all — resolve identity/routing from cache but read status from the authoritative row via the AuthGuard/TenantGuard DB revalidation (TEN-01), so suspension can't be cached.

title: storageSigningSecret silently defaults to the session JWT secret in production
description: SESSION_SECRET is `required('SESSION_SECRET')` in non-dev (env.ts:139) but STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET is `optional('STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET', sessionSecret)` (env.ts:212) — in prod an operator who omits it signs storage download tokens with the exact same HS256 key as session cookies. The comment at env.ts:209 claims the separate secret exists to rotate independently, which the fallback defeats. Cross-token forgery is currently blocked only by distinct required-claim shapes: session verify demands `sub`+`role` (jwt-session.service.ts:57-65) and signed-url verify demands `tid`+`ref` (signed-url.service.ts:63-69); a token minted for one purpose fails the other's type guard. There is no boot warning when the fallback fires.
impact: Not exploitable today (per-purpose claim guards hold), but it collapses two trust domains onto one key: a leak of either secret compromises both session auth and file-download authorization, and prevents independent rotation. A future loosening of either claim check turns this into a real forgery path.
fix: Require STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET in non-dev (same treatment as SESSION_SECRET/ADMIN_SESSION_SECRET), or at minimum log a loud boot warning when it falls back to the session secret in prod. Keep the per-purpose claim guards regardless.

title: Authenticated storage download / signed-URL minting (and delete) is gated by TenantGuard only — any tenant member incl. volunteer can read/mint/delete any file
description: GET /t/:slug/storage/:resourceType/:filename (line 88-89), GET .../signed-url (line 115-116), DELETE .../:filename (line 103-104) and POST .../storage-admin/recompute (line 143-144) all use `@UseGuards(TenantGuard)` with no RolesGuard/@Roles. RESOURCE_TYPES (line 26-34) includes `members` (member photos) and `attachments`. So any authenticated tenant user including `volunteer` (schema.prisma:45 'limited rights') can read any file, mint signed download URLs valid up to 86400s (ttlSec cap at line 127), and delete any file. Cross-tenant is NOT possible: TenantGuard pins req.tenant and the signed token binds `tid`, re-resolved via resolveTenantById(payload.tid) (lines 162,181-203) — no Host trust. NOTE: this matches the app's overall coarse model — members.controller.ts:43, loans, catalog all lack RolesGuard too, so a volunteer can already mutate those — so the storage gap is consistent with (not worse than) the documented role design. Kept at low.
impact: Intra-tenant only. The least-privileged role can read, hand out day-long bearer download links for, and delete member-photo/attachment files a librarian/admin might consider restricted. Consistent with the app's existing volunteer-can-write posture, so it's a hardening gap rather than a privilege-escalation breach.
fix: Decide the intended read/delete authority for storage; if member photos/attachments are sensitive, add a `@Roles('librarian','admin','owner')` floor on download/signed-url/delete and cap ttlSec lower for member-PII resource types. Also confirm the *-demo controllers (storage-demo, tenant-demo, plan-demo) are intended to ship to production at all.

title: deactivate() and setRole() never bust the AuthGuard `authcheck:<userId>` cache — even where AuthGuard IS mounted, revocation lags up to 60s
description: AuthGuard caches a positive revalidation under `authcheck:<session.sub>` for 60s (auth.guard.ts:39,62). staff.service.ts deactivate() (line 120-125) and setRole() (line 109-112) mutate the user row but never `redis.del('authcheck:'+userId)`. On the two endpoints AuthGuard actually protects (/auth/me, /auth/complete-setup), and on any route AuthGuard is later applied to (the TEN-01 fix), a just-deactivated user keeps passing for up to the remaining 60s of the cache window. The remediation's own recommendation (auth.guard.ts is documented to bound DB load with the cache) implicitly requires an eviction-on-mutation that was never wired.
impact: Bounded 60s revocation lag rather than instant. Minor on its own today (AuthGuard guards almost nothing), but it becomes the residual revocation window the moment TEN-01 is fixed by applying AuthGuard broadly — so it should be fixed together with TEN-01.
fix: In deactivate(), setRole(), resetCredentials() and any user-status/role mutation, call `await redis.del('authcheck:'+userId)` (best-effort). Centralize in a small helper so every staff mutation evicts the cache.

title: Admin JWT verify skips per-claim type checks that the tenant verify performs
description: AdminSessionService.verify only checks `if (!payload || typeof payload !== 'object') return null;` then returns the cast payload (admin-session.service.ts:43-44). The tenant JwtSessionService.verify additionally validates `typeof sub/tid/role === 'string'` and `typeof iat/exp === 'number'` (jwt-session.service.ts:57-65) before returning. Both correctly pin `algorithms: ['HS256']` (admin-session.service.ts:40; jwt-session.service.ts:54), so alg-confusion is not the issue — this is purely missing structural-validation parity on the higher-privilege path.
impact: Low in practice (we sign these tokens ourselves, so claims are present), but a future signing-path change or a malformed-but-validly-signed admin token would flow unchecked into control-plane authorization. Inconsistent hardening between two equally-sensitive verify paths.
fix: Mirror the tenant verify: validate `typeof sub === 'string' && (role === 'owner' || role === 'support') && typeof iat === 'number' && typeof exp === 'number'` before returning, else null.

title: No minimum length/entropy enforcement on SESSION_SECRET / ADMIN_SESSION_SECRET at boot
description: required() only rejects empty/whitespace: `if (!v || v.trim().length === 0) throw ...` (env.ts:121-123). In non-dev, sessionSecret/adminSessionSecret/impersonationSecret use required() (env.ts:139,170,188) with no length/entropy check; storageSigningSecret falls back to sessionSecret (line 212). mfaMasterKey is the only secret with a format check (64-hex enforced in MfaService constructor, mfa.service.ts:31). So `SESSION_SECRET=x` boots and signs HS256 JWTs in production. scripts/secrets.ts (per the finding) generates strong secrets but using it is optional.
impact: A weak/guessable HMAC secret makes tenant and admin session JWTs forgeable offline → full account/tenant or control-plane impersonation. HS256 security depends entirely on secret strength; the boot-time validator could catch this but does not.
fix: In loadEnv, for non-dev environments enforce a minimum length (>= 32 chars / 256 bits) on SESSION_SECRET, ADMIN_SESSION_SECRET, IMPERSONATION_SECRET, and STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET, and fail boot otherwise.

title: 60s positive auth cache delays deactivation/suspension enforcement and is not invalidated on revocation
description: AuthGuard caches a positive validation result in Redis for REVALIDATE_TTL_SEC=60 under `authcheck:${session.sub}` (auth.guard.ts:28,62) and short-circuits with `if (await this.redis.client.get(cacheKey)) return true;` (line 41). Nothing invalidates this cache when a user is deactivated, a tenant is suspended/archived, or a role/password changes. The guard's own doc claims it 'invalidates a disabled admin's existing session immediately' for the ADMIN guard, but the TENANT AuthGuard here defers any status-based revocation by up to 60 seconds.
impact: A user deactivated or whose tenant is suspended (e.g. for abuse, non-payment, or a security incident) can continue making authenticated tenant requests for up to 60 seconds after the change lands. Combined with AUTH-01 (no session-version revocation at all), the practical revocation latency for status changes is up to 60s and for password changes is the full token TTL. Low severity for the 60s window alone, but it undermines the stated 'immediate' invalidation guarantee.
fix: Delete the `authcheck:${session.sub}` key when a user is deactivated, tenant status changes, or credentials change (e.g. from the deactivate/suspend/reset code paths), or drop the positive cache for these sensitive transitions. Document the bounded staleness explicitly.

title: Session-log visibility uses the stale JWT role instead of the live DB role
description: `sessionLog` gates cross-admin access with `if (admin.role !== 'owner' && session.adminId !== admin.sub)` where `admin` is the `@AdminSess()` param = `req.adminSession`, i.e. the raw verified JWT payload (admin-auth.guard.ts:42-48). The JWT `role` is the role at sign-in time, explicitly documented as not authoritative: 'Role at signing time. The DB row is the source of truth at request time.' (admin-session.service.ts:12-13). Unlike AdminRolesGuard (admin-roles.guard.ts:42-49), this handler does NOT re-read the live role. A demoted owner→support keeps owner-level visibility into every admin's session logs until token expiry (ADMIN_SESSION_TTL_SEC).
impact: A just-demoted admin can read other admins' support-session action logs for up to the admin-session TTL. Low blast radius (read-only audit data), but inconsistent with the deliberate live-role re-read used by AdminRolesGuard everywhere else.
fix: Re-read the current role from `controlDb.adminUser` before granting cross-session log access, or split into an owner-only `@AdminRoles('owner')` all-sessions route plus a 'my sessions' route, so the live DB role governs visibility.

title: Retry sweep bypasses the Redis dedup lock, allowing concurrent double-processing with a live Stripe delivery (or another sweep)
description: The controller serializes via `redis.client.set(EVENT_KEY(id),'1','EX',TTL,'NX')` (controller:90-99). The sweep loop (stripe-retry.job.ts:66-69) calls `dispatch(billing, event)` directly with NO lock acquisition. Sweep runs every 5 min (registry.ts:34-36) and picks rows where `error IS NOT NULL OR receivedAt < now-5min` (job:42-44). An errored row with error set is eligible immediately (the OR), so it can be dispatched concurrently with a fresh Stripe retry delivery that hits the controller and independently holds the SETNX lock. recordPaymentFailure re-arms `graceUntil = now+N` on each run (billing.service.ts:408-412), so two interleaved runs can produce inconsistent grace/status writes.
impact: Concurrent double-application of a billing event. For idempotent syncStripeSubscription/handleStripeSubscriptionDeleted it is benign (last-writer-wins, same target). The only observable harm is grace-window jitter / a transient inconsistent status write — no money loss, no data corruption, no cross-tenant effect. Probability is low (handlers are fast DB-only ops; BullMQ won't overlap same-name repeat ticks unless one exceeds 5 min). Severity downgraded from medium to low accordingly.
fix: Have the sweep claim each row atomically before dispatch — e.g. an `updateMany` that stamps `processingStartedAt` only if currently null (row-level claim), or acquire the same SETNX lock the controller uses and release it after — so the controller and sweep cannot process the same event simultaneously.

title: Unvalidated BILLING_GRACE_PERIOD_DAYS produces an Invalid Date that crashes payment-failure / past_due webhooks
description: env.ts:240 `billingGracePeriodDays: Number(optional('BILLING_GRACE_PERIOD_DAYS','7'))` with no Number.isFinite/NaN guard (the only validation in env.ts is `required()` at line 122). `optional` returns the fallback only for empty/unset (env.ts:127-129), so a non-empty non-numeric value like '7d' flows through as NaN. recordPaymentFailure (billing.service.ts:408) then computes `new Date(Date.now() + NaN * MS_PER_DAY)` and the past_due branch of syncStripeSubscription (488-491) does the same. I verified at runtime: `Number('7d')` = NaN; `new Date(Date.now()+NaN*86400000)` is Invalid Date; `.toISOString()` throws `RangeError: Invalid time value`. Prisma serializes DateTime via toISOString, so the `subscription.update` throws. The epochSecsToDate guard (billing.service.ts:27-29) only covers Stripe-epoch fields, not this env-derived date.
impact: Misconfiguration-gated latent bug: if BILLING_GRACE_PERIOD_DAYS is set to a non-numeric value, EVERY invoice.payment_failed and every past_due subscription webhook throws, is recorded as an error row, and retries indefinitely (until the 30-day prune). Tenants whose cards decline are never moved to past_due/grace and keep paid features for free. Severity low because it requires an operator typo in an optional env var; the default ('7') is safe.
fix: Validate at boot: `const n = Number(...); env.billingGracePeriodDays = Number.isFinite(n) && n >= 0 ? n : <throw or fall back to 7>`. As defense-in-depth, also clamp/guard the Date construction in recordPaymentFailure and the past_due branch of syncStripeSubscription.

title: Non-numeric ttlSec query param throws an uncaught 500 in the signed-URL endpoint (jwt.sign rejects expiresIn: NaN)
description: Line 127: `const ttlSec = ttlSecRaw ? Math.max(60, Math.min(86400, Number(ttlSecRaw))) : undefined;` — for `?ttlSec=abc`, Number('abc')=NaN and `Math.max(60, Math.min(86400, NaN))=NaN` (confirmed `Math.min(5, NaN-0) => NaN`). NaN is neither null nor undefined, so in SignedUrlService.sign `const ttl = input.ttlSec ?? this.defaultTtlSec` (signed-url.service.ts:43) keeps NaN and calls `jwt.sign(..., { expiresIn: NaN })` (lines 44-48, no callback → synchronous). Verified jsonwebtoken@9.0.3 sign.js:20 validates expiresIn via `isInteger(value) || (isString(value) && value)`, and I confirmed `lodash.isinteger(NaN) === false`, so validateOptions (sign.js:59-60) throws synchronously `Error('"expiresIn" should be a number of seconds...')`. The throw is uncaught in the `signedUrl` handler → 500 for a client-sendable query param.
impact: User-triggerable 500 / noisy error log from a malformed ttlSec query param. No security/data impact (auth still enforced, no leakage), but a crashy path that should degrade gracefully.
fix: `const n = Number(ttlSecRaw); const ttlSec = ttlSecRaw && Number.isFinite(n) ? Math.max(60, Math.min(86400, n)) : undefined;` (or throw BadRequestException for non-numeric input).

title: storageUsedBytes decrement has no floor at zero — counter can go negative and inflate effective quota
description: delete() does `storageUsedBytes: { decrement: size }` (line 151) with no lower bound. Schema column is `storageUsedBytes BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0` (init migration migration.sql:80) with NO CHECK >= 0 (the only CHECK constraints in that migration are on slugs/keys/feature-override types, lines 635-698, none on storage). The put() increment is explicitly best-effort — only `.catch(warn)` on failure (lines 97-101) — so a lost increment can leave the counter stale-low, and repeated decrements (or races with recompute) then drive it negative. A negative currentBytes makes `currentBytes + newSize > limitBytes` (line 70) under-evaluate, raising the effective quota until the nightly recomputeUsage overwrites it (lines 162-169).
impact: Quota under-counting / silent over-allowance; compounds STG-03. Low blast radius and self-heals on recompute.
fix: Floor the decrement (GREATEST(0, storageUsedBytes - $size) via raw SQL, or decrement min(size, current) in a tx) and add a DB CHECK (storageUsedBytes >= 0). Make the put() increment non-best-effort or reconcile more aggressively.

title: recomputeUsage counts orphaned .tmp-* partial-upload files, inflating storageUsedBytes
description: put() writes to `${target}.tmp-${randomBytes(6).toString('hex')}` then atomically renames (local-driver.ts:64-66). If the process crashes or the write is interrupted between createWriteStream and rename, the `.tmp-*` file is orphaned on disk and never cleaned up. walkSize() (the basis of recomputeUsage) sums ALL files in the tree with no name filter (lines 158-166), so it counts these orphans. recomputeUsage then overwrites the authoritative counter with the inflated total (storage.service.ts:162-169), permanently raising the tenant's apparent usage (and shrinking their effective quota) until the orphans are manually removed. There is no startup/periodic sweep of `.tmp-*` files.
impact: Orphaned temp files from interrupted uploads inflate storageUsedBytes after the nightly recompute, eroding the tenant's usable quota with no self-heal. Low blast radius but a real accounting drift that worsens over time.
fix: Exclude `*.tmp-*` from walkSize (or write temp files outside the tenant tree / in a dedicated tmp dir), and add a periodic sweep that removes stale `.tmp-*` files older than N minutes.

title: Queue comment claims failed commits are resumable via re-run, but the code forbids it
description: import-queue.service.ts:33-35 sets attempts:1 with the comment 'the engine commits each row independently and is resumable via re-running with skip/update'. But after a commit failure the batch is 'failed' (import-worker.ts:218-224 fail() sets status 'failed') and requireRunnable only re-runs `['uploaded','validated']` (import.service.ts:322). So a 'failed' (or stuck 'committing') batch cannot be re-run through the API — the documented resume path does not exist; the operator must cancel+delete and re-upload (cancel has no status guard and remove allows deleting a non-running batch, so this fallback does work).
impact: Operators relying on the stated 'just re-run with skip/update' recovery cannot do so after a partial commit; partially-imported rows remain and the only supported path is cancel→delete→re-upload. Misleading invariant, no direct data/security harm.
fix: Either implement the promised resume (allow re-running a 'failed' batch — skip/update dedup makes already-written rows idempotent) or correct the comment to state that a failed commit requires cancel+delete+re-upload.

title: Money transform produces unbounded cents with no range check; int4 columns reject silently as opaque db_error
description: toMoneyCents returns `Math.round(value * 100)` with no bounds (transforms.ts:85-86); toInt likewise unbounded (transforms.ts:24-29). amountCents and priceCents are Prisma Int = Postgres int4 (schema.prisma:431 `amountCents Int`, :291 `priceCents Int?`; numPages :228, renewedCount :365 also Int). Values over 2,147,483,647 are rejected by Postgres at write; dbIssue (import-engine.ts:92) maps the failure to a generic `db_error` with a truncated raw message, not a precise per-field error. Critically the overflow is never caught in dry-run: commitFine returns before the create when dryRun (import-engine.ts:610), so validate passes clean and commit then fails — undermining the dry-run guarantee.
impact: Legitimately large fine/price values fail at commit with a cryptic 'db_error' after a clean validate, eroding trust in the dry-run. No data loss/corruption (Postgres rejects rather than truncates), limited to oversize numeric inputs.
fix: Range-check toMoneyCents and toInt against int4 bounds (and numPages/renewedCount) returning a precise TransformErr, so the dry-run catches it and the row issue is actionable.

title: Imported reservation queuePosition collides with live holds — duplicate positions corrupt hold ordering
description: nextQueuePosition seeds queueTop from `reservation.aggregate(_max queuePosition where status='queued')` ONCE per book (import-engine.ts:581-587) and then increments an in-memory counter. There is no DB-level uniqueness on (bookId, queuePosition); schema.prisma:418 only has `@@index([bookId, status, queuePosition])` (non-unique). If a queued hold is concurrently placed via the manual path while a 'queued' reservation import is running for the same book, both can compute the same next position, producing duplicate queue positions and a non-deterministic hold order.
impact: Imported holds can share a queue position with manually-placed holds during a concurrent import, corrupting the pickup queue order the reservations service relies on. Narrow window (concurrent import + manual hold on the same title), no money/cross-tenant impact.
fix: Compute queuePosition inside a transaction that re-reads the max under a row lock, or accept eventual reordering and renumber the queue after import; optionally add a unique constraint on (bookId, queuePosition) for queued holds.

title: Member email duplicate-detection is case-sensitive in the DB query, allowing duplicate members on commit
description: findMemberByEmail caches on `email.toLowerCase()` (import-engine.ts:690-691) but the actual DB lookup uses the raw email verbatim: `where: { email, archivedAt: null }` (import-engine.ts:693). If the existing member row stored the email with different casing than the imported cell (e.g. stored 'Jane@x.com', import cell 'jane@x.com'), the lookup misses an existing member and a duplicate member is created on commit — and quotaUsed is incremented (import-engine.ts:417), double-counting against max_members. The lowercased cache key only dedups within the same import run, not against the existing DB row.
impact: Case-mismatched emails between the source file and existing rows defeat duplicate detection, creating duplicate member records and inflating the quota counter. Limited to imports where stored email casing differs from the file.
fix: Match members case-insensitively (store/compare a normalized lower-cased email, or use a citext column / `mode: 'insensitive'` filter) so the DB lookup agrees with the lowercased cache key.

title: OpenLibrary fetch follows redirects with no protocol/host pinning (residual SSRF) and no response-size cap
description: fetchOpenLibraryBook() pins host to openlibrary.org with digits-only ISBN (lines 39-44) and sets a 5s AbortController (line 46) — good. But `fetch(url, { signal, headers })` (line 48) uses the default `redirect: 'follow'` (up to 20 hops) with no re-validation of the Location target, and `res.json()` (line 53) has no body-size cap. If openlibrary.org is MITM'd / DNS-rebound / compromised and returns a 3xx to http://169.254.169.254 or an internal address, the worker follows it; an oversized JSON body could also balloon memory. Reached at request time (IsbnLookupService) and in the book-metadata-refresh job. Genuinely low likelihood because it requires the trusted host to be subverted.
impact: Low-likelihood SSRF / cloud-metadata reach if the pinned host is compromised or returns attacker-controlled redirects; potential memory blow-up from an oversized response body.
fix: Pass `redirect: 'manual'` (or 'error') and treat 3xx as not-found, or re-validate each Location is https + openlibrary.org; cap the response body size before JSON.parse; optionally enforce a worker egress allowlist.

title: Formula-neutralization corrupts legitimate numeric data returned as strings by the pg driver (BigInt / numeric columns)
description: cellValue() (line 271) and toCsv()'s esc() (line 285) skip neutralizeFormula only for `typeof v === 'number' || 'boolean'`; everything else (incl. strings) is passed to neutralizeFormula, whose regex `/^[=+\-@\t\r]/` (line 264) matches a leading '-'. node-postgres returns int8/BigInt, numeric and decimal as JS strings (precision preservation), so a negative value like '-123' would be rewritten to "'-123". The control schema has Tenant.storageUsedBytes BigInt (schema.prisma:242). The comment 'number/boolean — safe, no neutralization needed' (line 285) is wrong for bigint/numeric which arrive as strings. Practically narrow today: storageUsedBytes is a byte count with @default(0) that is effectively never negative, so live corruption is unlikely now, but any future numeric/decimal column with a value starting -/+ is a latent silent-corruption bug.
impact: Exported bigint/numeric/decimal values that begin with - or + are silently apostrophe-prefixed (turned into text) in CSV/XLSX, producing incorrect data downstream. Narrow today, latent as the schema grows.
fix: Use res.fields[].dataTypeID to detect numeric/int8 columns and skip neutralization for them, or only neutralize strings that are not a valid number (`/^-?\d+(\.\d+)?$/.test(s)` left untouched), or register a pg type parser to coerce int8/numeric to number/BigInt.

title: import errors.csv (csvCell) omits formula-injection neutralization applied everywhere else
description: errorsCsv() emits cells [rowNumber, field, code, message] through csvCell() (import.service.ts:209), which only RFC-4180-quotes (`if (/[",\r\n]/.test(value))`, lines 383-386) and does NOT neutralize leading =+-@\t\r like export-processors.ts toCsv() does. Notably the `message` column DOES embed raw uploaded cell values — transforms.ts fails echo `raw`: `fail(\`not a yes/no value: "${raw}"\`)` (line 48), `fail(\`not a real date: "${raw}"\`)` (113/139), `fail(\`unrecognized date/time: "${raw}"\`)` (160), `fail(\`not a valid ISBN-13: "${raw}"\`)` (178), which flow into `message: \`${def.label}: ${result.reason}.\`` (row-mapper.ts:191). However, because the message is always prefixed by `${def.label}: `, no errors.csv cell ever BEGINS with a formula character today, so it is not currently exploitable — a defense-in-depth / consistency gap, confirming the finding's own low/theoretical assessment.
impact: No current exploit (cells are label-prefixed so never start with a formula char), but the only path producing CSV from semi-user data without neutralization; one wording change that lets a raw cell lead a message would introduce real Excel/Sheets formula injection.
fix: Share the neutralizeFormula helper from export-processors.ts and apply it inside csvCell() (neutralize before quoting) so every CSV-producing path is uniformly safe.

title: No per-tenant cap on queued export jobs — amplifies the concurrency-1 export DoS
description: createForTenant() unconditionally inserts a queued ExportJob and enqueues it (export.service.ts:39-51); there is no check for already-pending/running jobs for the tenant and no throttle on POST /t/:slug/exports (the controller has no rate limiter, tenant-export.controller.ts:43). Because the export worker is concurrency:1 (export-worker.ts:38) with no statement_timeout (see EXP-002), an owner/admin can fire many large 'sql'/'all'-adjacent or full-table exports back-to-back and saturate the single export slot, delaying every other tenant's exports indefinitely.
impact: An authenticated owner/admin can flood the global single-slot export queue, denying the export feature to all other tenants. Authenticated-only, hence low, but it compounds EXP-002.
fix: Reject a new tenant export when the tenant already has a queued/running job (or cap the count), and add a coarse per-tenant rate limit on POST /t/:slug/exports. Consider a per-tenant fairness policy or a dedicated worker pool.

title: No Content-Security-Policy anywhere despite dangerouslySetInnerHTML usage
description: next.config.mjs has no headers() function at all (only rewrites/redirects). The Caddy (security_headers) snippet (Caddyfile:40-51) sets HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options: DENY, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy — but no Content-Security-Policy. (The only CSP strings in the repo are inside apps/web/.next build artifacts — Next's internal image-optimizer CSP — not an app response header.) Two dangerouslySetInnerHTML sinks exist: token CSS at layout.tsx:48 and help article bodyHtml at page.tsx:64. Both inputs are currently platform-trusted: the token CSS is built by tokensToCssVars (packages/ui/src/tokens.ts:22) from /assets/theme/tokens.json (a platform file), and help bodyHtml comes from controlDb.helpArticle (help.service.ts:114-124), a control-plane/platform table, not tenant input. The tenant-supplied brandColor is validated by an anchored regex `^#[0-9a-fA-F]{6}$` (branding.controller.ts:22,44) AND is applied via a React CSSProperties object (`{ ['--color-primary']: brandColor }`, t/[slug]/layout.tsx:163), not via dangerouslySetInnerHTML — so it is not a sink. Confirmed: no live XSS injection today; this is purely the missing defense-in-depth layer.
impact: Clickjacking is already covered by X-Frame-Options: DENY. The gap is the missing XSS/script/connect containment layer: if any future change introduces an HTML sink (e.g. tenant-authored help/announcement HTML, or a regression that lets unsanitized content reach either dangerouslySetInnerHTML), there is no CSP to contain script execution or exfiltration. No current exploit.
fix: Add a Content-Security-Policy at the Caddy edge in (security_headers) so both hosts inherit it (minimum: default-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'). The injected token <style> needs a per-request nonce or style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' (prefer nonce). Roll out Report-Only first, then enforce.

title: tenant-relocate leaves the source DB fenced read-only on the success path with no automatic recovery if --drop-source is never run
description: Before the dump the script fences the source: line 126 `await fenceSourceReadOnly(tenant.dbUrl, dbName);` which runs `ALTER DATABASE "tenant_X" SET default_transaction_read_only = on` and terminates backends (lines 342-347). The success path (lines 154-182: transaction → bustResolverCache → closeEvent → done) never calls `unfenceSource`. unfenceSource (line 354) is reachable only on the failure path (line 189). So a relocated-away source DB remains `default_transaction_read_only = on` permanently.
impact: Limited blast radius: the abandoned source DB stays read-only. Intentional when the operator then runs --drop-source (the terminal step), but if they instead keep/reuse the old DB or relocate back without manual `ALTER DATABASE ... RESET default_transaction_read_only`, that tenant silently rejects writes at the Postgres level (opaque 500s, since the system-mode window was closed). Operationally confusing; not data loss.
fix: Record the fence in the audit afterJson so an operator can find/lift it, and/or lift the fence on the success path immediately after cutover (the tenant no longer uses that DB, so unfencing is harmless). Document --drop-source as the intended terminal step.

title: restore.sh storage untar is additive (no clean) — restored storage tree can contain stale/deleted files
description: Lines 70-71: `mkdir -p "$STORAGE_DIR"; tar -C "$STORAGE_DIR" -xzf "$dir/storage.tar.gz"` with no prior clearing of $STORAGE_DIR. The backup tars the tree with relative paths (backup.sh:60 `tar -C "$STORAGE_DIR" -czf "$dest/storage.tar.gz" .`). Untarring over an existing dir overwrites matching files but does not remove files present on disk yet absent from the archive.
impact: Restoring an older backup onto a non-empty/newer storage tree leaves orphaned/stale files (images for records the restored Postgres no longer references, or previously-deleted files reappearing). Non-faithful point-in-time restore; not data loss. Low severity (only diverges on a non-empty target). Compounds with DR-002/DR-003: restore.sh's STORAGE_DIR also defaults to the in-container path /srv/libriant/storage, so a default-path restore untars to a wrong/nonexistent host dir.
fix: Restore into a clean directory: move the existing $STORAGE_DIR aside (or rm -rf after confirmation) before untarring, or untar into a temp dir and atomically swap. At minimum document that storage restore is additive and the target should be emptied first.

title: backup.sh has no integrity test of the gzip/dump and restore.sh never validates the dump decompresses before DROPping live data
description: backup.sh validates only that postgres.sql.gz is >1024 bytes (lines 51-54); it never verifies the gzip stream is intact or that pg_dumpall actually succeeded (the `docker compose ... exec ... pg_dumpall | gzip` pipeline's exit status is the gzip's, not pg_dumpall's — under `set -o pipefail` a mid-stream pg_dumpall failure after some output could still yield a >1024-byte, truncated, non-restorable dump if gzip exits 0). restore.sh checks only that postgres.sql.gz exists and is a file (line 50); it then immediately pipes `gunzip -c ... | psql ... ON_ERROR_STOP=1` (lines 62-64), which begins issuing DROP DATABASE against live data before any proof the archive is decompressible/complete. A corrupt/truncated backup is only discovered mid-DROP, after destruction has begun.
impact: A silently-truncated nightly dump passes the >1KB check and is treated as a valid backup; the failure surfaces only during a real restore, partway through DROPping live databases — the worst possible moment. Low because pipefail catches the common pg_dumpall failure, but gzip-truncation/disk-full mid-write is not fully covered and there is no `gzip -t` pre-restore gate.
fix: In backup.sh, run `gzip -t "$dest/postgres.sql.gz"` after writing and abort on failure; consider asserting a known footer/last-line. In restore.sh, `gunzip -t "$dir/postgres.sql.gz"` (and optionally a dry decompress to /dev/null) BEFORE issuing any DROP, so a corrupt archive aborts the restore before it touches live data.

title: Lint gate is non-load-bearing — `pnpm lint` lacks `--max-warnings 0`, so configured rules can never fail CI/deploy
description: Root `"lint": "eslint ."` (package.json:13) with NO --max-warnings; this is exactly what verify runs (deploy.yml:70 `pnpm lint`, ci.yml:48). eslint.config.mjs sets the only correctness-adjacent rules as warnings: `'no-console': ['warn', ...]` (56), `'@typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any': 'warn'` (57), `'@typescript-eslint/no-unused-vars': ['warn', ...]` (58-61); only `no-var` is 'error' (48). I created a probe file under apps/api/src with `any`, `console.log`, and an unused var: `eslint` reported 3 warnings and exited 0; the same file with `--max-warnings 0` exited 1. So those rules can never fail the gate. Additionally every per-package lint is a no-op echo ('lint: ok') — confirmed across apps/api, apps/web, packages/db-control, db-tenant, i18n, shared, ui — so `turbo run lint` does nothing; only the root eslint . matters.
impact: The lint quality gate added in the remediation is advisory: any volume of `any`, unused vars, or stray console.log passes verify/CI unflagged. Tree is clean today but unprotected going forward.
fix: Run `eslint . --max-warnings 0` (or promote the rules to 'error'). Delete the no-op per-package lint scripts or wire `turbo run lint` to the real linter so the two paths don't diverge.

title: DEPLOY_KNOWN_HOSTS emptiness guard is dead code — an unset secret writes a 1-byte file that passes the `-s` check
description: Line 181 `printf '%s\n' "${{ secrets.DEPLOY_KNOWN_HOSTS }}" >> ~/.ssh/known_hosts` then line 183 `if [ ! -s ~/.ssh/known_hosts ]; then ... exit 1; fi`. I reproduced: `printf '%s\n' ""` writes a 1-byte file (just a newline); `[ ! -s file ]` is FALSE because the file is non-empty, so the intended explicit error NEVER fires. Security property still holds: `ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes` (lines 201, 243) rejects the unknown host because known_hosts has no real key — fail-closed, NO MITM exposure.
impact: Forgetting to set the pinned-hosts secret surfaces as a generic 'Host key verification failed' during an incident deploy instead of the clear diagnostic the guard was meant to give. No security impact.
fix: Guard the secret content before writing: `KH='${{ secrets.DEPLOY_KNOWN_HOSTS }}'; if [ -z "${KH// /}" ]; then echo 'DEPLOY_KNOWN_HOSTS is empty'; exit 1; fi`, or grep the file for an `ssh-` key line rather than relying on `-s`.

title: No .dockerignore; API/web build contexts COPY whole workspace dirs, risking stale node_modules/.next/.turbo + any stray apps/*/.env
description: Confirmed no .dockerignore exists anywhere in the repo (find returned nothing). Build context is the whole repo (`context: .` deploy.yml:109/121; `context: ../..` prod.yml:153). Dockerfiles do scoped per-workspace COPYs: api `COPY apps/api apps/api` (Dockerfile:51), web `COPY apps/web apps/web` (Dockerfile:30) + `COPY assets assets`/`COPY locales locales` (39). I verified the working tree currently contains apps/web/.next, apps/web/node_modules, apps/api/node_modules, apps/api/dist (all gitignored, so absent on a clean CI checkout but present locally). The compose `build:` blocks (prod.yml:152-154/182/212) let an operator build images locally where these artifacts WOULD be baked into the build layer. Root .env.local is NOT copied (no top-level COPY of it) — the finding correctly acknowledges this; no stray apps/*/.env exists today.
impact: On a developer/operator-built image (compose build:), local .next/node_modules/dist get embedded — bloated, cache-unstable images and a stale build risk; a future stray apps/*/.env could be shipped. No impact on the clean CI build path.
fix: Add a .dockerignore covering **/node_modules, **/.next, **/.turbo, **/dist, **/coverage, **/.env*, .git, .dev-storage — shrinks the context and removes the latent chance of an env file or stale build entering an image.

title: Empty PORT/WORKER_PORT env var binds the API/worker to a random ephemeral port (Number('')===0), defeating the deploy health check
description: Distinct from the NaN case in CFG-03: `optional('PORT','3001')` returns the fallback only when PORT is unset OR empty (`v && v.length`), so an EMPTY PORT is harmless. BUT if PORT is set to a value that `optional` returns verbatim yet coerces to 0 — e.g. `PORT='0'` or `PORT=' 0 '`-style — `Number()` yields 0 and `app.listen(0)` binds a RANDOM ephemeral port. The compose api healthcheck hits a fixed `http://localhost:3001/readyz` (prod.yml:173) and the deploy health poll hits `http://localhost/healthz` via Caddy upstream :3001 — neither would reach a process listening on a random port, so the container is marked unhealthy and the deploy times out at 150s (deploy.yml:257) with a confusing failure. Same pattern for the worker (worker.ts:41 `Number(process.env.WORKER_PORT ?? '3002')`, listen at :114). The 'valid or fail loudly' contract should range-check ports to a fixed expected value or reject 0.
impact: A `PORT=0`-style misconfiguration (or any value coercing to 0) silently binds a random port; the fixed-port healthchecks never connect and the deploy fails opaquely after the full 150s timeout. Low likelihood (operators rarely set PORT in this stack), low blast radius.
fix: Range-check port via the same `num()` helper proposed in CFG-03 (assert 1 <= port <= 65535), or hard-pin the listen port from the image ENV and ignore env overrides in production.

title: Expiry-job promotion does not rebalance queuePositions, leaving non-contiguous gaps (divergent from service paths)
description: Confirmed. When the expiry job promotes `next` from queued->ready it sets `queuePosition: null` (line 159) but does NOT run the `queuePosition = queuePosition - 1` rebalance that the service paths run (returnLoan loans.service.ts:427-433 and promoteNextHoldInTx reservations.service.ts:515-521 both issue `UPDATE reservations SET queuePosition = queuePosition - 1 ... WHERE status='queued' AND queuePosition > 0`). After the job promotes position-1, remaining holds keep positions 2,3,4... I verified this does NOT violate the CHECK constraint `reservations_queue_position_when_queued` (20260526184041_init/migration.sql:529-534), which only requires queued rows to have queuePosition >= 1 — gaps are allowed. Ordering still drains correctly (orderBy queuePosition asc; back-of-queue inserts use max+1 in placeHold reservations.service.ts:238-242). So it is cosmetic/divergent-from-contract, not functional.
impact: No incorrect circulation outcome today, but position numbers shown to staff become misleading after a cron-driven expiry, and the data diverges from the service-layer contract, raising the risk of a future regression in any code that assumes contiguous 1-based positions.
fix: After the promotion update in the expiry job, run the same `queuePosition - 1 WHERE bookId=... AND status='queued' AND queuePosition > 0` rebalance the service paths use, so all promotion paths keep positions contiguous.

title: Overdue 'days' are 24h wall-clock blocks from the exact dueAt instant, not calendar days in the library timezone
description: Confirmed. Return computes `const overdueMs = Math.max(0, returnedAt.getTime() - loan.dueAt.getTime()); const daysOverdue = Math.floor(overdueMs / MS_PER_DAY)` (loans.service.ts:376-377) and the accrual sweep computes `Math.floor((now.getTime() - loan.dueAt.getTime()) / MS_PER_DAY)` (fine-accrual.job.ts:89) — both raw-millisecond differences with MS_PER_DAY=86_400_000. dueAt inherits the checkout time-of-day: checkout sets `dueAt = new Date(loanedAt.getTime() + settings.loanPeriodDays * MS_PER_DAY)` (loans.service.ts:149-151), not midnight-aligned. So overdue is measured in rolling 24h windows anchored to checkout time, not calendar days in the tenant locale. The two paths are mutually consistent (no divergent/duplicate charge), so this is a fairness/expectation gap rather than a defect or leak — as the finding itself characterizes it.
impact: Fine amounts can be off by one day relative to calendar-day billing expectations, and identical lateness can be charged differently depending on checkout time-of-day. Per-loan money impact is small and internally consistent.
fix: If calendar-day fines are intended, normalise dueAt and the comparison instant to start-of-day in the tenant timezone before computing daysOverdue, applied identically in both the return path and the accrual job. Otherwise document that fines accrue per 24h from checkout time.

title: Misleading P2002 messages: member 'or email' uniqueness and book 'these details already exist' don't match actual constraints
description: members.service.translateCreateError returns 'A member with this number (or email) already exists' on any P2002 (lines 464-467), but the init migration has only `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX members_member_number_unique_active ON members(memberNumber) WHERE archivedAt IS NULL` (migration.sql:475-477) and `CREATE INDEX members_email_idx ON members(email)` (line 329) — email is `@db.Citext` but only `@@index([email])` (schema.prisma:347), NOT unique, so email cannot raise P2002 and the '(or email)' clause is wrong. books.service.translateDbError maps P2002 to 'A book with these details already exists' (lines 545-547), but the Book model has no `@@unique` and only `@@index([isbn13])`/`@@index([isbn10])` (schema.prisma:251-252) with no partial unique index in migrations — this branch is dead/unreachable today.
impact: Confusing error messages for librarians (a member dup is always the number, never email); latent dead-code in books error translation that won't identify the field if a unique index is added later. No data-integrity impact.
fix: Drop '(or email)' from the member message (or add a real unique constraint if email should be unique). For books, remove the P2002 branch or make it constraint-name-specific like the existing CHECK-constraint handling (books.service.ts:548-559).

title: Custom url field type accepts javascript:/data:/file: schemes (latent stored-XSS if ever rendered as a link)
description: The 'url' validator (field-types.ts:225-233) only does `new URL(raw)` in a try/catch and returns the raw string. I verified in Node that `new URL()` ACCEPTS `javascript:alert(1)`, `data:text/html,<script>...`, `vbscript:msgbox(1)`, and `file:///etc/passwd`. The only current render path, BookDetail.tsx:243-251, renders the value via `String(value)` inside a `<dd>` (escaped text, no href), so React neutralizes it and it is NOT active XSS today. It is a latent trap: the moment any view renders a url custom-field value as `<a href={value}>` it becomes stored XSS, and the value already passes server validation.
impact: No active exploit in the audited render path. Real risk if/when a url field is rendered as a clickable link (the obvious intended UX for a 'url' type).
fix: Restrict the url validator to an allowlist of safe protocols (http/https, optionally mailto/tel) and reject the rest, so the stored value is safe regardless of how the frontend renders it.

title: /readyz ignores the maintenance and export workers — a failed-to-start consumer reports ready while its queue never drains
description: Readiness is `const ready = !shuttingDown && !!emailWorker && !!scheduledJobs && !!importWorker` (worker.ts:76) — `maintenanceWorker` and `exportWorker` are omitted. Each is started with `.then(handle => global = handle).catch(err => console.error(...))` (worker.ts:158-173), so a boot rejection leaves the global null with no retry, yet /readyz still returns 200. The comment at worker.ts:73-75 says readiness covers 'both BullMQ workers' — stale; there are five queues. /healthz reports the queues individually (worker.ts:60-66) but nothing keys readiness off maintenance/export.
impact: An orchestrator can treat the worker as ready while export and maintenance jobs pile up unconsumed. Downgraded to low: `startMaintenanceWorker`/`startExportWorker` are very unlikely to actually reject — ioredis connects lazily (no throw on `new Redis`) and BullMQ `new Worker(...)` is synchronous and non-throwing (maintenance-worker.ts:29-46, export-worker.ts:22-39), so in practice the globals get set even when Redis is down; the gap is the stale check/comment, not a likely live failure.
